entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical - WFLX
entry.summary: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical    WFLX
entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon. Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside. Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting. The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911. Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris’ waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris’ front pocket, police said. The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm. Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital. No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

entry.title: X-ray technician accused of sexually assaulting patient during MRI at HCA St. Lucie Hospital
entry.summary: A traveling X-ray technician has been accused of sexually assaulting a patient during an MRI procedure at HCA St. Lucie Medical Hospital, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Gabriel Cruz, 42, of Grant-Valkaria, was working as a contract technician at the hospital when the alleged assault occurred on Sept. 13. The victim, a female patient who was receiving treatment for fainting episodes, reported the incident to hospital administration the following day. According to the police report, the patient had been brought to the emergency room by her nephew on Sept. 11 for evaluation after experiencing fainting spells and head injuries. She underwent a CT scan and was scheduled for an MRI two days later to further assess her condition. The victim told investigators that Cruz made inappropriate comments before the procedure, allegedly telling her 'nobody can see what I can do to you.' During the MRI, the patient was given medication that made her drowsy. She reported waking up to find Cruz sexually assaulting her. Hospital security footage from Sept. 13 shows Cruz entering the MRI room with the patient and later exiting while carrying an unknown object and wearing purple latex gloves. The video confirms Cruz was the only person in the MRI room with the victim during the time period in question. According to the police report, Cruz had been working at the hospital on contract since August 2026. The case has been forwarded to the Criminal Investigation Division for further investigation. WPTV received this statement from HCA St. Lucie Medical Hospital on Sept. 17: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individuals assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Peloton is releasing its cheapest treadmill yet as it bets on running for a turnaround
entry.summary: Peloton is launching its cheapest treadmill yet, in the hope that runnings surging popularity will spur sales. The fitness equipment maker announced Tuesday it will soon release a $2,195 treadmill called the Tread Flex. Thats about $1,000 cheaper than its current lineup, and also the companys first-ever foldable device that contracts to roughly half its size. Peloton hopes the space-saving design will entice new customers, like those with apartments or smaller homes, to buy the companys pricey equipment. Focusing on walking and running is a major initiative for CEO Peter Stern, who has the massive task of transforming the beleaguered company. Once a pandemic-era success story, sales have slumped in recent years and its stock has fallen 42% since it last unveiled new products, in October 2025. That equipment ultimately failed to lure back shoppers and the company conducted another round of layoffs at the beginning of the year. entry.title: 'I'm not going back to prison': New details emerge in Palm City SWAT standoff - cbs12.com
entry.summary: 'I'm not going back to prison': New details emerge in Palm City SWAT standoff    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Before an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City , a man allegedly threatened to kill himself and his ex-girlfriend after she went to his home to check on him following their breakup, a new report reveals. According to an arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the ex-girlfriend of the suspect, Darrel Abbey, arrived at his home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts, according to the report. The woman told investigators Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated. The arrest report says Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman, "I should die, you should kill me," while holding a gun. Investigators said Abbey continued yelling at the woman while recording the interaction on his phone. The woman told investigators that Abbey pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey allegedly placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed, according to the report. Investigators said Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey allegedly continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. The report says that when Abbey picked up the gun again, he said, "This is really f***** dangerous now." Investigators said Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. As Abbey walked outside, the woman told investigators she heard several loud "pop" sounds. Abbey then returned inside to retrieve a rifle and allegedly tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. See also: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey allegedly told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it. At some point during the incident, Abbey allegedly began cleaning the firearms and said, "I gotta wipe all my fingerprints off, I gotta get the gunshot residue off of my hands, I'm not going back to prison." The report says Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink, prompting the woman to begin recording him. Investigators who reviewed the video said Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he allegedly reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her. Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Investigators also said Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

entry.title: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation - WPBF
entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Family seeks answers after pre-purchased burial plot in Delray Beach cemetery was sold to someone else
entry.summary: A Delray Beach family is demanding accountability from the city after discovering that a burial plot they had purchased years ago at the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery was sold and used to bury someone else. The discovery has caused significant heartbreak for Delila Kellum and her family, who were unable to fulfill her father's final wish to be buried next to his brother. 'It's just heartbreak; it's upsetting,' Kellum told WPTV. 'We can't bury him where he wanted, so we havent really decided what to do.' WPTV's Zitlali Solache has been covering multiple concerns involving the cemetery's overcapacity , maintenance , and record-keeping , pressing the city for answers. WATCH: Family seeks answers after pre-purchased burial plot was sold to someone else Delray Beach family demands answers after burial plot mix-up A painful discovery The issue began in 2010 when Kellum and her sister took their father to visit his late brother's grave. Their parents had purchased two adjacent plots. 'When we took him to there, we got out and looked at the stone and when we look over... we noticed somebody was buried in my mothers spot,' Kellum said. The family immediately contacted the city but were told the body could not be moved. According to Kellum, a supervisor offered them two different plots and promised to provide new deeds. 'To this day we've never seen them,' Kellum said. 'My sister tried to contact them when my father passed, but nothing.' When her father died in 2024, the family was faced with a devastating reality. 'We couldn't put him in his spot next to his brother, we had to get him cremated,' she explained, adding they skipped a proper funeral. Kellum said her mother suffers from dementia and is unaware of the distressing situation. 'Now were just gonna wait for my mother to pass and have it together,' she said. A history of problems This is not the first time the Kellum family has encountered issues with the cemetery's record-keeping. Kellum said they have also struggled to locate the grave of her grandfather, a Pearl Harbor veteran. Although the city initially denied he was buried there, Kellum stated that funeral home officials provided documents proving his interment at the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery. 'We went to go try to find him and we couldn't find him,' she said. The family has documents, including a deed from 1994, which they believe prove their ownership of the original plots. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half. 'The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'' Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks. entry.title: Port St. Lucie's $2.2 billion mobility plan aims to tackle traffic and keep up with growth
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie City Council is looking ahead to a sweeping infrastructure plan to address traffic congestion and accommodate rapid population growth but the city acknowledges a significant funding gap remains. The 2050 Mobility Plan carries a $2.2 billion price tag and serves as a road map for building infrastructure projects through 2050. WATCH BELOW: $2.2B mobility plan aims to keep up with Port St. Lucie growth Port St. Lucie's $2.2 billion mobility plan aims to tackle traffic and keep up with growth Those projects include new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. The city said more than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020. Residents like Laura Milsom said the growth is impossible to ignore on local roads. 'We're not in love with the traffic situation,' Milsom said. Milsom said that the rapid expansion has come with consequences. 'The population increased so rapidly,' Milsom said. 'A lot of traffic backups.' On Monday, City Council members approved the first reading of the Mobility Plan, updating the mobility fee schedule for the next four years and outlining the broader 25-year vision. entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a massive data center in Indiantown is back before the public with significant changes, but the developers’ new plan has not eased the concerns of many residents who fear the project will harm their community.Representatives for “Project Silver Fox,” a 606-acre data processing center proposed by developers Panatonni and Ferreira, held an open house Monday to present the plan. WATCH: Indiantown 'Project Silver Fox' data center plan returns with changes, resident concerns remainThe debate over the project highlights a familiar tension in growing communities: the promise of economic development versus the desire to maintain a community’s character, with a final decision by the Village Council expected to shape Indiantown's future for years to come.The project was initially withdrawn in April. Now, developers say they have directly addressed the public’s biggest worries.Adam Kramer, an executive with Project Silver Fox, said the new plan includes several key commitments intended to mitigate the facility's impact.“It’s a waterless data center,” Kramer stated, emphasizing that the project would not use Indiantown’s water resources. He also noted changes to the facility’s design and footprint. “We have commitments on how we are doing natural landscaping with retaining the trees there to kind of block the view of the data center, working on the size of the facility.”The project is slated for land already zoned for industrial use, the former site of a power plant. According to project officials, noise levels will remain within village code, there will be no ongoing vibrations, and local water pressure will not be affected.Proponents of the data center point to its potential to transform the local economy without costing taxpayers. Kramer said the project could represent a billion-dollar investment in the village.“What the project is, is an economic opportunity for the community and creating jobs, creating tax revenue,” Kramer said.That view is shared by Kloee Ciuperger, the CEO of the Economic Council of Indiantown.“I think a huge part of the benefits is gonna be that tax revenue,” Ciuperger said. “That’s gonna be able to go to youth, athletics, to parks, to the water infrastructure, to the wastewater infrastructure.”However, some residents at the open house remained skeptical of the developers' motives.“This is a money grab, a land grab and we do not want this,” said Penny Kaminsky-Preli. Despite the proposed changes, many who attended the meeting voiced continuing concerns about the impact of a large-scale data center on their daily lives.Penny Kaminsky-Preli, an Indiantown resident, said the facility is too close to homes and a local school.“First of all, they’re way too close to people. There’s a school within 2.2 miles from this place,” Kaminsky-Preli said. “You’re gonna subject teachers to that 5 days a week? The sound, The heat?”Concerns about constant noise, heat generated by the facility, and the overall impact on farmland and families were the primary reasons for the continued opposition.The future of the Project Silver Fox site plan now rests with the Indiantown Village Council, which is expected to make a decision in the coming months, according to Kramer.If approved, construction could begin in phases as early as 2027.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. entry.title: Police: Three Fort Pierce shootings that hit homes are connected and targeted - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Police: Three Fort Pierce shootings that hit homes are connected and targeted    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

entry.title: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation - WPBF
entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.title: Fort Pierce home hit by gunfire, bullet enters child's bedroom - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce home hit by gunfire, bullet enters child's bedroom    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cw34.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County High student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff Jon Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Sheriff Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" In 1987, Reaves was convicted of murder and sentenced to death, yet for nearly four decades, Reaves sat on death row while Marc stood beside his brother's grave, waiting and wondering."Wondering what's happened. Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." When DeSantis signed Reaves' death warrant, Marc said the weight of the wait finally lifted."It's finally over. It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. "All of that is very heavy on our agency, and knowing that this execution is coming in October gives a little weight lifted off. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. "Because I want to make sure the last thing he sees is an Indian River County Deputy uniform," said Flowers. Reaves' execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025, which set a modern-day record. The rapid pace has prompted concern from groups like Floridians Against the Death Penalty, who, along with capital defense attorneys, have raised concerns about how quickly executions are being carried out."One I think is around the transparency of this process. We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. Her own family member was murdered, and said she understands everyone processes that grief differently. "And far be it for me to tell any family how they should feel. I can only speak to my own experience and my family's experience of having a loved one who was murdered, and I can say that I came out of that feeling that another death and another family's pain was not going to give us closure or peace," said Hanna. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." For Marc, standing at his brother's grave — a place that will always hold pain — he's reminded of all he's lost. "The time I never got to spend with him," Marc said, holding back tears. "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. "For what he [Reaves] did to Richard, yes. What he did and the way he did it, yes, it gives me some closure, but still the pain will still always be there." entry.title: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation - wpbf.com
entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.article_text: A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told her, Nobody can see what I can do to you, before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. CBS12 News previously reported the arrest of Gabriel Cruz, 42, a traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. He faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. "In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. The criminal complaint says on Sept. 14, shortly after 8 a.m., officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital after a patient reported that a technician had sexually assaulted her, the report states. Officers met with the hospital’s director of patient safety, who said the patient reported being sexually assaulted by a male Hispanic imaging technician during the time of her MRI. The patient told investigators that Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County student thought bomb threat couldn’t be traced, investigators say    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old student is facing a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat targeting Martin County High School Tuesday morning. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the student later admitted he made the threat because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was arrested and charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. According to investigators, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL , a school safety reporting system, around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday, while a resource deputy was present. During a news conference, Sheriff John Budensiek read the message that prompted the investigation. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," the sheriff read. The sheriff said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating. Authorities say surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. According to an affidavit, another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students. However, deputies said he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. According to Budensiek, Taylor later explained why he made the threat. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class." Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 The arrest comes amid a string of bomb threats tied to Martin County High School. The sheriff said this is the fourth threat connected to the campus in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating, the sheriff added. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation. In a statement, Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact false threats can have on a school community. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek also warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences. "This individual has now been arrested, charged with a felony, getting expelled from school, likely. Getting a job down in the future is going to be very difficult for them because of the type of threat it is. These things that students think are funny can have long-term repercussions." The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. entry.title: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie weighs mobility plan for future growth    WPEC
entry.article_text: Years of rapid growth have brought thousands of new homes, businesses and drivers to Port St. Now, city leaders are confronting the cost of keeping everyone moving: approximately $2.2 billion. Council members on Monday approved Ordinance 26-89 on first reading, moving forward the city’s 2050 Mobility Plan , an updated mobility-fee schedule and guidelines for administering the program. The plan serves as a 25-year roadmap for new and wider roads, intersection improvements, sidewalks, trails, bicycle facilities and transit. It does not, however, guarantee every project will be built. Approximately $1.7 billion of the plan is currently unfunded. We know there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, a presenter told council during Monday’s meeting. The plan comes as Port St. Lucie has grown to more than 260,000 residents spread across approximately 120 square miles. City officials said the updated plan is intended to identify the transportation infrastructure that continued residential and commercial growth will require through 2050. Major road projects proposed by 2030 The plan divides proposed work into short-, mid- and long-term periods. The short-term plan, covering projects targeted through 2030, carries an estimated cost of approximately $403 million. Among the proposed short-term projects: Widen St. Lucie West Boulevard from four lanes to six between Interstate 95 and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen Torino Parkway from two lanes to four between Midway Road and Cashmere Boulevard. Widen California Boulevard from two lanes to four between St. Lucie West Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Lucie Boulevard from two lanes to four between Paar Drive and the Martin County line. Continue improvements along Floresta Drive between Prima Vista Boulevard and Crosstown Parkway. Widen Village Green Drive between Walton Road and Tiffany Avenue. Build or extend several roads intended to improve connections through growing areas of the city. Those projects remain part of a planning document. Their inclusion does not mean funding has been secured or construction will be completed by 2030. City officials also highlighted work already completed, underway or moving through design under the existing mobility program. That includes: A roundabout and widening near East Torino Parkway and Midway Road. Lucie Boulevard between Darwin and Gatlin boulevards. New sidewalks along Savage Boulevard and Selvitz Road. A sidewalk under construction on Kestor Drive. Traffic-calming improvements on Whitmore Drive. A feasibility study for improvements along St. An intersection project at Savona and Gatlin boulevards, with construction anticipated in 2027. Intersection improvements at Tradition and Village parkways. New development would pay more To help fund future projects, the ordinance updates the city’s mobility fees one-time charges tied to new development, redevelopment, additions and certain changes in property use. The fees are paid by developers, contractors or owner-builders, not existing homeowners. Developers could, however, factor the added expense into the prices of new homes, rents or commercial projects. The increase is not a blanket 50% hike for every development. Rates vary depending on the type of project and the area of the city where it is built. Under the proposal, the difference between the current fee and the newly calculated rate would be divided into four steps. The city would impose 25% of that difference in 2027, 50% in 2028, 75% in 2029 and the full calculated rate in 2030. For example, the current fee for a new single-family home east of I-95 is approximately $1.60 per square foot, up to 3,500 square feet. Under the updated schedule, it would rise to $1.80 per square foot in 2027 and $2.40 per square foot in 2030. For a new 2,000-square-foot home, that would mean an increase from approximately $3,200 today to $3,600 in 2027 and $4,800 by 2030. One council member raised concerns Monday about balancing the city’s infrastructure needs with the potential effect that higher development costs could have on housing affordability. Broader than road construction Port St. Lucie has used mobility fees since 2021. According to the city’s plan, the program collected more than $30 million between 2022 and 2024. Unlike traditional road impact fees, the money can support a broader range of transportation projects, including sidewalks, shared-use paths, trails, bicycle lanes, transit stops, mobility hubs and intersection improvements. The new plan extends the city’s previous transportation-planning horizon from 2045 to 2050. City officials said its short-, mid- and long-term road projects, multimodal improvements, intersection projects and transit plans remain largely unchanged from a version previously presented to council. The city held public workshops on the plan and proposed fee schedule Sept. 2 and 3 to gather input from residents, developers and other stakeholders. Because Monday’s vote was the ordinance’s first reading, it must return to City Council for final approval. If adopted, the ordinance and updated fee schedule would take effect Dec.
