entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.article_text: An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his K9 partner joined a search effort to locate a missing 84-year-old woman with dementia while attending a K9 certification course in Gadsden County near Tallahassee. Body camera footage from Deputy Sam Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area to assist in the search. Bloodhound search teams from across the state, including Indian River County, participated in the effort. "They had a rotated dog search, so Penny searched and some of the other dogs searched as well," Lt. Margaret Myles Ellis was reported missing on Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before. Officials said Ellis had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Ellis was found approximately 30 hours later in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety. They're coming out," the body camera footage captured. "They're nine counties away, and that's why we're proud of him and all of our deputies because no matter where they are, in the state or in the nation, they are always willing to help," Jaworski said. He expressed pride in the entire K9 unit, which includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. "Luckily, they were at the right place at the right time. We're extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and our entire K9 unit that, you know, goes out every day," Jaworski said. entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half. WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threat The arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. "The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks. Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus. When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement. "Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip." However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said. While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school. "The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case." Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious." This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - cw34.com
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.article_text: A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told her, Nobody can see what I can do to you, before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. CBS12 News previously reported the arrest of Gabriel Cruz, 42, a traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. He faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. "In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. The criminal complaint says on Sept. 14, shortly after 8 a.m., officers responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital after a patient reported that a technician had sexually assaulted her, the report states. Officers met with the hospital’s director of patient safety, who said the patient reported being sexually assaulted by a male Hispanic imaging technician during the time of her MRI. The patient told investigators that Spanish is her primary language and that she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. See also: Boynton woman accused of stealing $4,300 in skip-scan theft scheme that cost BJ's $18,000 According to the report, the patient was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. She said medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states that he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel. Another person later transported the patient back to her room. Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August, according to the report. "Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the report states the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time. We spoke with a local rape crisis counselor about the impact of something like this. "It is a very confusing time for people. It can bring upon people feeling ashamed, they can feel fearful, confused, guilty, angry. They can have difficulty relating with people close to them after the fact," said Julie Stoyka, Director, Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee. Their rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital. But, you know, truly you're not safe anywhere," Chief Niemczyk said. Lucie Hospital released a statement that says: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

entry.title: Fort Pierce home hit by gunfire, bullet enters child's bedroom - cw34.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce home hit by gunfire, bullet enters child's bedroom    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

entry.article_text: With just weeks to go before voters decide the fate of Amendment 3, one of the most talked-about questions across Palm Beach County remains the same: What does it mean for my wallet?WPTV has been following the debate for months as county leaders, residents and taxpayers weigh the potential benefits and drawbacks of the controversial property tax proposal that will appear on the November ballot.WATCH BELOW: Amendment 3 calculator to launch in Palm Beach CountyNow, Palm Beach County homeowners have a new tool aimed at answering that question with personalized numbers."We're excited to launch the Amendment 3 calculator, which will let residents, homesteaded residents, actually look up their own property and find out what their taxes could be after Amendment 3 passes, should it pass," Palm Beach County Property Appraiser Dorothy Jacks said.The new online Amendment 3 calculator allows homesteaded property owners to enter their address and see an estimate of how the proposed constitutional amendment could affect their property taxes, along with the potential revenue impact on local taxing authorities.Amendment 3 has become a regular topic at county meetings as officials discuss their budgets and what could happen if voters approve the measure.The amendment requires at least 60% voter approval on Nov. According to the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's Office, the exemption could increase to as much as $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School taxes would not receive the same increase.Supporters argue it would provide much-needed tax relief for homeowners dealing with rising costs."I plan to vote to eliminate property taxes," said Gillian Lieberman, a Palm Beach County property owner and real estate professional. "People work hard, and I think everyone that I work with, my colleagues, my friends, my clients, they work hard, and I'd like them to see that money back in their pocket as much as possible."Lieberman said she believes property owners could use the savings."We have such a great city, great infrastructure, great development, and I don't think eliminating property taxes is going to hurt that. I think it's going to allow owners to do more and purchase more so they have less stress when the tax bill comes," she said.Others are concerned about the potential loss of funding for community services.Logan Mroczkowski, a Palm Beach County homeowner, pointed to local parks and public amenities that benefit from property tax revenue."I work in Lake Worth, and I spent a lot of time at Bryant Park. I spent a lot of time there on my lunch breaks for work, and I know that the property taxes pay for a significant amount of the upkeep, the maintenance, stuff like that," Mroczkowski said. "I'm a big fan of when taxes are utilized to better the community."While acknowledging the referendum could save him money personally, Mroczkowski said he currently plans to vote against it."I am personally of the opinion that I'm probably going to vote no on the referendum. I know it could save me money, but unselfishly, I think it's more important that those taxes are used to better the community," Mroczkowski said.Jacks said the potential impact stretches far beyond individual homeowners.According to Jacks, that equates to roughly "$324 million in tax revenue that would go away."She noted that's only the county's share."And that's just the county. There's certainly many other taxing authorities that would also see similar reductions," Jacks said.The new calculator is designed to help residents understand both sides of that equation."We also wanted people to understand the two sides to Amendment 3, the one side that yes, I, as a homesteader, would save more, but also there's an impact to the many taxing authorities that each of us pay and to sort of share with them what that impact would be when you start bundling together 300,000 homesteads in Palm Beach County, not just my own," Jacks said.Residents with a homestead exemption can simply enter their address to generate an estimate."You would just put your address into this field here and then of course it just goes down and gives you the data," Jacks explained.The calculator will show current estimated taxes, projected changes for 2027 and 2028 if Amendment 3 passes, and estimated revenue impacts to local taxing districts.Jacks said the system will also indicate if a property does not have a homestead exemption and therefore is not eligible for the proposed tax benefit.The projections are based on 2026 certified property values and millage rates.She cautioned that future tax bills could still vary."That depends on the millage rates, which can change. They could go up, and it also depends on their value, which also could go up," Jacks said.Because the calculator uses parcel-level data, Jacks believes it can offer a clearer picture than broad statewide estimates."I think because we're able to do it at the parcel level, so individually, it's probably one of the more accurate," Jacks said.The tool also accounts for local differences."Absolutely, that's the point," Jacks said when asked whether results will vary depending on where someone lives. It's what you're paying."Jacks emphasized that the Property Appraiser's Office is not advocating for or against the amendment."It's really here to educate and nothing more," Jacks said.Instead, she hopes the calculator gives residents a way to move beyond campaign rhetoric and evaluate the proposal based on their own situation."So often these amendments appear on the ballot, and there isn't really a tool or a resource you can go to to say OK, well, how is that going to affect me and we thought this would be a good way to do that," Jacks said.Ultimately, she said, the goal is simple."We're hoping that the public will say, wow, you know, OK, let me look at my numbers and let me make a decision based on my numbers as opposed to all this chatter going on," Jacks said.For Palm Beach County voters still deciding how they'll cast their ballot in November, that personalized look may arrive just in time.The Amendment 3 Homestead Calculator is live now on the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser's website.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law? - WPEC
entry.summary: Causeway Cove project fight escalates: Can Fort Pierce push back against state law?    WPEC
entry.article_text: A proposed luxury waterfront development in Fort Pierce is drawing renewed attention after city commissioners approved a motion to explore hiring outside legal counsel to review whether the city has any options to challenge the project under Florida's Live Local Act. 14 vote comes as cities across Florida continue testing the limits of the state's Live Local Act and lawmakers implement the latest round of changes to the law. The proposed Causeway Cove development on South Hutchinson Island has become one of the Treasure Coast's most closely watched growth disputes, putting residents and local officials at odds with a state law that limits how much control cities have over certain housing projects. 14 meeting, the commission approved a motion to explore hiring an outside land-use attorney to determine whether Fort Pierce has any legal grounds to challenge the project under the Live Local Act. The city is also monitoring lawsuits filed elsewhere in Florida that seek to restore greater local control over development decisions. The move comes as Florida enters the latest phase of the law. Known as Live Local 4.0, the most recent changes took effect July 1, 2026, expanding eligible development sites and further clarifying protections for qualifying projects that include affordable housing. Qualifying developments must continue to reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years. Now, Fort Pierce finds itself at the center of a broader statewide debate over growth, affordable housing and home rule. The proposed redevelopment would dramatically transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive. According to city records, plans call for five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips. For residents like Edie Harrison, the project would change the area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems." Harrison and hundreds of other residents have raised concerns about the size of the development, traffic impacts and what they view as a lack of public input. At the center of the fight is Florida's Live Local Act, a law passed in 2023 to encourage the construction of affordable and workforce housing across the state. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the law and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. For critics, that process has become one of the most controversial aspects of the proposal. Fort Pierce Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. Critics argue the formula can produce rents that technically qualify as affordable under state guidelines but remain difficult for many local residents to afford. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city. Even some lawmakers who supported the legislation have raised concerns about how it is being applied. Dana Trabulsy, whose district includes parts of the Treasure Coast, has recently questioned whether developments of this scale reflect what legislators intended when they approved the measure. The Fort Pierce dispute is also part of a much larger battle unfolding across Florida. Several lawsuits challenging aspects of the Live Local Act are moving through the courts as cities seek to regain greater authority over local development decisions. Supporters of the law argue it is helping address Florida's housing shortage, while critics contend it has weakened local home-rule powers and limited communities' ability to shape growth. Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida , making the law one of the most significant growth and housing measures enacted in recent years. Related 2024 article: $100M Kanner Hwy development in Stuart: Affordable housing powered by Live Local Act If things move forward as anticipated, construction on the Causeway Cove development could begin before the end of the year. The property's owner, Palm Beach developer Ashton DePeyster, did not respond to requests for comment. This report is part of an ongoing CBS12 News I-Team investigation examining the impact of Florida's Live Local Act, the legal challenges surrounding the law, and how communities across the Treasure Coast are responding to large-scale development projects.

entry.title: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation - WPBF
entry.summary: 'I was surprised': Card skimmer discovered at Fort Pierce gas station prompts investigation    WPBF
entry.article_text: A Treasure Coast man discovered a card skimmer device at a 7-Eleven gas pump on Orange Avenue Monday morning, prompting an investigation by local police. Arlo Bess, who has a background in cybersecurity, said he normally checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps. "So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training," Bess said. After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added. A card skimmer is a device that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. Bess noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers, but he filed a police report to alert authorities. Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident, saying there hasn't been an incident like this in a while. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed." Santiago and Bess also warned that card skimmers can be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said. To identify card skimmers, Santiago recommended checking for tamper-evident seals, such as red or orange tape, on gas pumps. "If that seal is broken, don't use the system and alert the tenant," he said. Bess added that visual inspection can sometimes help. "Visually, you cannot tell. The other card readers, if you look at them on the gas pump, the original ones and even the original one on that one, they'll be slightly dirty, slightly dinged up a little bit," he said. Santiago advised paying for gas inside the store or using tap-to-pay at the pump to avoid potential skimmers. If investigators find the person responsible, that individual will face charges of fraud, attempting to and extract information from individuals' credit card information. "Depending on what we find, if we can connect how much money was actually stolen from this particular skimmer, there's always some charges that we can address when it comes to that point," Santiago said. entry.title: Police: Three Fort Pierce shootings that hit homes are connected and targeted - WPEC
entry.summary: Police: Three Fort Pierce shootings that hit homes are connected and targeted    WPEC
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18 according to police. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside. Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," said Major Mike Santiago. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold." A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," the teen's mother said. See also: Coast Guard offloads 7,250 pounds of cocaine, 2,082 pounds of marijuana in Port Everglades Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. CBS12 counted at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

entry.title: Man shot outside Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical now faces charges, police say - WPBF
entry.summary: Man shot outside Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical now faces charges, police say    WPBF
entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man who was shot during a confrontation outside a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie is now facing charges after investigators determined he was the primary aggressor in the encounter, according to police. Lucie Police Department said officers responded around 3:43 p.m. 19, to the restaurant at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard after receiving reports of a shooting. When officers arrived, they found Christopher Harris, 37, suffering from a gunshot wound to his upper torso. He was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where his injuries were determined to be non-life-threatening, police said. The other person involved, identified by police as Isaiah Davis, 25, was detained at the scene while detectives investigated. Officers also recovered a firearm. According to investigators, the encounter began after Harris and Davis had an interaction in the restaurant's parking lot. Police said surveillance video showed Davis entering the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order and Harris following him inside, despite Harris not appearing to place or pick up an order. Police said Harris then followed Davis back outside, where exterior surveillance video showed Harris pushing Davis and advancing toward him as Davis moved backward. Investigators said Harris was armed with a knife during the confrontation, and witnesses reported seeing him with a knife shortly before the shooting. Davis fired one round, striking Harris in the chest, according to police. Harris went back inside the restaurant, where people began providing aid and called 911. Investigators said one knife was recovered after it had been removed from Harris' waistband while people were helping him. Police said another knife was later found in his front pocket. After reviewing surveillance video, physical evidence and witness statements, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor and established probable cause to charge him with attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery based on a prior battery conviction, according to the department. Because Harris remained hospitalized, police said an arrest affidavit was submitted to the St. He is expected to be booked into the jail after he is medically released. Police said no criminal charges are currently pending against Davis. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates

entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - WPEC
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Crosswalk coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after safety study
entry.summary: A crosswalk is coming to Haverhill Road near Greenacres Elementary School after a county pedestrian safety study confirmed it's needed. Palm Beach County Engineering and Public Works is working to agree on the exact location either at Haverhill and Carver or Haverhill and 4th before submitting the design to the City of Greenacres. Once the crosswalk is installed, a crossing guard will be placed there. The city tells WPTV's Christy Waite they will allocate for the crossing guard(s). Waite has been investigating safety conditions along Haverhill Road across from Greenacres Elementary School for nearly a month. Brandon and Lynn Pote are among the parents who raised concerns about the stretch of road. 'Right here on Haverhill there's no school zone and it's 40 mph,' Pote said. The City of Greenacres tells WPTV: iWe have been in touch with PBC and are happy to hear they conducted a study and will be moving forward with the crosswalk. Being Haverhill is a county road, the review and permitting will be solely done by Palm Beach County rather than here at the city. When referencing the city, it is possible they will send a design to us as a courtesy which would just be a quick administrative review/feedback. We did have discussion with Palm Beach County and agreed to allocate a crossing guard(s). As this is not a identified 'school zone' and may not include flashing beacons, we did request some type of flashers to increase visibility for the safety of the students and crossing guards. The city will not be financially responsible for the project other than the crossing guards/i. Waite reached out to the Palm Beach County School District about the area being a school zone. The district said in a statement: iGreenacres Elementary School resides in a school zone, where traffic speeds are limited to 20 miles per hour along Jackson Avenue during arrival and dismissal times. With school in session, we remind drivers to allow extra commute time and exercise caution near schools. Please remain highly alert for students, school buses, and heavier traffic./i The crosswalk is expected to be completed early next year. entry.title: Department of Justice charges Utah postal worker with disposing mail-in ballots in the trash
entry.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice unsealed an indictment that charges a Postal Service employee in Utah with allegedly disposing of hundreds of mail-in ballots. Damon Matai Seei was arrested Tuesday and indicted a day later after officials said he 'did unlawfully secrete, destroy, and delay mail entrusted to him and which came into his possession.' Seei entered a not guilty plea and was released on his own recognizance. RELATED STORY | Trump slams the Supreme Court for rejecting his push to restrict mail ballots According to the department, the employee allegedly failed to deliver approximately 300 ballots to Utah County residents, along with other mail items not related to elections, and instead threw the ballots into a dumpster outside a church parking lot. entry.title: CROS Ministries hosts Hustle to End Hunger 5K as food insecurity rises in Palm Beach County
entry.summary: CROS Ministries is preparing for its annual Hustle to End Hunger 5K as the nonprofit warns food insecurity continues to rise across Palm Beach County. During WPTVs 'Shining A Light' segment Wednesday morning, executive director Ruth Mageria said more than 200,000 people in Palm Beach County do not have enough to eat. WATCH BELOW: Hustle to End Hunger 5K helps families facing food insecurity Hustle to End Hunger 5K helps families facing food insecurity 'The numbers are up in terms of who's food insecure,' Mageria said. '(About) 200,000 individuals here in Palm Beach County don't have enough to eat.' The Hustle to End Hunger 5K will take place Saturday, Oct. 3, at John Prince Park near Lake Worth Beach. The event raises money for CROS Ministries food assistance programs serving Palm Beach and Martin counties. Mageria encouraged community members to participate in the race or volunteer to support the organizations mission. 'What you can do to help is come to the Hustle to End Hunger 5K on Saturday, October 3rd at John Prince Park,' Mageria said. Registration for the event is available online, and viewers can receive a 15% discount using the code 'WPTV' or 'FOX29' in all capital letters, according to organizers. Volunteers spent the morning packing race bags and organizing supplies inside the CROS Ministries warehouse in Lake Worth Beach. The race is also drawing support from local community groups, including Pineapple Grove Run Club. 'Were bringing the two communities together to raise awareness for hunger, and were excited,' said Rob Cordoba, a founder of Pineapple Grove Run Club and CROS board member. CROS Ministries operates food pantries, meal programs and produce recovery initiatives throughout the region. The nonprofit has reported growing demand for food assistance amid rising grocery and housing costs. The organization also encourages residents to volunteer. Students can also receive volunteer service hours through the organization, according to volunteers at the event.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearance Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's patrol car, abandoning it on I-95 At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says - WPTV
entry.summary: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop - WPEC
entry.summary: Deputies: Vero Beach driver had Glock switch, loaded pistol, marijuana during traffic stop    WPEC
entry.article_text: Indian River County deputies arrested a Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of what authorities identified as a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. According to an Indian River County Sheriff’s Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after the driver, identified as 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes, lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier, according to the report. Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card, the affidavit said. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said. See also: 3 juveniles arrested after Riviera Beach teen fatally shot in alleged gun-sale robbery As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket, according to the report. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock . A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends. Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff’s office.

entry.title: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer on Fort Pierce gas pump - WPEC
entry.summary: Cybersecurity expert finds card skimmer on Fort Pierce gas pump    WPEC
entry.article_text: A man with decades of experience in cybersecurity found a credit card skimmer on a gas pump at a Fort Pierce 7-Eleven , and police are now investigating. Arlo Bess said he was stopping for gas at the 7-Eleven on the south side of Orange Avenue near Interstate 95 before heading back to Palm Bay when he found the device. Bess said he has worked in cybersecurity on and off for about 25 years. He said that background made him cautious at the pump. For years, he has tugged on the outside of the card reader every time he pays with a card at a gas station. He said this was the first time one came loose. "I was quite surprised when I went in there and pulled on it, just like I normally do, half not expecting anything to come out, and out pops this," Bess said. Bess said skimmers take almost no time to put on. "It literally takes about two to three seconds to put one in place and about the same amount of time to pull one out," Bess said. Bess said skimmers like this one are often held on with double-sided tape. A small chip inside reads the data on a card's magnetic stripe as it goes in. He said thieves usually leave a device in place for about a week and collect card numbers, expiration dates, and often security codes. They can then sell that information on the dark web or copy it onto other cards to make purchases at places like self-checkout kiosks or online. Bess took the device inside and showed it to the store manager, who called police. He said officers arrived a few minutes later and took a report, and they checked every pump at the station with him for more skimmers. Bess said neither the manager nor the responding officer had ever seen a skimmer in person. He said the manager also reported it to her supervisor with the company. The Fort Pierce Police Department confirmed it is investigating. Bess said you can't reliably spot a skimmer just by looking. "By looking at it visually, you can't tell the difference between a pump that's got a skimmer on it and one that doesn't," Bess said. See also: Is it illegal to drive with hazard lights on in the rain? It depends; here's the law The one he found looked newer and shinier than the scuffed readers on the other pumps. Still, he said the best check is a firm pull on the card reader with your hands, without using tools. He also said newer skimmers can sit inside the card slot, where they can't be seen at all. "My advice would be to tap your card, go inside and pay. It's much harder to put these skimming devices on card readers inside the store," Bess said. He also recommends not using a debit card at the pump. He said fraud protections for debit cards are different from those for credit cards, so it can take weeks to get stolen money back from a checking account. If you need to use a debit or ATM card, Bess suggests using a machine inside a bank lobby. He said outdoor machines, including drive-thru ATMs, are easier targets because thieves are less likely to be seen. We'll have an update on the investigation from the Fort Pierce Police Department, and we'll give you the details when they become available.

entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.title: 4 injured in stabbing at South Bay Correctional and Rehabilitation Facility
entry.summary: Four people in custody at the South Bay Correctional and Rehabilitation Facility were injured after a stabbing Tuesday evening, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue officials said. PBCFR was dispatched to the Geo Group-owned facility in the 600 block of U.S. Highway 27 in South Bay around 6:05 p.m., officials said. Two of the four injured people were triaged as trauma alerts and were taken to a trauma center, officials said. The other two people were taken to a local hospital. A Geo Group spokesperson said Wednesday that the victims' wounds were not life-threatening. Two of the people who were injured have since returned to the facility, while the other two remain under medical care. Officials did not immediately provide additional information about what may have led up to the incident. However, the Geo Group spokesperson said the Florida Department of Corrections is investigating the incident. Read the Geo Group's full statement below: 'On September 22, an incident involving four individuals in custody occurred at the South Bay Correctional amp; Rehabilitation Facility. Staff responded promptly and in accordance with established protocols. All four individuals were medically assessed onsite and taken to a local hospital for treatment of non-life-threatening injuries. Two have since returned to the facility, and two remain under medical care. The safety and security of our facility and those in our care is our highest priority, and we commend our staff for their swift response. The Florida Department of Corrections is investigating the incident, and we are unable to comment further at this time.'

entry.title: Tri-Rail fares set to increase 10% on Oct. 1
entry.summary: Tri-Rail fares will increase by 10% beginning Oct. 1, the South Florida Regional Transportation Authority (SFRTA) announced Wednesday. The fare adjustment was approved by the SFRTA Governing Board following a public hearing held on June 26, SFRTA stated in a press release. WATCH BELOW: Tri-Rail funding crisis threatens service for South Florida commuters Tri-Rail funding crisis threatens service for South Florida commuters The increase comes weeks after WPTV's Samantha Gutierrez reported that Tri-Rail is facing a severe funding crisis that threatens to disrupt or eliminate services. The commuter rail line is counting on $60 million in state funding that is currently stalled, leaving the future of the system uncertain despite a record-breaking year of 4.5 million passenger rides. SFRTA said the fare adjustment will help sustain long-term financial sustainability of the system. Tri-Rail continues to provide an important and affordable transportation option for residents, commuters and visitors traveling throughout the region, Diane Hernandez Del Calvo, SFRTA deputy executive director, said in the release. This fare adjustment is just one of the components to help sustain service and support the long-term financial sustainability of the system. The adjustment will apply to applicable fare products, including one-way fares and passes. Discounted fares will continue to be available for eligible passengers in accordance with Tri-Rails fare policies, SFRTA said. Tri-Rail remains committed to providing an affordable alternative to driving and connecting communities throughout Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties. The system also provides connections to the regions major airports and other transportation services. Passengers and members of the public are encouraged to familiarize themselves with the new fare structure by visiting Tri-Rails website www.tri-rail.com , or calling 1-800-874-7245.
