entry.article_text: Palm Beach County commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on the construction of new hyperscale AI data centers Thursday, completing the final vote in a process that began this summer.WATCH BELOW: This is an issue WPTV has been following closely for several months. The moratorium adds a definition for a large-scale data center use to the Palm Beach County Unified Land Development Code and establishes a temporary halt on new facilities that meet that definition. The county's zoning commission recommended approval of the measure in August.The temporary ban gives county officials and staff time to research and draft comprehensive regulations for the fast-growing industry, which has faced increasing public scrutiny. A study from the University of Pennsylvania indicates that approximately 60% of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities, a significant increase from earlier this year.The moratorium follows the commission's rejection of Project Tango, a controversial data center expansion proposal near the Arden community, back in July. Residents and commissioners cited concerns that the project could negatively affect nearby homes and Saddle View Elementary School.The county's action aligns with a national trend, as other local and state governments implement similar moratoriums to better understand and manage AI-related development.During a meeting earlier this year, commissioners and zoning staff discussed a range of potential rules that could be implemented following the one-year study period. Regulations under consideration include:Capping a facility's power consumption at 50 megawattsRequiring public disclosure of a data center's end-user or operatorEstablishing new restrictions on water use, noise levels and heat emissionsCreating a permanent task force to monitor the industry's evolutionPalm Beach County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she wants adequate time to hear from experts before the moratorium period ends."I want to hear from all the experts myself," Woodward said. "A year could fly by pretty quickly, and so I don't want to be at the end of this trying to cram it into another 12-hour meeting."Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores emphasized the importance of ongoing oversight."Whatever task force we put together should continue to study how this technology continues to evolve and what potential impacts it could play in the future," Flores said.With regard to data centers, the commission decided to look into hiring a consultant over establishing a committee. Either way, Woodward said the public needs to be involved."The public should come, listen, watch, show up, put in a card and speak every single time. I want to hear from them; we all want to hear from them, because this affects them just as much as it affects any of us," Woodward said. "A consultant or a committee, either way the public needs to participate in this."Palm Beach County Commissioner Gregg Weiss of District 2 said the vote reflects his responsibility to residents."It's in my responsibilities to look after the best interests of my fellow residents, and that means not just listening to their concerns but taking action," Weiss told WPTV's Joel Lopez. "And that is important when it comes to the health, safety of our community and when they're at risk," Weiss pointed to the rejected Project Tango proposal as a catalyst for the moratorium."Right here in Palm Beach County we recently had developers pushing for a hyper scale AI data center right next to a neighborhood and near an elementary school," he said. "Our community knew what happens when a data center comes to town, and we spoke up. Across the country, communities living near data centers have raised issues and concerns about water, electricity usage, wastewater discharges, and noise pollution."Weiss, a former technology executive who co-chaired a National Association of Counties committee on artificial intelligence in 2023, said he supports AI innovation but not at the expense of communities.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW:"One of the reasons why I voted to deny this project is the sound impact study behind it. We're using the wrong metric, one that misses the low hum these facilities produce around the clock. That hum affects somebody's ability to get a good night's sleep or enjoy a quiet time out on their porch," Weiss said. "Palm Beach County has a message loud and clear, and that was hell no on AI data centers near our neighborhoods. I believe the promise of AI, but embracing innovation doesn't mean ignoring impact on our communities."Weiss also addressed the race for Florida governor and contrasting candidates' positions on data center development."Byron Donalds has earned the nickname 'Data Center Donalds,' and it fits. He's told Florida that pristine land is wide open to data centers, and he's told families to trust the process to find the truth about Byron Donalds. Data center developers have sent nearly a million dollars in campaign checks. When your community takes a backseat to donors bankrolling your campaign. You're not looking out for Palm Beach and you're not looking out for Florida," Weiss said. "Families here need a process they can trust. They need a governor who will pause it, study it, and get it right. Floridians across party lines are on the same page. No data centers in our neighborhoods. Byron Donalds wants to rush these projects forward. David Jolly wants answers first, and he's right. That's why I'm proud to stand with David Jolly, and come Nov. 3, I think the voters will do so too."Several residents who spoke during and after the meeting said the moratorium is only the beginning of a much longer discussion about how Palm Beach County should regulate data centers.Palm Beach County Democratic Environmental Caucus President Reinaldo Diaz said the moratorium is an opportunity to pause and assess the industry's impact."The people who want data centers now and right away are the people who are poised to benefit and profit off of them. Regardless of the cost of the community," Diaz told WPTV's Joel Lopez.He also raised concerns about the environmental impact of data centers on the Everglades ecosystem, particularly regarding water temperature."Palm Beach County is the main connection of sending clean water south to the southern Everglades," Diaz said. "The system starts from the Kissimmee River and goes into Lake Okeechobee, then we ideally want to send it south where the water is nice and clean for the rest of the Everglades, so that it makes its way into Florida Bay."He said the proposed Project Tango site was particularly problematic from an environmental standpoint."If you look at our map and if you were to choose the most egregious spot where you would propose something that generates this amount of heat, it would be where this project is being proposed," Diaz said. "That's at the critical juncture of the L8 Canal, the C-51, and the stormwater treatment areas. That's where that's the only connection if you think of it as pipes, that's the only pipe we have right now that sends water south to the lower Everglades." Diaz warned that even a small temperature increase from a data center could have significant consequences."This is a data center that will raise the temperature to the surrounding area by just a couple of degrees as soon as they turn it on. That's so critically important to the Everglades in the environment raising the temperature by just a couple degrees on water that is already stressed by heat raising temperature of the environment," he said. "You're raising the risk of things like cyanobacteria blooms, other bacteria blooms, poor water quality. That compromises all the effort that has been put into Everglades restoration."Palm Beach County conservation advocate Sergey Kelley, who addressed commissioners during public comment, called the unanimous vote a significant victory for residents who opposed Project Tango and pushed for stronger oversight of the industry. Kelley argued that public pressure helped change the county's approach and urged officials to use the next year to develop regulations that prioritize environmental protections and local concerns."I'm thankful to people speaking up and defending their backyards," Kelley said. "If we didn't speak out and got essentially very mad about it, they would have approved Project Tango and never approved a moratorium."Kelley said he remains concerned about the potential demands hyperscale data centers could place on water supplies, power infrastructure and environmentally sensitive lands, including wetlands and areas near the Everglades. He also argued that future projects should bear the full cost of any necessary infrastructure and environmental safeguards rather than shifting those expenses to taxpayers or utility customers. "It should not come from our taxes," Kelley said. "The cost should be totally to developers."He also argued the county's moratorium does not go as far as measures adopted elsewhere in Florida. He noted that Palm Beach County's pause applies to hyperscale data centers as defined by the state at 50 megawatts, while some municipalities have adopted lower thresholds. "At least six other municipalities have passed a 5- or 10-megawatt ban," Kelley said. He suggested county officials consider stricter limits or a longer moratorium as they spend the next year studying potential regulations, arguing that "50 megawatts still allows a lot of these big buildings."Meanwhile, Gary Brown, a member of the county's Planning Commission who said he was speaking as a resident, focused on the need for expertise and careful planning before any long-term regulations are adopted. Brown said rapidly evolving technology, environmental concerns and safety considerations make it critical for the county to gather reliable information before making permanent policy decisions."This stuff is moving at warp speed," Brown said. "The information you have today is old in a matter of minutes."Brown supported the commission's interest in hiring a consultant to help evaluate potential impacts and develop recommendations, saying local staff, subject-matter experts and residents should all have a role in the process. He said finding a consultant that have give commissioners the most accurate information would be worth the cost as they decide how and where and how data centers could operate in Palm Beach County."Give them the best data to make the best decisions that will protect us all," Brown said.While Brown said he left the meeting with "more questions" about how the county's review process will ultimately work, he cautioned against rushing decisions involving a technology that is changing rapidly. Invoking a common carpenter's phrase, Brown encouraged county leaders to "measure twice, cut once" as they spend the next year studying the issue and weighing future regulations.Read more of WPTV's coverage below:

entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - WPEC
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    WPEC
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

entry.title: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says - wptv.com
entry.summary: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    wptv.com
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: CROS Ministries hosts Hustle to End Hunger 5K as food insecurity rises in Palm Beach County
entry.summary: CROS Ministries is preparing for its annual Hustle to End Hunger 5K as the nonprofit warns food insecurity continues to rise across Palm Beach County. During WPTVs 'Shining A Light' segment Wednesday morning, executive director Ruth Mageria said more than 200,000 people in Palm Beach County do not have enough to eat. WATCH BELOW: Hustle to End Hunger 5K helps families facing food insecurity Hustle to End Hunger 5K helps families facing food insecurity 'The numbers are up in terms of who's food insecure,' Mageria said. '(About) 200,000 individuals here in Palm Beach County don't have enough to eat.' The Hustle to End Hunger 5K will take place Saturday, Oct. 3, at John Prince Park near Lake Worth Beach. The event raises money for CROS Ministries food assistance programs serving Palm Beach and Martin counties. Mageria encouraged community members to participate in the race or volunteer to support the organizations mission. 'What you can do to help is come to the Hustle to End Hunger 5K on Saturday, October 3rd at John Prince Park,' Mageria said. Registration for the event is available online, and viewers can receive a 15% discount using the code 'WPTV' or 'FOX29' in all capital letters, according to organizers. Volunteers spent the morning packing race bags and organizing supplies inside the CROS Ministries warehouse in Lake Worth Beach. The race is also drawing support from local community groups, including Pineapple Grove Run Club. 'Were bringing the two communities together to raise awareness for hunger, and were excited,' said Rob Cordoba, a founder of Pineapple Grove Run Club and CROS board member. CROS Ministries operates food pantries, meal programs and produce recovery initiatives throughout the region. The nonprofit has reported growing demand for food assistance amid rising grocery and housing costs. The organization also encourages residents to volunteer. Students can also receive volunteer service hours through the organization, according to volunteers at the event.

entry.title: Martin County High School student arrested for false bomb threat at school - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County High School student arrested for false bomb threat at school    WPBF
entry.article_text: The Martin County Sheriff's Office announced on Tuesday, Sept. 22, that it arrested a 15-year-old Martin County High School student in connection with a false bomb threat made against the school. The sheriff’s office said its school resource officers and criminal investigations division traced the originator of the message back to the 15-year-old student, who is a sophomore at the school. WPBF 25 News is not publishing the name of the suspect because the student is under the age of 18 and has not been charged as an adult. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The sheriff’s office said the student confessed to sending the hoax threat. The student is facing a charge of false report concerning the planting of a bomb, which is a second-degree felony. “This arrest follows multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in our area over the past several weeks. Each threat is taken seriously and requires a significant response from law enforcement and emergency personnel, regardless of whether the threat ultimately proves to be a hoax,” the sheriff’s office said. It added that the suspect was only linked to the threat to the high school on Tuesday, Sept. “The Sheriff’s Office will thoroughly investigate these incidents and aggressively pursue those responsible when the investigation provides sufficient evidence to identify them. To anyone who thinks sending a threat anonymously, by text, online or through another form of electronic communication will automatically protect you from being identified and charged: that is not a safe assumption. These are not jokes, and will be treated as the crimes that they are.” Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. entry.title: 'Parents are having a hard time': Catholic school in Fort Pierce launches new educational program - WPBF
entry.summary: 'Parents are having a hard time': Catholic school in Fort Pierce launches new educational program    WPBF
entry.article_text: Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program on Thursday morning with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, marking the first program of its kind in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs. The program is called Morning Star, and officials with the diocese said it began as a pilot in August with seven students. The event included a ribbon-cutting ceremony and moments of interaction between students and Bishop Manuel de Jesus Rodriguez of the Diocese of Palm Beach, who attended the historic occasion. "It's the first of its kind, offering full experience of Catholic education to children with special needs," Rodriguez said. NEW BISHOP: 'I feel like we are connected': Dozens show up to welcome Diocese of Palm Beach Bishop-Elect The program aims to support families raising children with special needs, who often face unique challenges. "My gosh, right now, parents are having a hard time raising a special need . Sometimes they can feel alone and isolated. So, it's nice that we can open our doors to them and be able to offer the tools and resources for them, not only to assist them but also for them to understand the faith," the Rev. Principal Kevin Hoeffner explained how before the program's introduction, the school struggled to accommodate students with special needs. "So, I've been here 20 years here at St. Anastasia, and unfortunately, we've had to either let students go when they can't make it past a certain grade, or they come in the front door, and they really want a Catholic education, and we unable to provide that for them," Hoeffner said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates The Morning Star program includes sensory-friendly classrooms, a modified curriculum, small class sizes and individualized learning plans tailored to each student. "It is a gift to us, really. We think we're serving them, but they really are serving us," George said. The school hopes to expand the program to help more students and families in the community. Thursday's launch also marks the school's 100 years of Catholic education in Fort Pierce. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County.The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95.WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearanceAt around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard.Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118.During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia.Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft.The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

entry.title: Palm Beach County scraps resident task force for AI data centers, plans to hire consultants
entry.summary: Palm Beach County is changing course on how it will develop new regulations for AI data centers during its one-year moratorium, scrapping a planned resident-led task force and instead hiring outside consultants at a potential cost of up to $2 million to taxpayers. The decision marks a significant shift from the county's initial plan, which emphasized creating a resident task force to help guide the new rules. The pivot, made during Thursday's commission meeting, is drawing mixed reactions from residents who will ultimately foot the bill. A Shift from Task Force to Consultants Commissioners argued that the complexity of AI data center technology requires specialized knowledge that a volunteer committee may not possess. 'I dont know that we need a committee, I think what we need is a consultant thats an expert in the field,' said Commissioner Joel Flores, who originally championed the task force idea. Commissioner Marci Woodward agreed, suggesting that hiring experts would be more efficient. 'I fear we are adding an extra layer of work not only for the staff but also for interested parties and the public who want to participate in this as well,' she said. However, the expertise comes with a hefty price tag. Early estimates presented at the meeting place the cost of hiring a consulting firm between $200,000 and $2 million. Taxpayers React to the Cost The decision to spend taxpayer money on outside experts rather than empower a resident committee is not sitting well with everyone. 'If it's going to cost taxpayer money, to me, it seems like it's a superfluous use of that money,' said resident David Salvato. Taxpayer Juan Rivero expressed concern about losing direct public influence. 'Who's paying for them?' he asked. 'We don't have a voice on it, even though we're paying for it.' Other residents, like Vivian Diaz, believe it's a necessary expense. 'It's the best thing we can do as a community,' she said. 'Especially we paying for it.' What's Next for Public Input While the formal task force is off the table, residents can still voice their opinions during public comment periods at future commission meetings. For some, the core issue is ensuring the final regulations serve the community's best interests. 'It shouldn't be polarized. It's 'What's good for the community? What's the bottom line?'' Rivero said. 'Let's figure out how to make it happen.' The county aims to draft and approve the new data center regulations before the one-year moratorium expires on Sept.

entry.title: State Road 70 intersection raises safety concerns in Okeechobee; residents demand traffic light
entry.summary: Okeechobee residents say the intersection at State Road 70 and NE 128th Avenue is deadly, and families are now demanding the Florida Department of Transportation install a traffic light. However, the state has different plans. At State Road 70 and Berman Road, the number of trucks driving by is hard to miss with many of them headed to the Okeechobee landfill. Leah Suarez, a resident, said she recently lost a loved one to a fatal accident at the intersection. 'You have these fully loaded trucks coming not stopping or just a little quick tap on the breaks and then go, and so it makes it pretty dangerous,' Suarez said. Suarez said 24-year-old Luis Rivera, a beloved member of the Okeechobee High School band community, collided with a semi-truck back in August. 'He was just so special. Just such a great kid. He graduated with my son,' Suarez said. 'How could his life be snuffed out like that?' Suarez said she wants FDOT to install a traffic light to make the intersection safer. 'We can't let this tragedy, not provoke change,' Suarez said. She is not alone. At an Okeechobee County Let's Hear It event, residents shared the same concerns. 'You take your life in your hands every time you hit that intersection,' resident Deborah O'Donnell-Puckett said. The issue was recently addressed at an Okeechobee County Commission meeting, where staff explained a 2025 traffic study showed a traffic signal was needed. 'FDOT does not agree with that traffic study and wants to do a second traffic study,' county staff said. 'They've brought some suggestions about putting in some flashing lights, putting in some traffic deterrents and some other items to help start the process to see if it improves the intersection.' County staff explained one FDOT proposal included traffic deterrents in the intersection so vehicles cannot get across State Road 70 without turning right and then making a U-turn. Commissioner Terry Burroughs pushed back on that idea. 'When you tell me that they're going to make trucks a number of trucks do U-turns out there, somebody has lost their mind,' Burroughs said. County Commissioner Frank DeCarlo said over the phone Wednesday that the county is actively working with FDOT to improve safety at the intersection. When we reached out to FDOT, a spokesperson told us: 'FDOT is currently evaluating the intersection and continues to consider a traffic signal installation. In the interim, we are actively implementing signing and pavement marking enhancements as quickly

entry.title: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first rate hike since 2011 - WFLX
entry.summary: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first rate hike since 2011    WFLX
entry.article_text: Parking in Vero Beach is free, but overstaying your welcome is about to cost significantly more. Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. WATCH BELOW: Vero Beach doubling parking fines Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain the same at $200 per violation. The city said the increases are the first since 2011. Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would "encourage motorists to abide by the regulations." Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. "We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move," Kerensky said. "It creates turnover and can benefit from that." For residents like Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, the change hits close to home. "The free parking is great...when it's free," Gage said. "We've been tagged multiple times for not moving it after two hours." Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. "There's only so much parking, and it's usually on a beach day here, it's very [full] there's enough cars here that it's almost impossible," Wapnick said. Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. "You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they're going to get their money anyway," Billero said. With property taxes on the ballot this November, Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate. "I think we did it at the opportune time," Cotugno said. "Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress." Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions. "I think that's something that possibly should come up for discussion," Cotugno said. The new fines take effect Oct.

entry.summary: Martin County High School student, 15, arrested for bomb threat made to 'get out of class,' sheriff says    WPTV
entry.article_text: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a felony after officials say he confessed to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he "was just tired of being in class," according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident is the fourth threat leveled against the school in just a week and a half.WATCH: Martin County High student arrested for allegedly making fake bomb threatThe arrest comes as the school district is only six weeks into the academic year, and authorities are sending a clear message that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the school's resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday."The tip said, 'I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today,'" Budensiek said, reading from the alert. The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.Investigators immediately reviewed security camera footage and were able to quickly trace the electronic submission of the tip back to a 15-year-old student on campus.When first confronted, the student, who WPTV is not naming due to his age, denied any involvement."Initially, he denied knowing what had taken place," Budensiek said. "Alibied for himself, saying that maybe somebody else sent the tip."However, after further questioning, the student confessed, according to the sheriff. "He gave the explanation... as he just wanted to get out of third-period class," the sheriff said.While an arrest has been made in Tuesday's case, Sheriff Budensiek confirmed it is not connected to three other recent threats against the school."The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia," Budensiek said. "And then the last two, we're still investigating, and we could potentially be making some more arrests on that case."Budensiek issued a stern warning to any student who might consider making a similar threat as a joke."This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion... and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting - wpbf.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. entry.title: 'Parents are having a hard time': Catholic school in Fort Pierce launches new educational program - wpbf.com
entry.summary: 'Parents are having a hard time': Catholic school in Fort Pierce launches new educational program    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program on Thursday morning with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, marking the first program of its kind in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs. The program is called Morning Star, and officials with the diocese said it began as a pilot in August with seven students. The event included a ribbon-cutting ceremony and moments of interaction between students and Bishop Manuel de Jesus Rodriguez of the Diocese of Palm Beach, who attended the historic occasion. "It's the first of its kind, offering full experience of Catholic education to children with special needs," Rodriguez said. NEW BISHOP: 'I feel like we are connected': Dozens show up to welcome Diocese of Palm Beach Bishop-Elect The program aims to support families raising children with special needs, who often face unique challenges. "My gosh, right now, parents are having a hard time raising a special need . Sometimes they can feel alone and isolated. So, it's nice that we can open our doors to them and be able to offer the tools and resources for them, not only to assist them but also for them to understand the faith," the Rev. Principal Kevin Hoeffner explained how before the program's introduction, the school struggled to accommodate students with special needs. "So, I've been here 20 years here at St. Anastasia, and unfortunately, we've had to either let students go when they can't make it past a certain grade, or they come in the front door, and they really want a Catholic education, and we unable to provide that for them," Hoeffner said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates The Morning Star program includes sensory-friendly classrooms, a modified curriculum, small class sizes and individualized learning plans tailored to each student. "It is a gift to us, really. We think we're serving them, but they really are serving us," George said. The school hopes to expand the program to help more students and families in the community. Thursday's launch also marks the school's 100 years of Catholic education in Fort Pierce. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Wanted man found hiding under bed at Port St. Lucie hotel, police say - WPEC
entry.summary: Wanted man found hiding under bed at Port St. Lucie hotel, police say    WPEC
entry.article_text: You can run, but according to Port St. Lucie police , you cannot hide especially under a hotel bed. Police said officers went to a hotel on Village Parkway on Tuesday after receiving information that 41-year-old Kenneth Robert Ferow II, who was wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant, was inside a room. Ferow’s wife told officers he was not there, police said. But officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room. That's when officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there, police said. Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident. Police said officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine . Two children, ages 14 and 8, were also inside the hotel room. See also: Deputies: Woman with pipe bomb in stolen car hits school bus while fleeing traffic stop Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding warrant, police said.

entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - cw34.com
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

entry.title: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying - WPBF
entry.summary: ‘We’re about to fight’: Teens, dad clash at Indiantown bus stop over pizza and bullying    WPBF
entry.article_text: A confrontation between teenagers at an Indiantown school bus stop escalated into a man pulling a gun on two teens, according to a Martin County Sheriff’s Office report. The incident happened Friday morning near Southwest 174th Court and Southwest 175th Court as students were preparing to board a bus headed to South Fork High School. The sheriff’s office ultimately determined that no criminal charges would be filed as investigators believe the man who displayed the gun was legally allowed to defend himself under Florida’s Stand Your Ground Law. Sheriff John Budensiek said detectives spent the entire day Friday investigating the incident, interviewing students who were on the bus and the people involved. He said the investigation found the father had gone to the bus stop after his 16-year-old son reported being bullied by a 14-year-old student on the bus the day before. "The misinformation is of zero value. Actually, it's counterproductive to the safety of our citizens of Martin County," Budensiek said. According to the sheriff, the initial dispute happened Thursday when the 16-year-old got on the bus carrying a pizza. Budensiek said a 14-year-old student began asking the teen for pizza, eventually threatening him and hitting him in the head after he refused to give him some. The 16-year-old then went home and told his father what happened. Budensiek said the father returned to the bus stop that afternoon and spoke with the female bus driver, who told him she would try to address the situation. Confrontation at the bus stop The next morning, on Friday, the father drove his son to the bus stop. Budensiek said the 14-year-old involved in the previous day's incident was already on the bus when they arrived. As the 16-year-old got on the bus, his father began speaking with the driver again. According to the sheriff, that is when the 14-year-old got off the bus and confronted the father. "Now you have students on the bus that are yelling. You have the 14-year-old boy that came off the bus that's yelling, screaming at the dad," Budensiek said. Budensiek said other students on the bus then called another teenager to come to the scene. There were actually two 16-year-olds involved, according to the sheriff: the father's son, whom he described as the victim, and another 16-year-old who was already suspended from school and was not on the bus that morning. That second 16-year-old came to the bus stop after being summoned by students on the bus, Budensiek said. "So now you have two young men who look like grown men that are happening upon the dad, going at the dad and yelling at the dad," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father initially held his hand up and repeatedly told the teenagers to stay back. "They got all the way up on him before he pulled out a concealed weapon and told them to get back, which he's legally allowed to do," Budensiek said. He said both teenagers backed away, the father put the gun away and the confrontation ended. The father then drove around the corner, flagged down a deputy and immediately explained what had happened. Dad drives right around the corner, flags down a deputy, says, 'This is what happened, this is what I did, this is why I did it,'" Budensiek said. No criminal charges Budensiek said detectives interviewed students who witnessed the incident, including students on the bus and the two teenagers who approached the father. He said investigators found the accounts were consistent. "Everybody said the consistent story," Budensiek said. The sheriff said investigators would have sought warrants for the 14-year-old and the other 16-year-old who approached the father if the father had wanted to pursue charges. "We would have filed for warrants on the 14-year-old and the 16-year-old that went after the dad, except for the fact that the dad did not want to press charges," Budensiek said. The sheriff said the father's actions may not have been how he would have handled it, but investigators determined he did not break the law. "While it may not have been how I would have handled it, did not do anything illegal. You are allowed to stand your ground whether the person coming after you is 16 or 24 or 34," Budensiek said. Budensiek also said the father is a security guard and was legally carrying a concealed firearm. It's my understanding that he was a security guard and was carrying the gun," Budensiek said. He emphasized that the weapon was concealed before the confrontation. Budensiek said the father has since pulled his son out of school and plans to homeschool him. "He just was going to protect himself and his son at all costs," the sheriff said. Teenagers dispute sheriff's account The two teenagers who were in the video told WPBF 25 News a different version of what happened, disputing the sheriff’s narrative and saying they were frightened when the gun was pointed at them. RJ McIntyre and Trevor Ivory spoke with WPBF 25 News about what they say happened. McIntyre said he was walking to the bus stop Friday morning when someone called him and told him there was "an old man here looking for you." He said that when he got closer, he saw the man near the bus. McIntyre said he boarded the bus and noticed the father pointing toward him through the window. He said a back-and-forth exchange then began between him and the father's son, who had been involved in the pizza dispute the previous day. McIntyre said the bus driver eventually told both teenagers they needed to get off the bus. He said they dropped their backpacks and appeared ready to fight. "We dropped our backpacks. We're about to fight," McIntyre said, recalling the confrontation. Ivory said he was not originally at the bus stop but received a call from his younger brother. "My brother called me and he was like, 'There's a grown men at the bus stop. He's looking for somebody,'" Ivory said. Ivory said he went to the bus stop because he felt responsible for his younger brother. "I'm supposed to look after him," Ivory said. He said he spoke with the adult man before the teenagers got off the bus. "I was like, 'What's up with you? Like, who are you looking for?'" Ivory said. He said he eventually saw McIntyre and the man's son come off the bus. He said he could tell they were fighting and told the man to give them space. "I'm telling the dad, I'm like, 'No, just let them two fade,'" Ivory said. Seconds later, Ivory said a gun was drawn. "And the next thing you know, he put his son behind him, and he pulled a gun out on us," he told WPBF. McIntyre said he remembers what was going through his head when he saw the gun. "I can't process anything. I'm just like, am I going to make it home? It's life or death right now. It's a gun," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he grew up in the area and had never experienced anything like it. Ivory said he was also stunned. "In the moment, I was just like, it's crazy," Ivory said. Both teens put their hands up as they backed away. The dispute the day before McIntyre acknowledged he had interacted with the other student the previous day, but disputed the sheriff's characterization of that interaction as bullying. He said the encounter started when the other teen brought pizza onto the bus. McIntyre said he asked if he could buy a slice for a dollar. Instead, he said, the other student responded disrespectfully. "He screamed in my face," McIntyre said. McIntyre said he continued trying to talk to the student about the interaction during the ride home. He acknowledged that he used profanity and said he could have handled the situation differently. I think, like, when I was asking for pizza and he told me, you know, the first time, I think I should have left it there," McIntyre said. Questions over the gun The teenagers said they believe the father should be held accountable for bringing a firearm to the bus stop. McIntyre said the presence of the gun was particularly concerning because there were other children nearby. "I feel like under any circumstance, however you felt, no firearms should be displayed at a bus stop where there's a bunch of kids on a bus looking forward to going to school," McIntyre said. He said students on the bus could be heard reacting to the incident. "As you all can hear in the video, 'Oh Lord, please Lord, I hope they don't get shot,'" McIntyre said. The sheriff, however, said the father did not pull the gun until after the teenagers had approached him despite repeated warnings to stay back. He said the incident would not have happened if the 14-year-old had remained on the bus. "If he had stayed on the bus and kept his mouth shut and everybody had not called the other friend over there, there would have been no issues," Budensiek said. Sheriff blasts social media video The sheriff also criticized the spread of a partial video of the confrontation on social media. He said the video did not show the entire context leading up to the firearm being displayed. "There was a video that was put out on social media that was a half of a video and a half of a fraction of the story that actually took place and that grew legs and got spread around, and that's extremely counterproductive," he said. Budensiek said the social media posts created confusion in the community and questioned the work of investigators. "It unsettles the community. It undermines our law enforcement job that we're out there investigating it," Budensiek told WPBF. The sheriff said his agency conducted a thorough investigation and would have arrested the two teenagers if the father had wanted to press charges. "We did a thorough investigation, and you are allowed to stand your ground," Budensiek said. The sheriff ultimately characterized the father as the victim in the incident and said there will be no criminal charges. "To recap it, the individual with the gun was the victim in this case," Budensiek said. He said the father has since taken his son out of school to be homeschooled. "He did not want to press charges. He just wants to be left alone. He wants his son to be left alone," he said. McIntyre and Ivory, meanwhile, maintain they were not the aggressors and question why the father came to their bus stop armed. This is a developing story. entry.summary: 'Parents are having a hard time': Catholic school in Fort Pierce launches new educational program    WPBF
entry.article_text: Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program on Thursday morning with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, marking the first program of its kind in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs. The program is called Morning Star, and officials with the diocese said it began as a pilot in August with seven students. The event included a ribbon-cutting ceremony and moments of interaction between students and Bishop Manuel de Jesus Rodriguez of the Diocese of Palm Beach, who attended the historic occasion. "It's the first of its kind, offering full experience of Catholic education to children with special needs," Rodriguez said. NEW BISHOP: 'I feel like we are connected': Dozens show up to welcome Diocese of Palm Beach Bishop-Elect The program aims to support families raising children with special needs, who often face unique challenges. "My gosh, right now, parents are having a hard time raising a special need . Sometimes they can feel alone and isolated. So, it's nice that we can open our doors to them and be able to offer the tools and resources for them, not only to assist them but also for them to understand the faith," the Rev. Principal Kevin Hoeffner explained how before the program's introduction, the school struggled to accommodate students with special needs. "So, I've been here 20 years here at St. Anastasia, and unfortunately, we've had to either let students go when they can't make it past a certain grade, or they come in the front door, and they really want a Catholic education, and we unable to provide that for them," Hoeffner said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates The Morning Star program includes sensory-friendly classrooms, a modified curriculum, small class sizes and individualized learning plans tailored to each student. "It is a gift to us, really. We think we're serving them, but they really are serving us," George said. The school hopes to expand the program to help more students and families in the community. Thursday's launch also marks the school's 100 years of Catholic education in Fort Pierce. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical - wptv.com
entry.summary: Man charged after confrontation leads to shooting at Port St. Lucie Pollo Tropical    wptv.com
entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon.Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside.Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting.The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911.Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said.The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm.Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

entry.article_text: A year after WPTV first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman's Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination.The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was "likely contaminated" and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages.But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing.Those results are now in.According to site assessments obtained by WPTV, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WPTV said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming."I don't think it's necessarily something to be too concerned with," said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute.Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination.But WPTV Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal.Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development.Emails obtained by WPTV in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million.Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract.In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was "likely contaminated" and that the cost of "remediation" essentially "eliminates" his damages claim.At the time, however, FDEP's environmental investigation was still underway.The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself.Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination.FDEP's site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida's residential and industrial cleanup targets.Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property's historical industrial use."Personally, there's not really much in the report that alarmed me," Beckler said. "I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site."One sample, however, stood out.FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida's residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property.But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli.Shelli's proposed development property sits across the street.FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli.Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target.Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils."The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren't that high above it," Beckler said.The distinction could become important in Shelli's lawsuit.FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property.The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli.That is notable because the city's earlier letter specifically cited "remediation" when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli's damages.Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight.Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase."You're still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence," Torcivia said.Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP's findings to him or his legal team.The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers.In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli.During a public meeting, the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney's fees and other expenses under Florida's proposal-for-settlement rules.Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected."Maybe it's in everybody's best interests if they go to mediation," Torcivia said.WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation.For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom.Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman's Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years.Jenkins said he was shocked when WPTV told him last year that contamination had become part of the city's legal argument."This place was clean," Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago.He worries that simply associating Fisherman's Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners."You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that's going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners," Jenkins said. "I shouldn't have been in this situation."Shelli's lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department.And while FDEP's testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use.For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman's Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil.What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County - wflx.com
entry.summary: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County    wflx.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff’s Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff’s Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m.

entry.title: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested - cw34.com
entry.summary: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. entry.article_text: A 37-year-old man is facing charges after police say he was the aggressor in a confrontation that ended with him being shot at a Port St. Lucie restaurant Saturday afternoon.Christopher Harris faces attempted aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony battery charges following an incident at the Pollo Tropical located at 1365 NW St. Lucie West Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.The shooting happened around 3:45 p.m. 19 when a 25-year-old man had entered the restaurant to pick up a food delivery order when Harris followed him inside, despite not appearing to place or pick up an order himself. When the man left the restaurant, Harris followed him outside.Outside surveillance footage showed Harris pushing the man and advancing toward him while the victim backed away, according to police. Witnesses reported seeing Harris with a knife just before the shooting.The 25-year-old fired one round, striking Harris in the chest. Harris then went back inside the restaurant, where bystanders began providing aid and called 911.Officers responding to reports of gunfire found Harris suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso. He was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.During the investigation, officers recovered a knife that had been removed from Harris' waistband while he was receiving medical attention. A second knife was later found in Harris' front pocket, police said.The shooter was detained at the scene while detectives investigated and recovered the firearm.Based on evidence, witness statements and surveillance footage, detectives determined Harris was the primary aggressor in the confrontation. He will be booked into the St. Lucie County Jail upon his medical release from the hospital.No criminal charges are pending against the shooter at this time.

entry.title: Martin County barn fire destroys building, 6 vehicles; 1 firefighter taken to hospital
entry.summary: A barn that caught fire in Martin County on Thursday caused large flames and sent black smoke into the air that could be seen for miles. The fire occurred on a ranch in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown at about 5:30 p.m., according to a social media post by Martin County Fire Rescue. Large barn fire destroys building, 6 vehicles No horses or residents were injured. However, one firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms, Fire Rescue said. Officials said the barn and about six vehicles were a 'total loss,' including a side-by-side and a small front-loader tractor. Southwest Allapattah Road is back open after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

entry.summary: World Market celebrated the grand opening of its Palm Beach Gardens location Friday, bringing its signature collection of globally-inspired home goods and international foods to South Florida. entry.title: State Road 70 intersection raises safety concerns in Okeechobee County; residents demand traffic light
entry.summary: Okeechobee residents say the intersection at State Road 70 and Northeast 128th Avenue is deadly, and families are now demanding the Florida Department of Transportation install a traffic light. However, the state has different plans. At State Road 70 and Berman Road, the number of trucks driving by is hard to miss, with many of them headed to the Okeechobee landfill. WATCH BELOW: Residents demand traffic light at deadly intersection Residents demand traffic light at deadly SR-70 intersection in Okeechobee Leah Suarez, a resident, said she recently lost a loved one to a fatal accident at the intersection. 'You have these fully loaded trucks coming not stopping or just a little quick tap on the brakes and then go, and so it makes it pretty dangerous,' Suarez said. Suarez said 24-year-old Luis Rivera, a beloved member of the Okeechobee High School band community, collided with a semi-truck back in August. 'He was just so special. Just such a great kid. He graduated with my son,' Suarez said. 'How could his life be snuffed out like that?' Suarez said she wants FDOT to install a traffic light to make the intersection safer. 'We can't let this tragedy not provoke change,' Suarez said. She is not alone. At an Okeechobee County Let's Hear It event, residents shared the same concerns. 'You take your life in your hands every time you hit that intersection,' resident Deborah O'Donnell-Puckett said. The issue was recently addressed at an Okeechobee County Commission meeting, where staff explained a 2025 traffic study showed a traffic signal was needed. 'FDOT does not agree with that traffic study and wants to do a second traffic study,' county staff said.
