entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - cbs12.com
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

entry.title: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election. Senior Advisor for the Jolly-Graham campaign Mark Riddle sent a statement saying: Byron Donalds is panicked about David Jolly's momentum and is trying to fool Florida voters with a desperate website change, but the reality is that Byron Donalds is nothing more than Trump's yes man," Riddle said. "He and Byron are tied at the hip for an agenda that has sent costs soaring. Florida voters are angry and ready for change, and David Jolly is ready to deliver. Donalds' stop in Martin County came after he appeared at an economic summit in Fort Lauderdale earlier in the day. Donalds and Democrat David Jolly spoke separately at the event, laying out different approaches to issues including property taxes and Florida's insurance market.

entry.title: Amendment 3 sparks concerns over water quality funding in Martin County - WPBF
entry.summary: Amendment 3 sparks concerns over water quality funding in Martin County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A presentation at Stuart City Hall this week highlighted concerns about the potential impact of Amendment 3 on funding for waterway protection projects in Florida. The Rivers Coalition, which works to protect the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon, heard from environmental policy adviser Eric Draper about how reduced property tax revenue could affect water management districts responsible for water supply, flood control and water quality. Mark Perry, president of the Rivers Coalition, said the amendment could lead to reduced services funded by property taxes. "What you have to do is evaluate. I'm going to get, reduce my tax liability over the next few years with this amendment. But is that worth the services that are going to be reduced?" Perry said. During the meeting, data showed that the South Florida Water Management District could lose approximately $98 million in annual revenue by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes. Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard expressed concern about the potential impact on water quality projects. "The projects that improve water quality, that improve stormwater treatment, will be impacted, will be defunded," Heard said. Perry explained that local projects funded by property tax revenue, such as retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems, play a vital role in improving water quality by removing elements like nitrogen and phosphorus, which can prevent algae blooms. He said the passage of Amendment 3 would force local governments to decide whether to cut back on these projects or find alternative funding sources. "We're going to have a growing state and growing community here with growing runoff. That is going to happen," Perry said. A board member from the South Florida Water Management District told the Rivers Coalition that if Amendment 3 passes, it would affect the next fiscal year's budget, not the current one. However, they could not specify which projects might be impacted at this time. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.summary: High surf and dangerous swimming conditions are hitting areas throughout Palm Beach County as a Nor'easter churns off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic. At the Juno Beach Pier, high winds, rough seas, and a double red warning flag marked the scene Friday. Palm Beach County Ocean Rescue says the high surf is expected to stick around through the weekend. While beaches will remain open, they are recommending swimmers stay out of the water. WATCH BELOW: Dangerous surf hits beaches as Nor'easter churns offshore Dangerous surf hits Juno Beach amid nor'easter swells Most beachgoers were heeding those warnings. Anastasia Goldenberg, a resident, described the scene from the shoreline. 'Beautiful, you know, nature, powerful,' Goldenberg said. 'We're not going in. We're just going close to the water.' Fellow resident Jim Hooker took one look at the water and made the same call. 'I was like, I'm not sure if I'm going to live if I try and get in this water,' Hooker said. Hooker also noticed that not everyone was staying away. 'I see all these people swimming around out there. They should just have gotten in with a life preserver on because I'm not sure they're going to make it back,' Hooker said. The big swells are tied to the Nor'easter intensifying off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic, according to the WPTV First Alert Weather team. Logan Has, a local surfer, said he knew conditions would be tough to surf in, but that didn't stop him. 'Right now there's a lot of side shore current pushing us down the beach, so it's a lot of work we're paddling a ton,' Has said. Despite the challenge, Has said the waves were worth the fight. 'I was ready for it, but so excited. It's been flat all summer, so just glad to surf something,' Has said. entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - WPEC
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    WPEC
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

entry.title: Wanted man found hiding under bed at Port St. Lucie hotel, police say - WPEC
entry.summary: Wanted man found hiding under bed at Port St. Lucie hotel, police say    WPEC
entry.article_text: You can run, but according to Port St. Lucie police , you cannot hide especially under a hotel bed. Police said officers went to a hotel on Village Parkway on Tuesday after receiving information that 41-year-old Kenneth Robert Ferow II, who was wanted on a Martin County simple battery warrant, was inside a room. Ferow’s wife told officers he was not there, police said. But officers said they had credible information he was inside and continued investigating before getting permission to check the room. That's when officers looked beneath one of the beds and found Ferow hiding there, police said. Officers ordered Ferow to come out with his hands visible, and he was taken into custody without incident. Police said officers found a substance on Ferow that field-tested positive for methamphetamine . Two children, ages 14 and 8, were also inside the hotel room. See also: Deputies: Woman with pipe bomb in stolen car hits school bus while fleeing traffic stop Ferow was arrested on charges of possession of a controlled substance and two counts of child neglect, in addition to the outstanding warrant, police said.

entry.article_text: A barn that caught fire in Martin County on Thursday caused large flames and sent black smoke into the air that could be seen for miles. The fire occurred on a ranch in the 13000 block of Southwest Allapattah Road near Indiantown at about 5:30 p.m., according to a social media post by Martin County Fire Rescue. No horses or residents were injured. However, one firefighter was taken to the hospital with minor overexertion symptoms, Fire Rescue said. Officials said the barn and about six vehicles were a “total loss,” including a side-by-side and a small front-loader tractor. Southwest Allapattah Road is back open after earlier closures. The State Fire Marshal is investigating the cause of the blaze.

entry.article_text: WPTV is learning more details about what led up to a shooting at a Pollo Tropical in Port St. Lucie last weekend.According to the incident report, the shooting stemmed from a dispute over a parking space. Multiple witnesses provided accounts of the incident to responding officers.One witness told police he was sitting at a high-top table inside the restaurant when he heard a verbal argument between two men outside. The witness said he observed Christopher Harris, 37, push another man and after continuing the verbal argument, the witness said he saw the man discharge a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris, listed as a victim in the report, then came back inside and asked someone to call 911.One witness told police he was sitting at a high-top table inside the restaurant when he heard a verbal argument between two men outside. The witness said he observed Christopher Harris, 37, push another man and after continuing the verbal argument, the witness said he saw the man discharge a firearm, shooting Harris in the chest. Harris, listed as a victim in the report, then came back inside and asked someone to call 911.Another witness who came to pick up an Uber order said she observed a man pull into a parking space before another vehicle pulled into the space in front of them. She said the man was staring while he walked to the door, and when she looked away and got out of her vehicle to pick up the order, the man began yelling. The witness said that while exiting Pollo Tropical, the man was following someone out, calling them names and lunging toward them. She said she observed something in the man's hand and continued to lunge. The witness said the man was so close to the other person that they were almost touching before she saw the other person pull out a firearm and shoot.A witness picking up a DoorDash order said Harris came into Pollo Tropical yelling at another man over a parking space. The witness said the man exited to get his order, and Harris continued to yell, telling the man to "come outside." The witness said Harris held the door open and then approached the man before he heard a gunshot. The witness said the man stated that Harris "ran up on him with a knife."Officers recovered a 9mm handgun from the scene.The Port St. Lucie Police Department confirmed with WPTV that Harris, despite being the victim of the incident, faces charges of battery and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

entry.title: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested - WPEC
entry.summary: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested    WPEC
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. entry.title: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable - WPEC
entry.summary: Gubernatorial Candidate Byron Donalds talks costs, insurance at Martin County roundtable    WPEC
entry.article_text: With just six weeks until Florida voters choose their next governor, Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds brought his campaign to Martin County on Wednesday for a roundtable discussion focused on affordability and other issues facing residents. For about an hour inside a small meeting room at the Martin County Chamber of Commerce in Stuart, Rep. Donalds took questions from about a dozen Martin county voters, including insurance agents, realtors and homeowners. Rather than deliver a formal speech, Donalds encouraged an open discussion with community members. "Let's go around, introduce yourself and let's just have a dialogue," Donalds said at the start of the event. Questions centered largely on the rising cost of living, including homeowners insurance and healthcare costs. One homeowner asked Donalds what could be done about rising insurance costs. "What about homeowner's insurance because it's literally pricing people out of staying in their homes," the woman said. See also: Brightline may file Chapter 11 bankruptcy as soon as this week, reports say Donalds said higher construction costs have played a role in rising insurance premiums and outlined proposals he says would help lower costs for Floridians. The congressman also discussed his support for reducing property insurance premiums by 20% to 25% and his long-term goal of eliminating homestead property taxes. When another attendee raised concerns about increasing application fees and other costs imposed by local governments, Donalds said local officials should review their budgets and identify areas where spending can be cut. Throughout the discussion, Donalds emphasized making Florida more affordable for families, highlighting issues including insurance, housing and healthcare. "In healthcare, it's making sure we deal with stuff like dealing with in-network, out-of-network, prior authorizations," Donalds said. In an exclusive one-on-one interview with CBS12 News, Donalds was also asked about recent changes to his campaign website that removed prominent references to President Donald Trump's endorsement. "We're not distancing ourselves from President Trump," Donalds said. "We've been planning on making website changes for about two months now coming out of the primary. We wanted the website to be purely on the issues that we're campaigning on." Donalds added that he remains grateful for Trump's endorsement. Ron DeSantis has also endorsed Donalds in the race for governor. Donalds will face Democrat David Jolly in the November general election. Senior Advisor for the Jolly-Graham campaign Mark Riddle sent a statement saying: Byron Donalds is panicked about David Jolly's momentum and is trying to fool Florida voters with a desperate website change, but the reality is that Byron Donalds is nothing more than Trump's yes man," Riddle said. "He and Byron are tied at the hip for an agenda that has sent costs soaring. Florida voters are angry and ready for change, and David Jolly is ready to deliver. Donalds' stop in Martin County came after he appeared at an economic summit in Fort Lauderdale earlier in the day. Donalds and Democrat David Jolly spoke separately at the event, laying out different approaches to issues including property taxes and Florida's insurance market.

entry.title: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. entry.title: Nor'easter brings dangerous surf and rough conditions to Juno Beach through the weekend
entry.summary: High surf and dangerous swimming conditions are hitting areas throughout Palm Beach County as a nor'easter churns off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic. At the Juno Beach Pier, high winds, rough seas, and a double red warning flag marked the scene Friday. Palm Beach County Ocean Rescue says the high surf is expected to stick around through the weekend. While beaches will remain open, they are recommending swimmers stay out of the water. WATCH BELOW: Dangerous surf hits beaches as nor'easter churns offshore Dangerous surf hits Juno Beach amid nor'easter swells Most beachgoers were heeding those warnings. Anastasia Goldenberg, a resident, described the scene from the shoreline. 'Beautiful, you know, nature, powerful,' Goldenberg said. 'We're not going in. We're just going close to the water.' Fellow resident Jim Hooker took one look at the water and made the same call. 'I was like, I'm not sure if I'm going to live if I try and get in this water,' Hooker said. Hooker also noticed that not everyone was staying away. 'I see all these people swimming around out there. They should just have gotten in with a life preserver on because I'm not sure they're going to make it back,' Hooker said. The big swells are tied to the nor'easter intensifying off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic, according to the WPTV First Alert Weather team. Logan Has, a local surfer, said he knew conditions would be tough to surf in, but that didn't stop him. 'Right now there's a lot of side shore current pushing us down the beach, so it's a lot of work we're paddling a ton,' Has said. Despite the challenge, Has said the waves were worth the fight. 'I was ready for it, but so excited. It's been flat all summer, so just glad to surf something,' Has said. entry.title: Animal hoarding cases on the Treasure Coast raise questions about prevention efforts
entry.summary: Two high-profile animal hoarding cases in Martin County this summer and a third in Palm Beach County have prompted questions about whether more can be done to prevent animal neglect before it reaches a crisis point. The answers, experts say, are not simple. On July 20, Martin County deputies rescued more than 100 cats and dogs from a house near Hobe Sound. Exactly three weeks later, on Aug. 10, the same group of deputies rescued 36 border collies from a Palm City house piled with feces and rot. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, which was still handling rescue efforts of the previous case, then said this was the worst hoarding case they'd ever seen. On Sept. 16, Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputies, serving an unrelated arrest warrant near Lantana, rescued 13 dogs from another feces-filled home. According to the affidavit, seven of the dogs were confined inside 2 cages. Cesar Perea, vice president of the American Humane Society, said cases like these are not unusual. 'It's typically well-intentioned, whether it's a breeding operation or a rescue operation that just eventually just goes wrong,' Perea said. The American Humane Society monitors cases like these across the U.S. and assists law enforcement and local animal rescues when called upon. entry.summary: The West Palm Beach GreenMarket is returning to the downtown waterfront for its 32nd season, and for many vendors, the market represents more than a Saturday tradition. It has become a launching pad for local business growth across Palm Beach County. This season's theme, 'The World, Right Here,' highlights international flavors and cultures represented throughout the market, which returns Saturday, Oct. 3, to the Great Lawn at 100 N. Clematis St. WATCH BELOW: West Palm Beach GreenMarket returns with global flavors West Palm Beach GreenMarket Returns With Global Flavors 'It's the world right here,' said Kaitlynn Kenney with the City of West Palm Beach Community Events team. Several vendors featured during WPTVs 'Shining A Light' segment shared how the GreenMarket helped expand their businesses from weekend booths to permanent storefronts. Mauricio Sanchez of Sanvel Coffee said the company sources coffee directly from Colombia before roasting it locally each week. 'Our coffee is sourced directly in Colombia,' Sanchez said. 'We roast here every week.' Sanvel Coffee began at the GreenMarket and has since expanded into two brick-and-mortar locations in Wellington and Riviera Beach. French bakery Caf Marseille has experienced similar growth after building a customer base at the market. 'A lot of our customer base are customers that we actually met through the GreenMarket,' owner Jean Marseille said. 'So it's been tremendous for us.' The bakery recently opened its permanent caf location after first introducing customers to its pastries at the waterfront market. Luv's Kitchen Seasoning also brings international inspiration to the market with seasonings influenced by Jamaican flavors and cooking traditions. entry.title: 'That's going to scare everybody': New contamination findings raise questions in Fort Pierce waterfront fight - WFLX
entry.summary: 'That's going to scare everybody': New contamination findings raise questions in Fort Pierce waterfront fight    WFLX
entry.article_text: A year after WFLX first investigated a contentious legal battle over the future of Fisherman’s Wharf, newly released environmental testing is raising fresh questions about a key argument in the dispute: contamination. The city of Fort Pierce previously told developer Chris Shelli that the waterfront property at the center of his lawsuit was “likely contaminated” and suggested the cost of remediation could essentially eliminate his claim for damages. But the city made that assertion before the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had completed its testing. According to site assessments obtained by WFLX, FDEP found arsenic above state residential cleanup targets in two soil samples on city-owned land sold to Shelli. However, both samples were less than twice the residential cleanup target, and an environmental researcher who reviewed the findings for WFLX said the results on the development property did not appear particularly alarming. “I don’t think it’s necessarily something to be too concerned with,” said Jordon Beckler, an associate research professor at Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute. Shelli purchased approximately 3.2 acres around Fisherman’s Wharf with plans to transform the waterfront into a new destination. But WFLX Investigates previously uncovered a significant complication with the deal. Roughly half of the property was subject to a state right-of-reverter restriction, meaning the land could revert to the state if it were sold for private development. Emails obtained by WFLX in our first investigation showed Fort Pierce commissioners did not learn until 2023 — about two years after the sale — that removing the restriction could cost nearly $2 million. Shelli ultimately sued the city for breach of contract. In 2025, an attorney for the city sent Shelli a letter arguing the property was “likely contaminated” and that the cost of “remediation” essentially “eliminates” his damages claim. At the time, however, FDEP’s environmental investigation was still underway. The environmental concerns extend beyond the Fisherman’s Wharf property itself. Land immediately north of Fisherman’s Wharf was once home to a citrus packing house. Lucie County purchased that property in 2018 and designated it as a brownfield site — a designation used for property where redevelopment may be complicated by actual or perceived environmental contamination. FDEP’s site assessment found several soil samples at the former citrus packing house contained arsenic above Florida’s residential and industrial cleanup targets. Beckler said those findings were consistent with the property’s historical industrial use. “Personally, there’s not really much in the report that alarmed me,” Beckler said. “I think the findings are consistent with the past industrial uses of the site.” One sample, however, stood out. FDEP found an arsenic concentration roughly 148 times Florida’s residential cleanup target at a location along the northern portion of the former citrus packing house property. But that hot spot was not on the land sold to Shelli. Shelli’s proposed development property sits across the street. FDEP did send letters to seven surrounding property owners warning about possible off-site contamination. One of those letters went to the city of Fort Pierce and identified arsenic above the residential cleanup target in two soil samples on city-owned property sold to Shelli. Those exceedances, however, were far smaller than the hot spot found at the former packing house. Both were less than twice the residential cleanup target. Beckler also noted that environmental cleanup standards are intentionally conservative and that naturally occurring arsenic is present in Florida soils. “The vast majority of those samples, while, yes, they were above that residential standard, they weren’t that high above it,” Beckler said. The distinction could become important in Shelli’s lawsuit. FDEP identified remediation plans for five parcels included in its assessment, but those parcels are associated with the former citrus packing house property. The agency did not identify a remediation plan for the waterfront development property sold to Shelli. That is notable because the city’s earlier letter specifically cited “remediation” when arguing that contamination would essentially eliminate Shelli’s damages. Government law attorney Glen Torcivia, who is not involved in the lawsuit, reviewed the dispute for WPTV and said the new information does not necessarily resolve the legal fight. Instead, he said questions could remain over what the city knew — or should have known — and what responsibility Shelli had to investigate the property before the purchase. “You’re still going to have a dispute over whether the city knew or should have known that there were issues, and the city would argue from the developer standpoint, he should have done some due diligence,” Torcivia said. Shelli told WPTV that the city has not provided FDEP’s findings to him or his legal team. The lawsuit has potentially significant financial implications for Fort Pierce taxpayers. In March, commissioners were presented with a $6 million settlement offer from Shelli. During a public meeting , the city attorney warned commissioners that if they rejected the offer and Shelli later recovered at least $7.5 million, the city could also potentially become responsible for attorney’s fees and other expenses under Florida’s proposal-for-settlement rules. Commissioners took no action, and the offer was later deemed rejected. “Maybe it’s in everybody’s best interests if they go to mediation,” Torcivia said. WPTV reached out to the city for answers about its contamination claims and the status of the litigation. A spokesperson said the city does not comment on pending litigation. For Mike Jenkins, the dispute has consequences beyond the courtroom. Jenkins and his family own the property beneath 12A Buoy, a restaurant at Fisherman’s Wharf. He said his family has owned the property for roughly 50 years. Jenkins said he was shocked when WFLX told him last year that contamination had become part of the city’s legal argument. “This place was clean,” Jenkins said, adding that environmental testing had been conducted in the area decades ago. He worries that simply associating Fisherman’s Wharf with contamination could affect surrounding property owners. “You throw a word out like that — contaminated — that’s going to scare everybody, scare all the landowners,” Jenkins said. “I shouldn’t have been in this situation.” Shelli’s lawsuit against Fort Pierce remains pending as the city also navigates turnover within its legal department. And while FDEP’s testing did identify arsenic contamination in the broader area — including two exceedances on the city-owned property sold to Shelli — Beckler said the results he reviewed do not lead him to believe Fisherman’s Wharf is unsafe for recreational use. For now, the testing answers one question that has hung over Fisherman’s Wharf for more than a year: what is actually in the soil. What it means for the multimillion-dollar legal battle over the waterfront — however — remains unresolved. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said she is focused on helping Democrats including herself win reelection in 2026. entry.title: 2 killed, 2 critically injured in early morning crash on Old Boynton Road
entry.summary: Two people were killed and 2 others were critically injured in a crash early Saturday morning in unincorporated Boynton Beach, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office (PBSO). The crash happened around 1:04 a.m. on Old Boynton Road just west of Calliandra Drive. Investigators said a 2023 Dodge Charger was traveling westbound on Old Boynton Road when its driver, Rose Lott, 28, of Boynton Beach, lost control of the vehicle. The Charger began to rotate and crossed into the eastbound lanes, entering the path of a 2012 BMW X3. The front of the BMW collided with the Charger, according to PBSO. Both vehicles came to rest in the eastbound lanes. Lott was killed in the crash. A passenger in the Charger, Ryan Moody, 32, of Lake Worth Beach, was also killed. The BMW's driver, Ronald Lowe, 53, of Boynton Beach, suffered critical injuries. A second passenger in the Charger, Shaquila Reed, 25, of Boynton Beach, was also critically injured. PBSO said the crash remains under investigation. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Amendment 3 sparks concerns over water quality funding in Martin County - wpbf.com
entry.summary: Amendment 3 sparks concerns over water quality funding in Martin County    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: A presentation at Stuart City Hall this week highlighted concerns about the potential impact of Amendment 3 on funding for waterway protection projects in Florida. The Rivers Coalition, which works to protect the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon, heard from environmental policy adviser Eric Draper about how reduced property tax revenue could affect water management districts responsible for water supply, flood control and water quality. Mark Perry, president of the Rivers Coalition, said the amendment could lead to reduced services funded by property taxes. "What you have to do is evaluate. I'm going to get, reduce my tax liability over the next few years with this amendment. But is that worth the services that are going to be reduced?" Perry said. During the meeting, data showed that the South Florida Water Management District could lose approximately $98 million in annual revenue by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes. Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard expressed concern about the potential impact on water quality projects. "The projects that improve water quality, that improve stormwater treatment, will be impacted, will be defunded," Heard said. Perry explained that local projects funded by property tax revenue, such as retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems, play a vital role in improving water quality by removing elements like nitrogen and phosphorus, which can prevent algae blooms. He said the passage of Amendment 3 would force local governments to decide whether to cut back on these projects or find alternative funding sources. "We're going to have a growing state and growing community here with growing runoff. That is going to happen," Perry said. A board member from the South Florida Water Management District told the Rivers Coalition that if Amendment 3 passes, it would affect the next fiscal year's budget, not the current one. However, they could not specify which projects might be impacted at this time. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting - wpbf.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. entry.article_text: Anastasia Catholic School in Fort Pierce officially launched the Morning Star program on Thursday morning with a ribbon-cutting ceremony, marking the first program of its kind in the Diocese of Palm Beach to provide a full Catholic education experience for children with special needs. The program is called Morning Star, and officials with the diocese said it began as a pilot in August with seven students. The event included a ribbon-cutting ceremony and moments of interaction between students and Bishop Manuel de Jesus Rodriguez of the Diocese of Palm Beach, who attended the historic occasion. "It's the first of its kind, offering full experience of Catholic education to children with special needs," Rodriguez said. NEW BISHOP: 'I feel like we are connected': Dozens show up to welcome Diocese of Palm Beach Bishop-Elect The program aims to support families raising children with special needs, who often face unique challenges. "My gosh, right now, parents are having a hard time raising a special need . Sometimes they can feel alone and isolated. So, it's nice that we can open our doors to them and be able to offer the tools and resources for them, not only to assist them but also for them to understand the faith," the Rev. Principal Kevin Hoeffner explained how before the program's introduction, the school struggled to accommodate students with special needs. "So, I've been here 20 years here at St. Anastasia, and unfortunately, we've had to either let students go when they can't make it past a certain grade, or they come in the front door, and they really want a Catholic education, and we unable to provide that for them," Hoeffner said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates The Morning Star program includes sensory-friendly classrooms, a modified curriculum, small class sizes and individualized learning plans tailored to each student. "It is a gift to us, really. We think we're serving them, but they really are serving us," George said. The school hopes to expand the program to help more students and families in the community. Thursday's launch also marks the school's 100 years of Catholic education in Fort Pierce. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

entry.title: Amendment 3 sparks concerns over water quality funding in Martin County - WPBF
entry.summary: Amendment 3 sparks concerns over water quality funding in Martin County    WPBF
entry.article_text: A presentation at Stuart City Hall this week highlighted concerns about the potential impact of Amendment 3 on funding for waterway protection projects in Florida. The Rivers Coalition, which works to protect the health of the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon, heard from environmental policy adviser Eric Draper about how reduced property tax revenue could affect water management districts responsible for water supply, flood control and water quality. Mark Perry, president of the Rivers Coalition, said the amendment could lead to reduced services funded by property taxes. "What you have to do is evaluate. I'm going to get, reduce my tax liability over the next few years with this amendment. But is that worth the services that are going to be reduced?" Perry said. During the meeting, data showed that the South Florida Water Management District could lose approximately $98 million in annual revenue by 2030 if Amendment 3 passes. Martin County Commissioner Sarah Heard expressed concern about the potential impact on water quality projects. "The projects that improve water quality, that improve stormwater treatment, will be impacted, will be defunded," Heard said. Perry explained that local projects funded by property tax revenue, such as retention areas and large stormwater treatment systems, play a vital role in improving water quality by removing elements like nitrogen and phosphorus, which can prevent algae blooms. He said the passage of Amendment 3 would force local governments to decide whether to cut back on these projects or find alternative funding sources. "We're going to have a growing state and growing community here with growing runoff. That is going to happen," Perry said. A board member from the South Florida Water Management District told the Rivers Coalition that if Amendment 3 passes, it would affect the next fiscal year's budget, not the current one. However, they could not specify which projects might be impacted at this time. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first rate hike since 2011 - WFLX
entry.summary: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first rate hike since 2011    WFLX
entry.article_text: Parking in Vero Beach is free, but overstaying your welcome is about to cost significantly more. Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain the same at $200 per violation. The city said the increases are the first since 2011. Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would “encourage motorists to abide by the regulations.” Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. “We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move,” Kerensky said. “It creates turnover and can benefit from that.” For residents like Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, the change hits close to home. “The free parking is great...when it’s free,” Gage said. “We’ve been tagged multiple times for not moving it after two hours.” Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. “There’s only so much parking, and it’s usually on a beach day here, it’s very [full] there’s enough cars here that it’s almost impossible,” Wapnick said. Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. “You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they’re going to get their money anyway,” Billero said. With property taxes on the ballot this November, Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate. “I think we did it at the opportune time,” Cotugno said. “Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress.” Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions. “I think that’s something that possibly should come up for discussion,” Cotugno said. The new fines take effect Oct.

At approximately 9:30 a.m. on Thursday, a corporal spotted a red vehicle parked in the woods along the state-owned median of I-95 near Mile Marker 159 in Vero Beach. Upon investigation, officers found Williams in the woods holding a white bag and plant pruners, actively cutting a stalk of berries from a saw palmetto tree. Williams was taken into custody after admitting he was harvesting the berries and revealing two other men were with him. A Fellsmere Police Department officer located Gabbard just south of Williams' location. Howard refused commands to come out with his hands up and was ultimately apprehended by the K9. entry.title: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting - WPBF
entry.summary: Fort Pierce brothers, ages 11 and 12, killed in Georgia shooting    WPBF
entry.article_text: Loved ones are grieving the loss of two young brothers who were shot and killed Sunday at an apartment complex in DeKalb County, Georgia. The boys, 11-year-old Jamarion Rolle and 12-year-old Ja'khi Clark, grew up in Fort Pierce before moving to Georgia with their family. Their aunt told WPBF 25 News that both boys were straight-A students and were born and raised in Fort Pierce. Their mother also told WPBF 25 News they did everything together as a family, and both boys loved Roblox and being with their siblings and family. DeKalb County police Chief Gregory Padrick announced the arrest of 18-year-old Julian Ellis, who is charged in connection with the brothers' deaths. "Two children should still be alive today," Padrick said during a news conference. According to police, the shooting stemmed from an altercation that began while the boys were playing a backyard football game days earlier. The mother of the two boys told WPBF 25 News that the suspect and a few others showed up to their apartment Sunday and began trying to fight the boys before shots were fired. Two women were also shot in the incident. Police said both survived and received treatment for their injuries. Family members said one of the women underwent surgery on Thursday. "No family should have to endure the senseless loss of children," DeKalb County CEO Lorraine Cochran-Johnson said. As the investigation continues in Georgia, the boys' family and members of the Fort Pierce community are focused on bringing them home to be laid to rest. "No mother or father should have to bury their children. It truly goes against the laws of nature and expectation in our society," Cochran-Johnson said. The Fort Pierce community is rallying around the grieving family through donations and other forms of support. A GoFundMe is raising money to help bring the boys home to Florida. entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - cbs12.com
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

entry.title: Woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's cruiser, fleeing to St. Lucie County
entry.summary: A Fort Lauderdale woman was arrested Tuesday night after allegedly stealing a marked Broward County Sheriff's Office patrol car and abandoning it on Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County. The incident began at 9:30 p.m. when authorities issued a BOLO alert for the stolen Dodge Charger, which was traveling northbound on I-95. WATCH BELOW: Shannon Marie Dillon makes her first appearance Fort Lauderdale woman arrested after stealing Broward Sheriff's patrol car, abandoning it on I-95 At around 9:40 p.m., deputies with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Patrol Operations Bureau, along with officers from the Port St. Lucie Police Department and troopers from the Florida Highway Patrol, responded to I-95 after receiving information about the stolen patrol vehicle near Gatlin Boulevard. Within minutes, FHP located the abandoned patrol vehicle on the I-95 northbound exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard at mile marker 118. During the response, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputies found Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, in the area wearing an outer ballistic vest displaying Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. Dillon now faces charges in St. Lucie County including grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces charges out of Broward County for grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft. The northbound I-95 exit ramp to SW Gatlin Boulevard was temporarily closed while crime scene investigators processed the scene. The ramp reopened at 12:45 a.m. Wednesday morning.

entry.title: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Stolen Broward deputy's car found on I-95 in St. Lucie County, woman arrested    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: A Fort Lauderdale woman is facing multiple charges after authorities located a stolen Broward Sheriff's Office patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County Tuesday night. According to the Broward Sheriff's Office, shortly after 9 p.m., Broward County Regional Communications received a report that a marked BSO vehicle had been stolen from the public parking area of the Public Safety Building in Fort Lauderdale. Investigators, working with the Florida Highway Patrol, Port St. Lucie Police Department and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, tracked the vehicle to the northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Gatlin Boulevard in Port St. Deputies then spotted a woman nearby wearing an outer ballistic vest bearing Broward Sheriff's Office insignia. She was detained and identified as Shannon Marie Dillon, 42, of Fort Lauderdale. Lucie police said officers quickly established a perimeter after learning the suspect may have had access to a firearm. "The reason why the perimeter was established was because information was given to us that the female who had stolen the patrol vehicle had access to a firearm," Port St. Lucie Police spokesperson Brandon Martinez said. "PSLPD deployed both our K-9 unit and our drone resources." Drone video obtained by CBS12 News shows law enforcement officers from multiple agencies surrounding the stolen patrol vehicle along Interstate 95 before Dillon was arrested. Body camera video shows deputies ordering Dillon to get on the ground before she was taken into custody without incident. Dillon was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail and faces charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment, unlawful use of a police badge or law enforcement vehicle, unlawful possession of four or fewer identification items, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon, driving while license suspended, and resisting an officer without violence. She also faces Broward County charges of grand theft of law enforcement equipment from an authorized emergency vehicle and grand theft, according to investigators. The Broward County Sheriff's Office issued a statement crediting the coordination between agencies for bringing the incident to a safe end. The great coordination between all the agencies involved brought this incident to a peaceful conclusion. Nothing is missing from the vehicle. The deputy was on duty, and he reported his mark unit missing. The Internal Affairs Unit is investigating the incident to determine exactly what happened and if any agency policy was violated. See also: Can Florida police pull you over for a license plate frame? What the new law says Investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and the Broward Sheriff's Office are still working the case.

entry.summary: 3 arrested after saw palmetto berry harvest turns into K9 search along I-95 in Vero Beach    WPEC
entry.article_text: Three Okeechobee men allegedly drove to Vero Beach before sunrise Thursday, crawled into the woods along I-95, and illegally harvested 350 pounds of palmetto berries, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office . At approximately 9:30 a.m. on Thursday, a corporal spotted a red vehicle parked in the woods along the state-owned median of I-95 near Mile Marker 159 in Vero Beach. Upon investigation, officers found Williams in the woods holding a white bag and plant pruners, actively cutting a stalk of berries from a saw palmetto tree. Williams was taken into custody after admitting he was harvesting the berries and revealing two other men were with him. A Fellsmere Police Department officer located Gabbard just south of Williams' location. See also: 2 killed, 2 critically hurt in head-on crash on Old Boynton Road Gabbard admitted that he and the others drove from Okeechobee before sunrise in his sister's car to harvest the berries. A search then began for the third suspect, identified only as "Ray". Deputies initially deployed a drone, but technical issues forced it down. Law enforcement issued loud verbal warnings before bringing in a Florida Highway Patrol K9 unit. The K9 tracked Howard to a thick canopy of razor-sharp saw palmetto trees. Howard refused commands to come out with his hands up and was ultimately apprehended by the K9. Howard later claimed he was napping and did not hear officers yelling, though deputies noted the sharp, serrated limbs and rough ground made his claim highly unlikely. All three men admitted post-Miranda that they did not have permission to be on state land nor did they hold required harvesting permits from the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS). Throughout the wooded median, authorities recovered multiple large bags filled with freshly cut saw palmetto berries weighing approximately 350 pounds total. Inside and around the vehicle, officers found additional pruning shears, empty bags, headlamps, and flashlights. All three suspects were booked into the Indian River County Jail . All three suspects are being held without bond.

entry.title: Vero Beach doubles most parking fines starting Oct. 1, first rate hike since 2011
entry.summary: Parking in Vero Beach is free, but overstaying your welcome is about to cost significantly more. Vero Beach City Council voted Tuesday to double most parking fines starting Oct. 1. WATCH BELOW: Vero Beach doubling parking fines Vero Beach raising parking fines Fines for timed parking violations will increase from $20 to $40, while other miscellaneous infractions will rise from $30 to $60. Handicap violations will remain the same at $200 per violation. The city said the increases are the first since 2011. Vero Beach police sent a letter to the City Council in August requesting the rate increase, saying it would 'encourage motorists to abide by the regulations.' Lt. Brian Kerensky said the goal is to keep parking spaces moving and bring more foot traffic to the city. 'We have to kind of sometimes give them an incentive to move,' Kerensky said. 'It creates turnover and can benefit from that.' For residents like Wendy Gage, who regularly parks along Beachland Boulevard, the change hits close to home. 'The free parking is great...when it's free,' Gage said. 'We've been tagged multiple times for not moving it after two hours.' Neighbor Corey Wapnick said the increase is not fair because there are not enough spaces available to move to. 'There's only so much parking, and it's usually on a beach day here, it's very [full] there's enough cars here that it's almost impossible,' Wapnick said. Eugene Billero, who parks outside his real estate office, said a permit system could offer a better long-term solution for business owners and employees who need to park close to work. 'You could do a permit for the month and charge X amount of dollars, and they're going to get their money anyway,' Billero said. With property taxes on the ballot this November, Mayor John Cotugno said the timing of the fine increase was deliberate. 'I think we did it at the opportune time,' Cotugno said. 'Some of those courtesies that you paid, especially from a fee standpoint, we had to readdress.' Cotugno left the door open to exploring permit options and other long-term parking solutions. 'I think that's something that possibly should come up for discussion,' Cotugno said. The new fines take effect Oct. 1.

entry.title: Why Trump's attendance at Texas-Tennessee could affect the game
entry.summary: President Donald Trump is expected to attend this weekends SEC matchup between No. 1 Texas and No. 14 Tennessee in Knoxville. His attendance could affect communication on the field. Texas coach Steve Sarkisian told reporters Thursday that the presidents attendance could affect communication systems used between coaches in the press box and those on the field. That could create challenges in relaying play calls from the booth to players. The one thing we have to be aware of when the president goes to any game is that any time he enters the stadium or leaves the stadium or changes locations within the stadium, they cut all communication, Sarkisian told reporters. So they cut your headsets. They cut the headsets to coaches. They cut headsets to coach-to-player communication. So you have to have a plan for that, if and/or when it happens, and you get no warning. It just gets cut out. Sarkisian said he learned that firsthand when Trump attended a game between Alabama and LSU in 2019. Sarkisian was Alabamas offensive coordinator at the time. RELATED STORY | Senate college sports bill faces critical two-week stretch He also said the presidents presence could affect when players arrive at the stadium and alter their pregame routines. Texas reached the No. 1 ranking this season after defeating then-No. 1 Ohio State two weeks ago in a thrilling comeback victory. Now, the Longhorns face their biggest road test of the season. The University of Tennessee Police Department urged fans to arrive early for the noon matchup. Ticketed attendees are strongly encouraged to arrive significantly earlier than they would for a typical game, the department said. Enhanced security screening will be conducted before entry by the Secret Service Police at all stadium gates. Fans should expect increased wait times as kickoff approaches. RELATED STORY | Trump's executive order reshapes college athletics amid the NIL era Trump has frequently attended college football games. He was at last year's Army versus Navy game, then was on hand for the College Football Playoff finale between Miami and Indiana.

entry.title: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters - WPEC
entry.summary: From parks bonds to trash pickup: Local questions facing Palm Beach, Treasure Coast voters    WPEC
entry.article_text: Voters in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast will decide eight local ballot questions on Nov. 3, ranging from hundreds of millions of dollars in bonds to trash pickup, mosquito control and the future of public land. The questions are separate from candidate races and the three statewide constitutional amendments . Some apply countywide, while others are limited to Stuart, Port St. Palm Beach County Palm Beach County voters will consider three countywide funding questions. The first would authorize up to $280 million in general-obligation bonds , repaid through property taxes over no more than 20 years. The money would modernize aging parks, recreation facilities and botanical gardens; expand sports complexes; improve beach access and trail connections; and help develop new regional parks. A second question would authorize up to $175 million in general-obligation bonds for the Palm Beach County Library District. The money would be used to acquire, build, renovate, expand, improve and equip library facilities. The bonds would be repaid through property taxes within the library district over no more than 20 years. The third question asks voters to continue the School District of Palm Beach County’s existing 1-mill property-tax levy from July 1, 2027, through June 30, 2031. One mill equals $1 for every $1,000 of taxable value. The levy would fund school safety and police, mental-health services, teachers in arts, music, physical education and career and choice programs, and improved teacher pay. An independent citizens-and-experts committee would oversee spending. Martin County Martin County’s local ballot questions are limited to Stuart voters. One proposed charter amendment would require voter approval before the City Commission could sell, convey or lease for more than one year any city-owned property containing recreational ballfields. The second question concerns an undeveloped 1.97-acre city parcel on U.S. 1 opposite North River Shores Boulevard. Voters would decide whether to rescind a 2011 referendum requiring the city to commercially lease the land to fund maintenance of the Haney Creek Preserve. If approved, the city could convert the parcel to conservation land and add it to the preserve. Lucie County has three local issues, although they do not all apply to every voter. The countywide question would extend the existing half-cent infrastructure sales surtax for 10 years, from Jan. The current tax is set to expire in 2028. See also: Dead rodent in kitchen, 260 droppings & no hand-washing: 7 South Florida restaurants shut Revenue would continue to fund capital projects such as road improvements, traffic-congestion relief, drainage, flood control, sidewalks and water-quality work. Lucie voters also will see a nonbinding straw poll asking whether the city should change from once-a-week to twice-a-week trash pickup for an added fee . The city previously estimated the second pickup day would cost about $131 a year. The vote would not itself change collection service or rates. It is intended to gauge residents’ preferences before the City Council decides whether to pursue the change. Lucie County issue is a binding referendum on expanding the St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District by about 95,000 acres. The referendum is not countywide or citywide. Only qualified voters living in the area proposed for addition to the district will vote on it. If approved, those properties would be added to the district and become subject to its property-tax levy. Indian River and Okeechobee counties No countywide, municipal or special-district ballot question has been identified in the currently available Nov. 3 election materials for Indian River or Okeechobee counties. Voters there will still decide statewide constitutional amendments and candidate races, but there are no known local bonds, referendums or advisory questions to add to the local ballot-issues list.

The high surf advisory remains in effect until 8 a.m. Saturday, while the high rip current risk continues through Saturday evening. Some water could reach low-lying roads and properties, and localized beach erosion is possible.
