entry.article_text: The Miami Dolphins showed improvement in Sunday's 24-10 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, but they will be without De'Von Achane for the rest of the season after the star running back suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament in the first quarter.The knee injury happened on an 11-yard run on Miami's first drive. Achane got up quickly after a tackle, then stood still while flanked by a couple of teammates. He walked to the Miami sideline under his own power, was checked out in both the team's medical tent and locker room, and eventually returned to the Dolphins' sideline."My heart breaks for the guy," coach Jeff Hafley said Monday. "Since I've gotten to know him, watching him grow and develop, earning the captain role, becoming a leader of the team, becoming such great energy, such a great teammate. I mean, I just love his energy. I love his enthusiasm."General manager Jon Eric Sullivan has said that Achane — who agreed earlier this year to a four-year, $64 million extension with $32 million guaranteed — will be a key part of the Dolphins' rebuild. He is seventh on the team’s all-time rushing list despite playing only 47 games and led the NFL with an average of 5.7 yards per carry last season.Achane was expected have a hefty workload this season for the new-look Dolphins. He was either the ball carrier or the intended receiver on four of Miami’s first five plays Sunday before getting hurt and had 34 carries for 127 yards on the season.The Dolphins will now turn to backup Jaylen Wright — who was inactive on Sunday because of a stinger — and second-year running back Ollie Gordon, who had 17 carries for 41 yards and a touchdown. Miami also used speedy receiver Malik Washington at running back on Sunday.Gordon, who in college won the Doak Walker Award given to the top running back in the country, was praised by Hafley and teammates for taking over ball-carrier duties with no other tailbacks active following Achane's injury."I'm super proud of him," Willis said. "I told him in the game, I was like, 'Bro, you had to just man the ship alone.' He had to do this side of the oars, this side of the oars. I was like, ‘Dang, he had to do it all today.'"Despite Achane's injury, the Dolphins stuck with their plan of running the ball, keeping it out of the hands of Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs' potent offense.Hafley said that philosophy won't change going forward."I want to run the football. That's important, and we have the offensive line to do it," he said. "I have a lot of confidence in those backs, so this isn’t like, 'We can't run the ball anymore.' These are NFL players.'"Hafley said he liked the way Miami's defense responded after giving up some big plays and touchdowns early, which allowed it to keep the game close in the second half unlike in previous weeks. After giving up touchdowns on Kansas City's first two drives, the Dolphins stopped Mahomes & Co. on three straight possessions, including denying running back Kenneth Walker III on fourth down.The Dolphins are still committing too many penalties in critical moments. An illegal shift negated a touchdown in the third quarter. Rookie safety Michael Taaffe was flagged for an illegal contact that wiped out what would have been the Dolphins' first sack of the season. Chop Robinson and Zach Sieler were flagged for penalties that extended a Chiefs drive that ended in a field goal.Linebacker Jacob Rodriguez. The rookie second-round draft pick has had a strong start to his NFL career. Rodriguez had a diving interception of Mahomes in the second quarter on Sunday and finished with a team-high three tackles for loss and a pass breakup.Secondary. Mahomes carved up Miami’s young secondary, completing his first 11 passes until Rodriguez came up with the pick on a deflection off receiver Rashee Rice. The Dolphins have improved their run defense over the past two games, holding the NFL's leading rusher in Walker under 100 yards for the first time this season, but they’re still giving up explosive plays.Wright and WR Caleb Douglas (ankle) are day-to-day.23 — Number of penalties the Dolphins have committed through three games.The Dolphins will try to get healthy when they travel to face Minnesota on Sunday. The status of star Vikings receiver Justin Jefferson may be in question after he left in the first quarter of Sunday's win at Tampa Bay with an ankle injury.

entry.title: IGNITE uses grilling to spark stronger bonds between fathers, sons and mentors
entry.summary: I visited Love, Hope Healing Inc. to learn more about IGNITE: The Father Son Grill Challenge , an event built around mentoring, communication and creating stronger relationships between young men and the adults who support them. While the event includes grilling and friendly competition, organizers say the larger goal is helping fathers, sons, mentors and mentees spend meaningful time together. West Palm Beach IGNITE builds bonds through grilling 'We will have what we call the Fire Circle, where we will have a therapist-led session, and we're talking about some of these conversations that fathers and sons need to have, but rarely have and don't know how to have,' said Donte Bates, co-founder and executive director of Love, Hope Healing Inc. 'So we're creating that space for them to actually talk about it.' Yolanda Bates, CEO of Love, Hope Healing Inc., said events like IGNITE help strengthen relationships that can have a lasting impact on young people. 'Fathers and sons, they need to create these bonds where these young men can have these experiences and the leadership and mentorship as they grow,' she said. One of the organizations supporting the effort is United Way of Palm Beach County. Gwynette Williams, vice president of mentoring, said relationship-building is at the heart of the organization's mission. 'It's important to make sure that we are building relationships between adults and young people all over Palm Beach County,' Williams said. 'That's really what we do all day long.' Williams also summed up one of the event's unique attractions with a smile. 'You can't go wrong with men and meat,' she said. Mentor Bruce Lewis said his involvement is rooted in helping young men see a positive path forward. 'It's serving as a positive role model for the young African American males who really need that, giving them a good pathway to success,' Lewis said. 'I look forward to helping them build their futures.' His mentee, Nate, said he's excited about both the experience and the opportunity to grow. 'I'm looking forward to making friends and having a better bond,' he said. The event's presenting partner, Lowe's Home Improvement, is providing a grill and supplies for participating teams. 'We're in the community, and we're for the community,' said David Territo, a Lowe's store manager. entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man accused of stabbing father, admits intent to kill    WPBF
entry.article_text: Lucie police say a 44-year-old man stabbed his father three times in the chest and admitted to authorities that he wanted to kill him. Body camera footage shows officers responding to a home on NW Blackbird Drive on Sunday, where they arrested the suspect, identified as Cartavion Merritt. "Our suspect was actually the 911 caller in this situation," said Port St. Lucie Police Department spokesperson Brittany McNally. McNally said Merritt admitted to stabbing his father with two different knives, which were later found in the kitchen sink. "It was revealed that he had some long-standing feeling towards this family member, meaning there was some resentment that was building up from what was described, and in comparison to other family members, he felt as if he wasn't exactly treated fairly," McNally said. Police found the 79-year-old victim inside the home with three stab wounds to the chest. He remains hospitalized and intubated, according to authorities. Court records show Merritt pleaded guilty to a stabbing in West Palm Beach in 2012, where officials said he stabbed his roommate twice with a kitchen knife. Merritt is being held on charges of attempted homicide and aggravated battery. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

entry.title: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest - WPEC
entry.summary: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest    WPEC
entry.article_text: More than two years after his arrest, jury selection is underway in the trial former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Nick Mimms. Prospective jurors are being asked in court what they know about the case, if they've reached any conclusions about Mimms' guilt or innocence, if they can put aside any information they may have heard or read about the case and base their verdict solely on the evidence presented in the courtroom. Mimms, 53, was arrested in August 2024 and accused of bid tampering and official misconduct in connection with a city bidding process involving two vacant, city-owned lots in Fort Pierce’s Lincoln Park area. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the investigation began after the agency received a complaint alleging inappropriate conduct involving a request for proposals to develop the property. FDLE accused Mimms of using his position to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals secure a lease for the lots. Investigators said the nonprofit was formed by two city employees, including Mimms’ niece. Investigators also accused Mimms, who served as project manager for the request for proposals, of influencing the language and evaluation criteria used in the bidding process and sharing nonpublic information with the nonprofit before the bid became public. The property, located at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D, was intended to become a community center called The Root, with plans that included a library, classroom space and pop-up markets. The lease was later terminated in 2024 after Lincoln Park Young Professionals told the city it was no longer pursuing the project. Mimms had served as Fort Pierce city manager since 2015 after previously working as deputy city manager and project engineer for the city. The prospective jurors were told Monday the trial may take one to two weeks. Outside the courtroom Monday, Mimms had no comment. CBS12 News will continue following the case as the trial moves forward. This is a developing story.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie pauses Flock program; 18 cameras set for removal Sept. 30 - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie pauses Flock program; 18 cameras set for removal Sept. 30    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Lucie officials said 18 Flock cameras installed in county and state rights-of-way are scheduled to be removed by the vendor by Sept. 30, as the city pauses its automated license plate reader program amid continued privacy concerns. The update came during public comment at a City Council meeting on Monday, where several residents urged council members to permanently remove the cameras and prohibit future permits for Flock and other automated vehicle-tracking systems. Casey Honeycutt called for a citywide ban on Flock cameras and similar systems, arguing they pose privacy and surveillance concerns. Lucie resident Jorge Borgess directly asked council members to remove the cameras and take further action. He asked the city to stop issuing permits for automated license plate readers and other vehicle-tracking systems in city-owned or city-controlled rights-of-way, and to pursue removal of existing cameras. Lucie police announced Sept. 1 that the department would pause the program and remove seven cameras. He told council he counted eight of 22 cameras still standing at locations he believed required state right-of-way review. Steven Grier also addressed the council, saying he has sued the city, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock in federal court. His lawsuit allegations were not discussed by the council during the meeting. See also: Sheriff’s office warns of renewed inappropriate activity at DJ Wilcox Preserve Later, Port St. Lucie resident James Reynolds joined the criticism, telling council members the city had previously achieved its public safety goals without Flock cameras. We need to make sure there’s punishments for misuse; we need to make sure that retention periods are addressed; our audit is complete, Bonna said. I know there have been local incidents of misuse, and so this isn’t something abstract. Bonna said he was not calling for all cameras to be taken down immediately. What I’m calling for is to pause the program, and when I say pause, I mean pause, and let’s get this policy right, so it protects both our liberties and safety, Bonna said. During the discussion, city officials said the police chief’s white paper calls for nine cameras in county rights-of-way and nine in state rights-of-way to be removed by the vendor. The city can’t take them down; the vendor needs to take them down, an unidentified city official said. Those 18 cameras will be taken down. An unidentified city staff member later confirmed the scheduled removal date. 30 that the cameras will be taken down, the staff member said. Lucie police had previously announced an operational pause on its Flock and Axon license plate reader systems after the Florida Department of Transportation revoked approvals for the technology in state highway rights of way. At that time, police said seven city cameras located in FDOT rights-of-way would be removed. The city’s pause limits use of the remaining systems to cases involving an immediate threat to life, including missing or endangered people, with authorization from Police Chief Leo Niemczyk . The discussion follows a broader debate in St. Earlier this month, county commissioners voted 3-2 to stop new permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers in county-controlled rights of way, review existing permits and issue removal notices where appropriate. The county action went beyond FDOT’s order, which applied only to state highway rights-of-way. The county vote did not apply to cameras on private property or devices mounted in law enforcement vehicles. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office would comply with the state directive while tightening internal rules for deputies’ use of the technology.

entry.title: Tiny satellite tags help solve mystery of where baby sea turtles go after disappearing into Atlantic
entry.summary: We watch baby sea turtles emerge from nests along South Florida's beaches and make their way toward the Atlantic. But once they disappear beneath the surface, one big question remains: Where do they go? entry.article_text: We watch baby sea turtles emerge from nests along South Florida's beaches and make their way toward the Atlantic.But once they disappear beneath the surface, one big question remains: Where do they go?Researchers at Florida Atlantic University's Marine Science Laboratory at the Gumbo Limbo Environmental Complex are using tiny satellite transmitters to help answer that question.WATCH BELOW: Gumbo Limbo Nature Center tracking young sea turtlesThe trackers are small, some roughly the size of a thumbnail, but the information they can send back could help scientists better understand one of the least visible stages of a sea turtle's life."We've been working on how to satellite tag the littlest life stages," said Jeanette Wyneken, professor of biological sciences and director of the FAU Marine Science Laboratory. "We have some little tiny satellite tags — they’re about the size of my thumbnail."For researchers, knowing a turtle’s location is only the beginning.Tracking can help scientists understand where young turtles travel after release, which parts of the ocean they use, and what types of conditions they encounter along the way.That information may also reveal whether their routes take them into healthier habitats or areas where they face greater risks.Wyneken describes it as figuring out whether the turtles are moving into the ocean's "good neighborhoods" or its "bad neighborhoods.""Are they going to the good neighborhoods, the bad neighborhoods — the bad ones being ones with lots of garbage or lots of fisheries bycatch issues?" she said.Those threats can include marine debris, plastics, discarded fishing gear, and areas where turtles may be at greater risk of becoming unintentionally caught in fishing activity.By identifying where young turtles spend time, researchers can begin building a better picture of which ocean habitats may be especially important during their early lives.The satellite tags give researchers a way to continue collecting information after the turtles leave the laboratory.Researchers have also learned more about how long they can continue receiving data as the turtles grow.Wyneken said the tag attachment allows young loggerheads to grow several centimeters before the transmitter eventually falls away.Under temperatures similar to those the turtles experience in the Gulf Stream, researchers estimate that can provide roughly 70 days of tracking data.That gives scientists a limited but valuable window into the turtles’ lives after they return to the ocean.Some of this season’s turtles are already giving researchers clues."We just released some leatherbacks with satellite trackers, and they got into the Gulf Stream," Wyneken said. "And last I checked, they were still in the Gulf Stream."The Gulf Stream runs just offshore of Florida’s Atlantic coast, carrying warm water northward through the Atlantic.For researchers, seeing the turtles enter that current is more than an interesting point on a map.It helps show how young turtles move through the ocean after leaving South Florida and provides another piece of information about the habitat they use during a critical stage of their development.That information can help scientists better understand which ocean habitats young sea turtles depend on — and where conservation efforts may be most useful.Researchers say funding is an important part of continuing and expanding this work.Support helps cover the care of turtles being studied as well as equipment used for research, including satellite-tracking technology.FAU’s Marine Science Laboratory provides information about its sea turtle research, ways to support the program and opportunities for the public to learn more about the work.The laboratory also works with Upwell, a nonprofit organization involved in sea turtle tracking and conservation research.You can also learn more about the lab’s sea turtle research and visit the public gallery at the Gumbo Limbo Environmental Complex in Boca Raton. Support FAU’s Marine Science Laboratory at Gumbo LimboViewers can also help protect sea turtles by keeping beaches clean, removing trash and discarded fishing line, limiting artificial light near nesting beaches, and give hatchlings and nesting turtles plenty of space.

entry.article_text: Lucie man was arrested after police said he called 911 and admitted to stabbing a 79-year-old man during a domestic-related incident Saturday night. Police said Cartavion Jermaine Merritt called 911 about 11:01 p.m. to report a stabbing inside a home in the 11200 block of Northwest Blockbird Drive. Lucie police, Merritt told dispatchers he used two knives to stab the victim in the chest and wanted to kill him. He also told dispatchers the two men were the only people inside the home and that he had put the knives in the kitchen sink. Body-camera video released by police shows officers arriving in the neighborhood, establishing a perimeter and escorting a man away from the home. Police said Merritt exited the house about eight minutes after the 911 call and was taken into custody without incident. Once officers entered, they found the 79-year-old victim with multiple apparent stab wounds to his upper chest, police said. Officers and paramedics provided emergency care before the victim was flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital as a trauma alert. See also: Airport security concerns resurface after perimeter breaches in South Florida The victim was later reported stable but intubated, police said. Investigators said they found two knives in the kitchen sink and blood on bedsheets in a bedroom, where they determined the stabbing occurred. Police said Merritt later told detectives that he intended to kill the victim. Merritt was arrested on charges of attempted second-degree murder without premeditation and aggravated battery on a person 65 or older, both domestic-related charges.

entry.title: 2028 Olympic torch relay to begin in Atlanta and travel through all 50 states
entry.summary: The torch relay for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics will begin in Atlanta, home of the last U.S. Summer Games in 1996, and travel through all 50 states, organizers announced Tuesday. The Olympic flame will be lit in Olympia, Greece, the birthplace of the Olympic Games, before beginning its journey around the United States in spring 2028. The full route for the torch relay will be announced in 2027. LA28 organizers say the relay will be one of the largest in Olympic history, passing through iconic and internationally renowned landmarks, stopping at major cultural and sporting events and hosting festival celebrations in select cities nationwide. 'Every Olympic Games begins with a single flame, and carrying that flame to Los Angeles is an honor and privilege that we'll share with every corner of the country, as Americans in all 50 states carry the flame on its path to our Opening Ceremony,' LA28 chair and president Casey Wasserman said in a statement. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT |  Olympic athletes to get cash grants from new $100M fund created by IOC Atlanta Mayor Andre Dickens said the city will be proud to welcome the Olympic flame back 32 years after hosting the centennial Summer Games. 'Atlanta looks a little different. We are bigger. We are more connected to the world. So, when the flame returns to the U.S., Atlanta will be ready,' Dickens said in a statement. 'Ready to welcome it from Greece. Ready to celebrate the spirit of the Games together as a community. And ready to send it forward toward Los Angeles and the next chapter of America's Olympic story.' The Paralympic torch relay will follow the end of the Olympics in August 2028, with the flame originating in Stoke Mandeville, England, the birthplace of the Paralympic movement. The relay's U.S. starting location will be announced later. Both torch relays will be sponsored by Coca-Cola, JPMorganChase, Allstate and Xfinity.

entry.title: Florida is set to execute a 77-year-old man convicted of a 1995 murder
entry.summary: A 77-year-old Florida man convicted of beating a woman to death with a hammer is scheduled Tuesday to become the 16th person executed this year in the nation's busiest death chamber. Curtis Wilkie Beasley was sentenced to death after being convicted of first-degree murder, robbery and grand theft auto in a 1995 attack on Carolyn Monfort. The Florida Supreme Court last week rejected appeals that executing a man his age who is suffering from cognitive decline would amount to cruel and unusual punishment. Beasley, who would become Florida's seventh prisoner over the age of 70 to be executed this year, is set to receive a three-drug injection at the state prison starting at 6 p.m. It was one of two executions scheduled this week in the U.S. Tennessee plans to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years on Wednesday by administering a lethal injection to Christa Pike, 50, who was convicted of killing a classmate in a jealous rage when they were both teens. Arrested while working under a fake name According to court records, Beasley had been staying at Monforts Dundee home, south of Orlando, in August 1995 while he was pressure washing and painting nearby apartments owned by her son-in-law. Monfort's daughter went to her home after being unable to reach her for two days and found her body in a blood-splattered laundry room. Monfort suffered multiple blunt-force trauma injuries to the head, and a bloody hammer head was found wrapped in a towel nearby, according to investigators. Authorities began searching for Beasley after a witness reported seeing him driving what turned out to be Monfort's car. Investigators determined Beasley had traveled to Miami and later relocated to Alabama, where he was arrested while working under a fake name for an electrical company, officials said. Dr. Heather Barron, Chief Science Officer and Director of Conservation Medicine at Loggerhead Marinelife Center, expressed excitement about this particular release, noting that Jurassic represents a milestone for the facility as the first adult green male tagged by the facility. 'It's so exciting, and I think this one, Jurassic, is particularly exciting. He's a full-grown adult breeding male, and he has a satellite tag on, so we'll actually be able to see how he's doing,' Dr. Barron said. The satellite tag, provided by the U.S. Navy, will allow researchers to track Jurassic's movements and behavior patterns once he returns to his natural habitat. Unlike the center's typical satellite tags, which are usually posted publicly on their website, this Navy tag operates differently. 'This one is a little bit different, and so they'll provide us with updates, and then we'll share those with the public when it's appropriate,' Dr. Barron explained. entry.title: FHP seeks help finding driver who hit, killed man in Okeechobee County
entry.summary: The Florida Highway Patrol is asking for the public's assistance in locating a driver involved in a fatal hit-and-run crash that claimed the life of a pedestrian Monday night. The deadly incident occurred at 8:22 p.m. along US Highway 441 Southeast near Southeast 42nd Place in Okeechobee County. According to investigators, the victim was standing in the roadway in front of his residence when he was struck by a southbound vehicle. Pedestrian struck on US Highway 441 in Okeechobee County The driver of the unknown vehicle fled the scene immediately after the collision, continuing south on U.S. Highway 441 SE without stopping to render aid or report the crash. A witness reported hearing the impact and the sound of a vehicle speeding away from the scene, though they did not see the fleeing vehicle. Emergency responders took the pedestrian to HCA Florida Raulerson Hospital in Okeechobee County, where he later died from his injuries. The victim's identity has not been released pending notification of family members. Vehicle Description Investigators have recovered vehicle parts from the crash scene that indicate the suspect vehicle is likely a pickup truck manufactured between 2014 and 2026 either a Chevrolet Silverado or GMC Sierra. The suspect vehicle would be easily identifiable due to significant damage, including: Missing right-side mirror (entire assembly) Possible damage to the headlight Possible damage to the fog light Additional damage to the right side of the vehicle Investigation Ongoing The Florida Highway Patrol's investigation into the fatal crash remains active. Authorities are urging anyone with information about the incident or who may have seen a damaged pickup truck matching the description to come forward immediately. Anyone with information is asked to contact Cpl. Bradley Meer with the Florida Highway Patrol at (772) 467-3507 or by email at bradleymeer@flhsmv.gov . Information may also be provided anonymously through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers by calling 1-800-273-TIPS (8477). Tips provided through Crime Stoppers may be eligible for a cash reward. Hit-and-run crashes involving fatalities carry severe criminal penalties in Florida, including potential felony charges that could result in significant prison time for the driver responsible.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby - WPEC
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest - WPEC
entry.summary: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest    WPEC
entry.article_text: More than two years after his arrest, jury selection is underway in the trial former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Nick Mimms. Prospective jurors are being asked in court what they know about the case, if they've reached any conclusions about Mimms' guilt or innocence, if they can put aside any information they may have heard or read about the case and base their verdict solely on the evidence presented in the courtroom. Mimms, 53, was arrested in August 2024 and accused of bid tampering and official misconduct in connection with a city bidding process involving two vacant, city-owned lots in Fort Pierce’s Lincoln Park area. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the investigation began after the agency received a complaint alleging inappropriate conduct involving a request for proposals to develop the property. FDLE accused Mimms of using his position to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals secure a lease for the lots. Investigators said the nonprofit was formed by two city employees, including Mimms’ niece. Investigators also accused Mimms, who served as project manager for the request for proposals, of influencing the language and evaluation criteria used in the bidding process and sharing nonpublic information with the nonprofit before the bid became public. The property, located at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D, was intended to become a community center called The Root, with plans that included a library, classroom space and pop-up markets. The lease was later terminated in 2024 after Lincoln Park Young Professionals told the city it was no longer pursuing the project. Mimms had served as Fort Pierce city manager since 2015 after previously working as deputy city manager and project engineer for the city. The prospective jurors were told Monday the trial may take one to two weeks. Outside the courtroom Monday, Mimms had no comment. CBS12 News will continue following the case as the trial moves forward. This is a developing story.

entry.title: I-95 North in Martin County reopens after deadly crash involving sedan, box truck
entry.summary: A deadly crash Monday morning shut down lanes of Interstate 95 North in Martin County, with closures lasting over seven hours. The crash occurred at around 3:40 a.m. at mile marker 91, involving a Honda Civic and a Hino box truck. Deadly early-morning crash shuts down lanes of I-95 North in Martin County According to the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), both vehicles were traveling northbound when the Honda Civic collided with the rear of the box truck in the outside lane. The sedan lodged underneath the back of the tractor-trailer and engulfed in flames. Despite lifesaving efforts, the Honda driver was pronounced deceased on scene. The driver of the box truck was not injured in the crash. FHP has not identified the deceased driver. All northbound lanes of I-95 were closed until just before 11 a.m. Monday.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year - WPTV
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year    WPTV
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie pauses Flock program; 18 cameras set for removal Sept. 30    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Lucie officials said 18 Flock cameras installed in county and state rights-of-way are scheduled to be removed by the vendor by Sept. 30, as the city pauses its automated license plate reader program amid continued privacy concerns. The update came during public comment at a City Council meeting on Monday, where several residents urged council members to permanently remove the cameras and prohibit future permits for Flock and other automated vehicle-tracking systems. Casey Honeycutt called for a citywide ban on Flock cameras and similar systems, arguing they pose privacy and surveillance concerns. Lucie resident Jorge Borgess directly asked council members to remove the cameras and take further action. He asked the city to stop issuing permits for automated license plate readers and other vehicle-tracking systems in city-owned or city-controlled rights-of-way, and to pursue removal of existing cameras. Lucie police announced Sept. 1 that the department would pause the program and remove seven cameras. He told council he counted eight of 22 cameras still standing at locations he believed required state right-of-way review. Steven Grier also addressed the council, saying he has sued the city, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock in federal court. His lawsuit allegations were not discussed by the council during the meeting. See also: Sheriff’s office warns of renewed inappropriate activity at DJ Wilcox Preserve Later, Port St. Lucie resident James Reynolds joined the criticism, telling council members the city had previously achieved its public safety goals without Flock cameras. We need to make sure there’s punishments for misuse; we need to make sure that retention periods are addressed; our audit is complete, Bonna said. I know there have been local incidents of misuse, and so this isn’t something abstract. Bonna said he was not calling for all cameras to be taken down immediately. What I’m calling for is to pause the program, and when I say pause, I mean pause, and let’s get this policy right, so it protects both our liberties and safety, Bonna said. During the discussion, city officials said the police chief’s white paper calls for nine cameras in county rights-of-way and nine in state rights-of-way to be removed by the vendor. The city can’t take them down; the vendor needs to take them down, an unidentified city official said. Those 18 cameras will be taken down. An unidentified city staff member later confirmed the scheduled removal date. 30 that the cameras will be taken down, the staff member said. Lucie police had previously announced an operational pause on its Flock and Axon license plate reader systems after the Florida Department of Transportation revoked approvals for the technology in state highway rights of way. At that time, police said seven city cameras located in FDOT rights-of-way would be removed. The city’s pause limits use of the remaining systems to cases involving an immediate threat to life, including missing or endangered people, with authorization from Police Chief Leo Niemczyk . The discussion follows a broader debate in St. Earlier this month, county commissioners voted 3-2 to stop new permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers in county-controlled rights of way, review existing permits and issue removal notices where appropriate. The county action went beyond FDOT’s order, which applied only to state highway rights-of-way. The county vote did not apply to cameras on private property or devices mounted in law enforcement vehicles. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office would comply with the state directive while tightening internal rules for deputies’ use of the technology.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: More than two years after his arrest, jury selection is underway in the trial former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Nick Mimms. Prospective jurors are being asked in court what they know about the case, if they've reached any conclusions about Mimms' guilt or innocence, if they can put aside any information they may have heard or read about the case and base their verdict solely on the evidence presented in the courtroom. Mimms, 53, was arrested in August 2024 and accused of bid tampering and official misconduct in connection with a city bidding process involving two vacant, city-owned lots in Fort Pierce’s Lincoln Park area. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the investigation began after the agency received a complaint alleging inappropriate conduct involving a request for proposals to develop the property. FDLE accused Mimms of using his position to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals secure a lease for the lots. Investigators said the nonprofit was formed by two city employees, including Mimms’ niece. Investigators also accused Mimms, who served as project manager for the request for proposals, of influencing the language and evaluation criteria used in the bidding process and sharing nonpublic information with the nonprofit before the bid became public. The property, located at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D, was intended to become a community center called The Root, with plans that included a library, classroom space and pop-up markets. The lease was later terminated in 2024 after Lincoln Park Young Professionals told the city it was no longer pursuing the project. Mimms had served as Fort Pierce city manager since 2015 after previously working as deputy city manager and project engineer for the city. The prospective jurors were told Monday the trial may take one to two weeks. Outside the courtroom Monday, Mimms had no comment. CBS12 News will continue following the case as the trial moves forward. This is a developing story.

entry.title: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

"Our suspect was actually the 911 caller in this situation," said Port St. Lucie Police Department spokesperson Brittany McNally. McNally said Merritt admitted to stabbing his father with two different knives, which were later found in the kitchen sink. entry.title: Mayor rallies Westlake community to surprise Station 22 firefighters with a crew-sized table
entry.summary: WPTV reporter Christy Waite recently learned that Westlake firefighters at Station 22 were in need of a bigger table to fit all of their staff. On Tuesday, the station got a surprise months in the making a handmade table that will give them a place to finally sit down together for breakfast, lunch, dinner and even holiday meals. WATCH BELOW: Westlake firefighters receive new table Westlake surprises firefighters with a handmade table When Mayor J.P. O'Connor learned the fire station needed a bigger table to accommodate everyone, he jumped into action, rallying community members and sponsors to make it happen. 'It's from a community that loves you and wants you to get the nourishment on this table that you need to go out and do what you guys do to keep us safe. We hope it's more than just a table; it's a symbol of love from the community,' Connor said. For District Chief Jose Garcia, the gift goes far beyond furniture. 'It's more than just a table. For the fire organization, it means a lot more. The kitchen table is where we solve all the world's problems, we come together as a family, we break bread and enjoy coffee together,' Garcia said. Garcia said the table is central to life at the station. 'It's pretty much the central hub of station living. For the city of Westlake to recognize how important it is to us. We have great gratitude for that,' Garcia said. The table was built by hand by Westlake resident Jordan San Jose, who said the project was a meaningful one. 'It's an honor to build something with my hands that will be here for a long time, happy to help and be a part of the community,' San Jose said. The new table will bring camaraderie, a place to debrief, connect and build memories. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo go one-on-one during first day of Miami Heat training camp
entry.summary: The Miami Heat are on the court. The team held day one of training camp on Tuesday at Florida Atlantic University. Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo went one-on-one during camp, with the former best defensive player in the league challenging the most versatile defender the Heat has ever seen. WATCH BELOW: Bam, Giannis take the court as Heat training camp begins Miami Heat training camp underway at FAU Head coach Erik Spoelstra said he welcomes that competitive energy between the two. 'I want that competitive spirit when they are going at each other,' Spoelstra said. But Spoelstra said getting the two stars playing together is just as important as the individual competition. 'We also need to get them on the same page, playing together. I want to get those reps, in this preseason,' Spoelstra said. That includes reps on defense, where the Adebayo-Antetokounmpo pairing could create serious problems for opposing offenses. 'We noticed that the last three, two, three, four years that teams were scheming against Bam's defense. Just like you have to scheme against Giannis' defense. Now we have two guys that can do both things. Hopefully that will really help I'll make our defense more dynamic,' Spoelstra said. Spoelstra said having both players on the floor at the same time opens up more opportunities defensively. 'It'll allow them each to make more plays, defensive plays in the paint, blocks, deflections, stops,' Spoelstra said. Adebayo and Antetokounmpo both said they plan to push each other in practice to elevate the team's defense. 'We're a fast team, but not only are we fast, we're switchable, we talk, we communicate, everybody can guard their yard. And that's one through five and from that standpoint, I feel like we're going to be really good.' Adebayo said. 'Because the defense is mindset and effort and I feel like we have guys around the team that have that,' Antetokounmpo said. On the offensive end, players including Davion Mitchell, Pelle Larsson and Klay Thompson got in plenty of shots during practice. Spoelstra said this year the team is turning the page and starting something new. The Heat will continue to practice at Florida Atlantic University throughout the week before heading to Toronto to face the Raptors in a preseason game Saturday.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade. Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services. 'Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars,' said Mayor Shannon M. Martin. 'By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible.' The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low. The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.
entry.article_text: Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

entry.title: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route    WPEC
entry.article_text: A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest - WPEC
entry.summary: Former Fort Pierce city manager Nick Mimms heads to trial nearly 2 years after arrest    WPEC
entry.article_text: More than two years after his arrest, jury selection is underway in the trial former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Nick Mimms. Prospective jurors are being asked in court what they know about the case, if they've reached any conclusions about Mimms' guilt or innocence, if they can put aside any information they may have heard or read about the case and base their verdict solely on the evidence presented in the courtroom. Mimms, 53, was arrested in August 2024 and accused of bid tampering and official misconduct in connection with a city bidding process involving two vacant, city-owned lots in Fort Pierce’s Lincoln Park area. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, the investigation began after the agency received a complaint alleging inappropriate conduct involving a request for proposals to develop the property. FDLE accused Mimms of using his position to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals secure a lease for the lots. Investigators said the nonprofit was formed by two city employees, including Mimms’ niece. Investigators also accused Mimms, who served as project manager for the request for proposals, of influencing the language and evaluation criteria used in the bidding process and sharing nonpublic information with the nonprofit before the bid became public. The property, located at 1134 and 1138 Avenue D, was intended to become a community center called The Root, with plans that included a library, classroom space and pop-up markets. The lease was later terminated in 2024 after Lincoln Park Young Professionals told the city it was no longer pursuing the project. Mimms had served as Fort Pierce city manager since 2015 after previously working as deputy city manager and project engineer for the city. The prospective jurors were told Monday the trial may take one to two weeks. Outside the courtroom Monday, Mimms had no comment. CBS12 News will continue following the case as the trial moves forward. This is a developing story.

entry.title: Nick Mimms trial: Prosecutor says former Fort Pierce city manager 'got caught with his hand in the cookie jar'
entry.summary: The trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms entered its second day Tuesday with opening statements and witness testimony. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city manager Former Fort Pierce city manager faces day two of trial During opening statements, the State Attorney's Office said Mimms knowingly rigged the bidding process for two vacant parcels of land along Avenue D in favor of a local nonprofit that his niece was on the board of, and kept it from the public. 'The defendant Nicholas Mimms just got caught with his hand in the cookie jar,' Assistant State Prosecutor Jonathan Bridges said. Bridges pointed to a paper trail of city documents, email correspondence, phone records and witness testimony. 'He made sure that the public was not privy to the information he shared with Miss Scott and her group. In doing so, the defendant made sure that the city-owned land would ultimately be leased by LPYP and no one else,' Bridges said. LPYP stands for the Lincoln Park Young Professionals, the local nonprofit involved in the case. The defense countered that Mimms showed no favoritism, and that a $500,000 grant provided by the Alleghany Franciscan Ministries toward the development of the site in Lincoln Park did not involve the city. 'They started work on the project, and it failed, and that's the sad truth. But it wasn't by the fault of any one person. It certainly wasn't a deliberate act by anyone,' defense attorney Donald Murrell said. The first witness called by the state was Ben Masondo, a local real estate broker from the Doyen Company, who also submitted a bid on the two vacant lots. Masondo said he felt the city's decision to move forward with LPYP was unfair. 'You have one that has a city employee involved. I felt that the judging was misguided. At one point, I think I had said clearly one of these people was the Russian judge, just decided not to score me fairly, and I looked at what was around, and yes, I was upset. I thought that was snake. They snaked me,' Masondo said. The trial is expected to last at least a week. If found guilty, Mimms could face a second-degree felony for bid tampering that carries a maximum of 15 years in prison and up to a $10,000 fine. Official misconduct is a third-degree felony that carries a maximum of five years in prison and up to a $5,000 fine.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year
entry.summary: The Port St. Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1. The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade. WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going down Port St. Lucie lowers property tax rate for 11th straight year Since 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value. Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services. 'Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars,' said Mayor Shannon M. Martin. 'By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible.' The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners. The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low. The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

entry.title: FHP seeks help finding driver who hit, killed man in Okeechobee County
entry.summary: The Florida Highway Patrol is asking for the public's assistance in locating a driver involved in a fatal hit-and-run crash that claimed the life of a pedestrian Monday night. The deadly incident occurred at 8:22 p.m. along US Highway 441 Southeast near Southeast 42nd Place in Okeechobee County. According to investigators, the victim was standing in the roadway in front of his residence when he was struck by a southbound vehicle. FHP seeks help finding driver who hit, killed man The driver of the unknown vehicle fled the scene immediately after the collision, continuing south on U.S. Highway 441 SE without stopping to render aid or report the crash. A witness reported hearing the impact and the sound of a vehicle speeding away from the scene, though they did not see the fleeing vehicle. Emergency responders took the pedestrian to HCA Florida Raulerson Hospital in Okeechobee County, where he later died from his injuries. The victim's identity has not been released pending notification of family members. Vehicle Description Investigators have recovered vehicle parts from the crash scene that indicate the suspect vehicle is likely a pickup truck manufactured between 2014 and 2026 either a Chevrolet Silverado or GMC Sierra. The suspect vehicle would be easily identifiable due to significant damage, including: Missing right-side mirror (entire assembly) Possible damage to the headlight Possible damage to the fog light Additional damage to the right side of the vehicle Investigation Ongoing The Florida Highway Patrol's investigation into the fatal crash remains active. Authorities are urging anyone with information about the incident or who may have seen a damaged pickup truck matching the description to come forward immediately. Anyone with information is asked to contact Cpl. Bradley Meer with the Florida Highway Patrol at (772) 467-3507 or by email at bradleymeer@flhsmv.gov . Information may also be provided anonymously through Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers by calling 1-800-273-TIPS (8477). Tips provided through Crime Stoppers may be eligible for a cash reward. Hit-and-run crashes involving fatalities carry severe criminal penalties in Florida, including potential felony charges that could result in significant prison time for the driver responsible.

entry.title: Decision not to charge parent in Indiantown bus stop gun incident sparks heated community debate - WPTV
entry.summary: Decision not to charge parent in Indiantown bus stop gun incident sparks heated community debate    WPTV
entry.article_text: Outrage and frustration boiled over at a community meeting in Indiantown, as residents packed a room to demand answers from the Martin County Sheriff's Office after a parent who pulled a gun on two students at a bus stop was not charged with a crime.The tense Monday night meeting, led by the Martin County NAACP and the sheriff, centered on the sheriff's determination that the father acted in self-defense. However, many residents argued that the man should have been arrested for the separate crime of possessing a firearm at a school bus stop.WATCH BELOW: Indiantown divided over bus stop gun incident, no-charge decisionSheriff John Budensiek laid out his office's account of the incident, which occurred just over a week ago. He said it began with a student being bullied and struck by another student on a school bus. The victim's father went to the bus stop to report the bullying to the driver.The situation escalated, Budensiek said, when the alleged bully and a friend "pushed past the bus driver and tried to confront the dad.""He puts his hand up and backs up, backs up, says 'stay away, stay away,' and they don't," Budensiek explained. "In fact, they’re yelling that they’re going to whoop his hind end... He pulls out a gun and all of a sudden they’re backing up, because they don’t want to get shot."The sheriff defended the lack of charges against the father, citing the state's self-defense laws. "In the state of Florida, you’re allowed to defend yourself against someone coming after you," he said.But residents at the meeting were furious, arguing that the father was committing a misdemeanor by possessing a gun at a bus stop, which they believe should negate his "Stand Your Ground" defense."Stand Your Ground cannot come into play because at the time you were committing a crime by being at that bus stop with a gun," one resident yelled.The sheriff countered that the law does not provide a clear legal definition of what constitutes a "bus stop," making that specific charge unenforceable in this case. The father also declined to press battery charges against the two students.Jimmy Smith, President of the Martin County NAACP, said the meeting was intended to inform the community about the laws that guided the sheriff's decision. He urged residents who are unhappy with the outcome to channel their anger toward changing those laws."These kids need to be loved and also protected on all ends," Smith said after the meeting. "Thank God nobody went home in a casket."He said that while there was disagreement, everyone shared one sentiment: "We can agree that this should have never happened."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
