entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District's attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership.Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the hazing investigation.Watch report from HusseyNearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which was called to address what board members described as a major gap in district policy: who investigates complaints against the district's own leaders."Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said. "They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those positions include the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." Months before the incident came to light, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it."That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. "I came up on the labor side, I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting."This system is so broken," one attendee said."Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. entry.title: Fact check: Donalds ad claims Jolly's hurricane insurance plan would cost Florida families $1,000 per year
entry.summary: With less than five weeks until Election Day, a campaign ad from Republican Byron Donalds claims Democrat David Jolly's hurricane insurance proposal would cost Florida families $1,000 a year in what the ad calls a 'hurricane tax.' An examination of the ad and the study it cites tells a more complicated story. The Donalds ad's claims The ad opens by asking, 'How much will David Jolly's hurricane tax cost Florida?' and cites a Florida State University study to support its assertion that Jolly's plan would run Florida families $1,000 per year. 'A giant bail-out for big insurance. A giant rip-off for you,' the 30-second spot says. RELATED: More political, election news What Jolly is proposing Jolly wants to create what he calls a 'sovereign wealth fund' to absorb all windstorm coverage in Florida, while allowing private insurers to handle other types of policies. When I asked him at an event in Fort Lauderdale recently to explain the concept, Jolly pushed back on the 'hurricane tax' framing. 'Well, there's currently a thousand-dollar hurricane tax on the books that Byron Donalds wants to continue. My model would actually repeal it,' Jolly said. What's actually on the books Florida does not have a specific 'hurricane tax' on the books. Jolly is likely referring to the assessments that Citizens Property Insurance is required to levy on Floridians in order to remain solvent. Jolly's campaign claims that if private insurers don't have to worry about windstorm policies, premiums would drop 60 to 70 percent. I was not able to independently verify that math. 'A state sovereign wealth fund can absorb the risk of hurricane coverage if we sufficiently capitalize it,' Jolly said. What the cited FSU study actually says The Donalds ad cites a Florida State University study which I obtained via a public records request. It was commissioned by the policy research arm of the Florida Legislature and released in August. The 80-page report does not examine Jolly's specific proposal of a sovereign wealth fund. Instead, it looks into the feasibility of having Citizens Property Insurance bear all the risk for named windstorms, taking the burden off private insurers. entry.title: Race, then head home: Inside St. Lucie County’s P1 Motor Club - cw34.com
entry.summary: Race, then head home: Inside St. Lucie County’s P1 Motor Club    cw34.com
entry.article_text: The 650-acre development plans nearly 10 miles of driving surfaces, trackside homes and country club amenities. Membership currently starts at $192,000. P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month, offering an early taste of a community where owners will eventually be able to drive on a circuit and head home overlooking it. The 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road is taking shape on a former orange grove. Plans include multiple driving circuits, trackside homes, a motorsports business park and amenities ranging from a pool to walking trails. The easiest way to describe it that most people understand is think of a high-end golf club, but a racetrack, said Chris Duplessis, P1’s director of fun. So no golf balls, we’ve got fancy race cars instead. CBS12 News took a ride with Duplessis for a firsthand look at the three-mile track, which he said is about 85% complete. Remaining work includes finishing sections of guardrail while the newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on what visitors see today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals, he said. See also: Citadel CEO's historic $3 billion gift is bringing Carnegie Mellon to Miami Eventually, the property will have just under 10 miles of driving surfaces. A planned 4.5-mile circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself. Other plans include karting, rally and drifting areas. Duplessis said construction on the larger circuit and real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. P1 plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service. Homes with a view of the action For some members, P1 will be a place to spend the day. For others, it will become a home or weekend getaway. Duplessis said the club already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. The planned garage townhomes will combine ground-floor vehicle space with living areas upstairs. Each unit will overlook a track, he said. These are fully livable, garage on the ground level, beautiful living space upstairs, Duplessis said. Every unit is overlooking the track, so they all have track view as well as community view. P1 also plans trackside residences. Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, with many buyers expected to use them as second or third homes. Only members can purchase real estate. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues in addition. Duplessis quoted real estate at $1.4 million, purchased separately. Residents could begin moving in in about two years, he said. The full development is expected to take approximately five years to complete. A fleet of cars and coaching for beginners Members will not necessarily need to bring their own car to get behind the wheel. Duplessis said P1’s partnership with Mercedes will provide a fleet of vehicles for members to drive. He also described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences that would give nonmembers opportunities to use the track. While luxury cars are part of the appeal, Duplessis said the vehicles on the circuit could range from Mazda Miatas to Porsches, Ferraris and Mercedes models. Some members have racing experience. Others have never driven on a track. For beginners, P1 plans to provide instructors who teach driving fundamentals and track rules before building toward more advanced skills. We get them an instructor, an expert, teach them all the basics, all the rules of the road, let’s say, and then they start driving, Duplessis said. The circuit has no posted speed limit, but drivers will be expected to stay within their abilities. New drivers will work with coaches who control the pace as they learn. Members whose skills qualify them will also have opportunities to participate in club races. Beyond the racetrack The development’s plans include a clubhouse, pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes and walking trails. Duplessis said a rooftop bar at the clubhouse will offer views of the activity below. He said the team is also considering nature as it lays out the property, including pond locations intended to support bird life. An area with mature trees is planned for slower, technical off-road driving. The team is exploring water sports on the property’s lakes, though those activities are still being considered. P1 also plans space for motorsports-related businesses. Duplessis said the club intends to host community events where nonmembers can visit and watch, along with driving training for law enforcement. He said local workers and contractors are already involved in the project. For Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, the development is personal. He plans to make it his home. I will live right here, he said. It’ll be a big sense of community for all our members. Duplessis said P1 will bring jobs and use local contractors and businesses, noting a track he previously ran employed about 150 people; he did not provide a hiring estimate for P1. He expects little traffic impact, saying many homes will be used only occasionally and a busy day would draw about 100 members.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby - cw34.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. "To me, that is absolutely ludicrous. There's no way that that should happen in this community. So I'm very upset that that is in our neighborhood," said Gail Lucas, a neighbor. Lucas said she has seen three children at the house. She said she was saddened that police found drugs in the home where there were kids. It's just, oh, it gives me the creeps," Lucas said. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. "I'm glad that they did, you know, take care of that," Lucas said after she learned Francis has been arrested. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow - wpbf.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie removes 18 Flock cameras as privacy concerns grow    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: Florida's deadline to remove Flock cameras from highway rights-of-way is Wednesday, Sept. Lucie is also removing 18 cameras from city streets after pausing its program due to privacy concerns. Florida’s Department of Transportation mandated that local agencies remove Flock cameras from state highway rights-of-way by today. These cameras capture license plate information that law enforcement can use to investigate crimes. However, the state order does not apply to cameras on city streets or county roads, leaving local governments to set their own rules. Lucie, the city commission voted to have the vendor remove 18 cameras today after pausing its Flock program. During Monday’s city commission meeting, one resident said, "Mass surveillance is wrong and has a negative impact on those under that surveillance. We have become too comfortable with bleeding-edge technologies without proper research or testing." Critics have raised concerns about how the cameras store the data and who can access it. Flock, the company behind the cameras, said the agency using the system controls the data, not Flock. The company also said that data is deleted by default after 30 days and that every search is logged, including details about who conducted the search, why, and when. Another resident urged the city to take broader action, saying, "I'm asking you to remove the city's Flock cameras and take broader action in St. Lucie County has taken in its rights-of-way." While the state’s order applies only to cameras on state highways, Port St. Lucie is taking its own steps by removing the 18 cameras from city streets. The city’s decision reflects ongoing concerns about privacy and surveillance technology. entry.summary: Fort Pierce driver accused of fleeing police twice during targeted traffic enforcement    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A driver in Fort Pierce is accused of fleeing from police officers twice during a targeted traffic enforcement initiative, according to the Fort Pierce Police Department . 25, at around 4:45 p.m., during the traffic enforcement initiative taking place in the Okeechobee Road and Jenkins Road area, officers conducted a traffic stop on a blue Volkswagen Jetta. During the stop, they identified that the driver Leon Kevin Gentle-Coaxum, 21 was driving with a suspended license. Next, as the officer approached the vehicle, the Gentle-Coaxum suddenly fled the traffic stop, according to FPPD. He then was seen driving recklessly, speeding into oncoming traffic and around stopped vehicles using the grass shoulder. After finding the vehicle stopped in traffic at South 25th Street and Edwards Road, officers attempted another traffic stop and ordered Gentle-Coaxum out of the car. Instead, he refused once again and attempted to flee a second time by ramming a vehicle in front of him. See also: Unable to paddle against strong current, pair calls for help and is rescued in river canoe In an effort to stop the car, an officer broke Gentle-Coaxum’s driver’s side window. He then exited through the passenger side and took off on foot. FPPD says a nearby citizen intervened and tackled Gentle-Coaxum, allowing officers to take him into custody. Gentle-Coaxum is charged with fleeing and alluding with property damages, hit and run with property damages, operating a vehicle without a valid license and resisting without violence.

entry.title: Florida minimum wage rises to $15/hour in final scheduled increase, but workers say it's still not enough
entry.summary: Florida's minimum wage increased on Sept. 30 to $15 an hour. This is the fourth and last of the annual scheduled hikes from a 2020 approved referendum. The minimum wage for tipped workers also rose to $11.98. WATCH BELOW: Florida minimum wage hits $15/hour Minimum Wage Rises in Florida 'Minimum wage is going up but so is everything going up,' a young man named Neff told me Wednesday on Clematis Street. 'You have to have another hustle, or another job so that way you can create more revenue and income for your family; $15 an hour is not enough.' Starting in 2027, the state minimum wage will be adjusted for inflation annually. In South Florida, where the cost of living is high, a $25-an-hour wage is considered 'livable,' according to a Massachusetts Institute of Technology report. The higher wage can also mean more pressure on small businesses. 'I have to pass that cost on to the consumer; I cannot absorb a 7% increase in labor,' John Ries, owner of Hot Pie Pizza in West Palm Beach, said. Ries says that, as a policy, he pays his employees above the minimum wage, and he admits inflation on all aspects of his business make it tough to keep prices down.

entry.title: Palm Beach County school superintendent proposes salary freeze amid 'severe financial challenges'
entry.summary: The School District of Palm Beach County is proposing a district-wide salary freeze as it faces what Superintendent Mike Burke described as 'severe financial challenges,' including a $15 million budget shortfall and a $60 million loss in state revenue tied to declining enrollment. In messages sent to teachers and staff, Burke warned that the district's financial outlook could make salary increases difficult this year as negotiations continue with employee unions. WATCH BELOW: 'Severe financial challenges': School superintendent proposes salary freeze Superintendent proposes salary freeze amid 'severe financial challenges' 'Our District is navigating a severe revenue shortfall due to minimal state funding and declining student enrollment,' Burke wrote. 'With an even smaller operating budget than last year, funding salary increases is exceptionally difficult this year.' The district lost nearly 6,000 students this school year, according to Burke, resulting in an immediate $60 million reduction in state funding because Florida funds school districts largely on a per-student basis. RELATED: School District confirms layoffs have started as more cuts loom | School District cuts 244 positions following enrollment decline To help close the gap, Burke said the district eliminated 1,200 positions and implemented a hiring freeze. 'We are disappointed to have had to lay off some members of our team and still face a projected $15 million budget shortfall for the current year,' he wrote. The number of position cuts cited in the letter is nearly 900 more than reductions previously disclosed to WPTV, as we pushed for answers over the last several months. WPTV is working to learn more about those positions and how the district arrived at that figure. Given the budget outlook, Burke said district leaders have recommended a salary freeze. 'Given our existing $15 million budget shortfall, the District made the difficult recommendation of a salary freeze across all positions for the current school year,' Burke wrote. He added that approving raises while revenues continue to decline 'would require additional layoffs and drastic cuts to student services.' However, WPTV has been tracking the budget and learned in August that negotiations are already underway and that the proposed freeze is not final. Palm Beach County Classroom Teachers Association President Gordan Longhofer told WPTV the district's proposal is simply a suggestion from the superintendent as negotiations continue

"With an even smaller operating budget than last year, funding salary increases is exceptionally difficult this year."The district lost nearly 6,000 students this school year, according to Burke, resulting in an immediate $60 million reduction in state funding because Florida funds school districts largely on a per-student basis.RELATED: School District confirms layoffs have started as more cuts loom | School District cuts 244 positions following enrollment declineTo help close the gap, Burke said the district eliminated 1,200 positions and implemented a hiring freeze."We are disappointed to have had to lay off some members of our team and still face a projected $15 million budget shortfall for the current year," he wrote.The number of position cuts cited in the letter is nearly 900 more than reductions previously disclosed to WPTV, as we pushed for answers over the last several months. WPTV is working to learn more about those positions and how the district arrived at that figure. Given the budget outlook, Burke said district leaders have recommended a salary freeze."Given our existing $15 million budget shortfall, the District made the difficult recommendation of a salary freeze across all positions for the current school year," Burke wrote.He added that approving raises while revenues continue to decline "would require additional layoffs and drastic cuts to student services."However, WPTV has been tracking the budget and learned in August that negotiations are already underway and that the proposed freeze is not final. Palm Beach County Classroom Teachers Association President Gordan Longhofer told WPTV the district's proposal is simply a suggestion from the superintendent as negotiations continue between the district and the union.When asked whether raises were completely off the table, Longhofer responded, "no.""Offering a zero percent increase, that's really hard for teachers to accept with the track record we have for student success here in Palm Beach County," Longhofer said.Longhofer said negotiations are ongoing but believes long-term solutions must come from state leaders."Absolutely we're going to make the biggest change that way," he said. "And that requires a concerted effort on the part of district leaders, on school board members, building level principals, worksite leaders and teachers themselves standing in the arena with lawmakers to do what is right by the citizens in Florida."Despite the proposed freeze, Burke said a separate raise approved this summer for veteran educators remains on track.Under an agreement reached with the Classroom Teachers Association, qualifying instructional employees with at least 10 years of Florida public school experience will receive a 2.187% recurring increase to their base salary. The district said it also made additional budget cuts to extend the increase to approximately 1,600 teachers who fall outside the state's specific definition of a classroom teacher."While I am glad we secured this for our veteran educators, I'm disappointed the state excluded teachers with fewer than 10 years of experience from these dedicated funds," Burke wrote.Burke stressed that a salary freeze this year does not necessarily mean educators will go without raises in the future."A salary freeze does not mean teachers should expect to go without raises in future years," Burke wrote. "However, we must first address this current situation so that we can plan for raises in future years."The superintendent also pointed to the district's upcoming "1 Mill for Schools" referendum, which will appear on the November ballot. The district says the measure provides an average annual supplement of $8,000 for teachers and helps fund 900 teaching positions.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart - cw34.com
entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

WATCH BELOW: Fort Pierce city clerk takes the stand in Nick Mimms trial Fort Pierce city clerk takes the stand in Nick Mimms trial The jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire district attorney resigns amid hazing fallout; chief faces no-confidence vote
entry.summary: The St. Lucie County Fire District's attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership. Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the hazing investigation. WATCH BELOW: St. Lucie County fire district attorney resigns amid hazing fallout St. Lucie County fire district attorney resigns amid hazing fallout Nearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which was called to address what board members described as a major gap in district policy: who investigates complaints against the district's own leaders. 'Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves,' St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said. 'They being those positions have essentially been able to investigate themselves.' Those positions include the fire chief, assistant fire chief and district attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin were fired as a result. 'It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,' Hutchinson said. 'We're all still friends,' Boudrias said. 'Us and the victims, there was no ill intent.' Months before the incident came to light, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it. 'That's not a good process,' Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee. 'It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district,' Fowler said. 'So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message.' Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting."This system is so broken," one attendee said."Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. There is no word yet on when results will be released.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.summary: Martin County sheriff investigates toddler death in pond    WPBF
entry.article_text: The Martin County Medical examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy an accidental drowning. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County Sheriff John Budenseik said the child's parents called 911. "We received one of the most heart wrenching 911 calls you can get," Budenseik said. According to investigators, Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in the area of Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive in Port Salerno and was found unresponsive in a pond on his family’s property in Port Salerno. The toddler was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he went missing for a short time. According to investigators, the child slipped out of sight for a short time. When Pablo’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and ultimately found him in the pond. "At some point there had been a fence around the pond, but it had been trampled down or broke down over time, so it wasn't really a functional fence,' Budensiek said. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, but despite lifesaving efforts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said. Charlene Lyons is the President and CEO for the YMCA Treasure Coast. She said she was devastated when she heard the news, "I started at the Y as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me,' Lyons said She wants the public to know they can contact the Y for information about swimming lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time. For more information about swimming lessons, log on to the YMCA Treasure Coast website posted here. entry.title: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart - WPEC
entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    WPEC
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

entry.title: Toddler drowns in pond near family home in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Toddler drowns in pond near family home in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo. According to the sheriff's office, the boy was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and started searching. They found him in a pond on the property. Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two year old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. He said investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. The district has declined further comment while the contractual proceedings are ongoing. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

entry.title: ‘Akeem should be remembered as a hero’: WPB police reveal minister drove passenger to safety after being shot
entry.summary: New details from the West Palm Beach Police Department reveal that Minister Akeem Moores final act was one of heroism, as he drove his passenger to the safety of a fire station moments after being fatally shot. WATCH: Police Call killed WPB Minister Akeem Moore a Hero Police Call Slain WPB Minister Akeem Moore a Hero At a news conference, Police Chief Tony Araujo detailed the investigation into the 31-year-olds murder, painting a picture of a selfless man whose courage never wavered. 'Akeem should be remembered as a hero,' Araujo stated. A Selfless and Courageous Final Act According to police, Moore and a passenger were in a parked car on the 500 block of Ontario Place just after midnight Sunday when they were approached by 38-year-old Hugh Earp Milner Jr. The passenger knew and recognized Hugh and immediately believed he was mistaking them for another person, Araujo said. The situation escalated quickly. Hugh pulled a handgun from his waistband and pointed it at the occupants, the chief explained. After shots were fired, Moore, though mortally wounded, focused on saving his passenger. 'Even after being shot, he acted selflessly and courageously, driving his passenger to safety at a nearby fire station,' Araujo said. Moore later died from his injuries at a local hospital. Technology's Role in a Swift Arrest Chief Araujo also revealed how technology was critical in tracking down the suspect. He said Milner, who is homeless, fled the scene in a vehicle. Flock license plate readers helped investigators track the car as it traveled south into Broward County. This real-time intelligence allowed the Broward Sheriffs Office to quickly locate and stop the car, Araujo said. Milner was taken into custody and remains in Broward County, awaiting transfer to Palm Beach County to face charges of first-degree murder and attempted first-degree murder. As the case progresses, Moore's family continues to process their loss while searching for closure. 'Whatever justice is, truth, answers understanding why this happened to such an innocent person,' said Malik Brown, Moore's cousin. Anyone with information about the case is asked to contact the West Palm Beach Police Department or Palm Beach County Crime Stoppers at 1-800-458-TIPS. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

entry.title: Fort Pierce city clerk testifies about meetings in former city manager Nick Mimms corruption trial - WFLX
entry.summary: Fort Pierce city clerk testifies about meetings in former city manager Nick Mimms corruption trial    WFLX
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. The jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization’s board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater. Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. “Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. “Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid. WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city manager Under cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms’ niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time. “You knew they were city employees,” Murrell said. “And it bothered you that they were doing this?” Murrell said. “I thought it was a little odd,” Cox said. “You didn’t raise any objections,” Murrell said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney’s presence at the meetings. “He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?” Murrell said. “He didn’t raise any objections or concerns, did he?” Murrell said. “Not at the meeting,” Cox said. Not that I know of,” Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

"They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those positions include the fire chief, assistant fire chief and district attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it."That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. entry.article_text: The Martin County Medical examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy an accidental drowning. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County Sheriff John Budenseik said the child's parents called 911. "We received one of the most heart wrenching 911 calls you can get," Budenseik said. According to investigators, Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in the area of Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive in Port Salerno and was found unresponsive in a pond on his family’s property in Port Salerno. The toddler was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he went missing for a short time. According to investigators, the child slipped out of sight for a short time. When Pablo’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and ultimately found him in the pond. "At some point there had been a fence around the pond, but it had been trampled down or broke down over time, so it wasn't really a functional fence,' Budensiek said. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, but despite lifesaving efforts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said. Charlene Lyons is the President and CEO for the YMCA Treasure Coast. She said she was devastated when she heard the news, "I started at the Y as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me,' Lyons said She wants the public to know they can contact the Y for information about swimming lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. entry.title: Toddler drowns in pond near family home in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Toddler drowns in pond near family home in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo. According to the sheriff's office, the boy was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and started searching. They found him in a pond on the property. Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two year old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. He said investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said.

entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    WPEC
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

entry.title: St. Lucie County fire district attorney resigns amid hazing fallout; chief faces no-confidence vote - WFLX
entry.summary: St. Lucie County fire district attorney resigns amid hazing fallout; chief faces no-confidence vote    WFLX
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District’s attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership. Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the hazing investigation. Nearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which was called to address what board members described as a major gap in district policy: who investigates complaints against the district’s own leaders. “Since this district’s inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves,” St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said. “They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves.” Those positions include the Fire Chief, Assistant Fire Chief, and District Attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result. “It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun,” Hutchinson said. “We’re all still friends,” Boudrias said. “Us and the victims, there was no ill intent.” Months before the incident came to light, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it. “That’s not a good process,” Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee. “It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district,” Fowler said. “So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that’s a pretty impactful message.” Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: “I’m glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue,” adding he “welcomes any investigation from any agency.” Per Sabol’s resignation, Lee said it’s a “sad day.” “She’s been a tremendous attorney for the district,” Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn’t have much to say until it’s over with “We’ll see what the men and women decide,” Lee told Hussey. “I came up on the labor side, I’ve always fought for our men and women on the line.” Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday’s meeting. “This system is so broken,” one attendee said. They want action,” said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins. As the union’s legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, “I think we might actually,” adding, “The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I’m going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What’s the process?” Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. There is no word yet on when results will be released. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: 'Ready to answer the call': Jupiter Fire Rescue officially in service, marking historic transition
entry.summary: The new Jupiter Fire Rescue Department is officially in service, taking over all fire and emergency response duties for the town as of 12 a.m. on Oct. 1. The historic transition from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue was marked by a ceremony where Fire Chief Darrel Donatto made the first official radio call, declaring the new agency 'in service and ready to answer the call.' The launch is the culmination of a months-long journey, closely followed by WPTV, from the initial swearing-in of firefighters to the traditional 'push-in' ceremony for the new fire engines. WATCH: Jupiter's new fire department officially launch at midnight. Jupiter Fire Rescue Department now in serviceA New Era of Service At a ceremony at the Jupiter fire station to mark the official start of operations, Chief Donatto addressed firefighters and the community, acknowledging the moment's significance. 'Jupiter Fire Rescue will assume official responsibility for providing fire and emergency services to this community,' Donatto said. 'We gather here to recognize those who came before us and to reflect on the responsibility that we now inherit and to reaffirm the mission and principles that will guide this department from its very first call.' 'Ready to Answer the Call' Just after midnight, the chief's voice came over the radio, making the transition official and signaling to dispatchers and surrounding agencies that the new department was operational. 'Jupiter Chief, thank you to everyone. We look forward to serving together. Jupiter Fire Rescue is in service and ready to answer the call,' Donatto announced. For residents, dialing 911 for an emergency will not change. However, calls will now be dispatched to the new municipal department, and a Jupiter Fire Rescue engine and crew will respond. The move gives the Town of Jupiter direct control over its emergency services, staffing, and equipment for the first time in decades. entry.title: Jupiter Fire Rescue Department now in service
entry.summary: The Town of Jupiter officially launched its own fire rescue department at 12:01 a.m. Thursday, marking a historic milestone for the community's emergency services. The Jupiter Fire Rescue Department (JFRD) has assumed full responsibility for fire suppression and emergency medical services throughout the town, operating from three strategically located stations. The new department represents the culmination of more than three years of intensive planning and preparation to build a municipal fire rescue operation from scratch. WATCH: WPTV speaks to Jupiter Fire Rescue Department minutes after official launch Jupiter Fire Rescue Department now in service JFRD operates from Station 10 at 500 N. U.S. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park, Temporary Station 11 at Abacoa Community Park, and Station 12 at 2197 W. Indiantown Road adjacent to Cinquez Park. The department employs 94 operational personnel, maintaining a minimum of 23 firefighters on duty during each shift to ensure round-the-clock coverage. Beyond emergency response, the town has also taken over fire prevention and inspection services through JFRD's Fire Prevention Division. This includes conducting fire inspections, reviewing building plans, and implementing other fire safety measures throughout Jupiter. Just before midnight, JFRD personnel gathered simultaneously at all three stations for ceremonial flag raisings and bell ceremonies. The traditional bell ceremony honored previous emergency responders while symbolically marking the beginning of JFRD's service to the community. Fire Chief Darrel Donatto officially placed the department in service after reading the department's mission statement and core values. JFRD operates under the mission statement 'Your Life, Our Mission.' Jupiter residents calling 911 for fire or medical emergencies will now be served exclusively by Jupiter Fire Rescue Department personnel.

entry.title: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart - cw34.com
entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

entry.title: Okeechobee family says 14-year-old daughter jumped from school bus to escape bullies, later attempted suicide
entry.summary: An Okeechobee family is demanding accountability from the school district after they say their 14-year-old daughter, in a desperate attempt to escape relentless bullying, jumped from a school bus window. The family says that after the girl returned home, she attempted to take her own life and was hospitalized for two days in the ICU. This family is now sharing their daughter's harrowing story to raise awareness and push for systemic changes to how bullying is handled. Their public plea and a planned protest aim to ensure that no other child has to endure what they say their daughter has gone through. A desperate escape captured on video The family of 14-year-old Estrella Ventura Meras, a seventh-grader at the Okeechobee Achievement Academy, says her bubbly personality has faded over the last month due to what they describe as escalating bullying by other girls at her school. The situation came to a head in an incident captured in a viral social media video, which WPTV is not showing. The video shows Estrella jumping from the bus window in the school parking lot and running away. 'She just feared for her life,' said Vanessa Sanchez, a family member. 'She didn't trust the bus driver to do anything. She didn't trust going out the front or back door, so she jumped out the bus window.' 'I'm tired of this' What the video doesn't show is what happened next. The family says when Estrella arrived home, she took a handful of medication and left a note saying, 'I'm tired of this,' in a suicide attempt. Her family found her in time to get her life-saving medical help. She is now recovering in a different hospital. 'Her mental state over the past month, has been degraded,' Sanchez said. A call for accountability The Okeechobee County School District released a statement acknowledging the incident, saying in part, 'Every student deserves to feel safe, and we take reports of bullying seriously.' The district confirmed it is investigating but stated that federal law limits its ability to comment on individual students. Estrella's family says this was not the first time they reported the bullying to the school and that they will not be sending her back. They are now focused on demanding change. entry.title: 'We're tired': Delray Beach residents confront consultant over cemetery failures, resold burial plots
entry.summary: Dozens of frustrated Delray Beach residents confronted a city-hired consultant at a heated community meeting Thursday night, demanding solutions for systemic failures at the Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery, including cases where burial plots were allegedly resold. The emotional meeting was a culmination of months of resident complaints and WPTV investigations into poor conditions, maintenance issues and significant record-keeping errors. The anger and frustration voiced by families underscore the deep personal impact of the cemetery's problems, which have left some unable to locate their loved ones' graves and others, like one woman who spoke to WPTV, discovering the plot she bought 18 years ago was sold to someone else. The city has now tasked an outside firm with creating a plan for immediate and long-term fixes. 'Fix what's broken right now' One by one, residents shared painful and personal stories with Stephen Kuehne of Kuehne Cemetery Consulting. I got six family members that had to be cremated because they couldnt be buried out there, resident Andre Andrews said passionately. Were tired! RELATED: Delray Beach woman searches for missing grandparents' graves Delray Beach woman searches for grandparents' graves at neglected cemetery Nicole Ivy described the anguish of many families. We have other people who cant find their loved ones out there, she said. Those are our ancestors, and we want to preserve and protect them. The community's demands were clear: a comprehensive audit of all records, competent on-site staff, a citizen oversight board, and for the city to purchase more land for expansion. Get something done, besides just saying Im gonna look into it, resident Stanley George said. You need to get these people some solutions. A resold final resting place The record-keeping failures are not abstract problems. For Sandra Owens, the issue is painfully specific. She first shared her story with WPTV's Zitlali Solache at a 'Let's Hear It' community meet-up in July. In 2006, a year after her parents were buried, Owens purchased the plot next to them. But during a visit in 2024, she found a stranger buried in her spot. 'I went to visit my parents' burial site, and lo and behold, there's some guy buried with the whole plot and everything,' Owens said.
