entry.title: Toddler drowns in pond near family home in Martin County - WPEC
entry.summary: Toddler drowns in pond near family home in Martin County    WPEC
entry.article_text: A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, who is remembered by loved ones for his bright smile and joyful spirit. Investigators say Pablo was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and began searching. They later found him in a pond on the property Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two-year-old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. One relative, Virginia Maldonado, said she hopes people remember Pablo by his smile and keep the family in their prayers. Others told CBS12 News Pablo was deeply loved by a large extended family spanning beyond Florida. According to the sheriff, investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said. A GoFundMe has been established to help Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo's family with expenses following his tragic death. Those who would like to support the family can donate here .

entry.title: ‘Akeem should be remembered as a hero’: WPB police reveal minister drove passenger to safety after being shot
entry.summary: New details from the West Palm Beach Police Department reveal that Minister Akeem Moores final act was one of heroism, as he drove his passenger to the safety of a fire station moments after being fatally shot. WATCH: Police Call killed WPB Minister Akeem Moore a Hero Police Call Slain WPB Minister Akeem Moore a Hero At a news conference , Police Chief Tony Araujo detailed the investigation into the 31-year-olds murder, painting a picture of a selfless man whose courage never wavered. 'Akeem should be remembered as a hero,' Araujo stated. A Selfless and Courageous Final Act According to police, Moore and a passenger were in a parked car on the 500 block of Ontario Place just after midnight Sunday when they were approached by 38-year-old Hugh Earp Milner Jr. The passenger knew and recognized Hugh and immediately believed he was mistaking them for another person, Araujo said. The situation escalated quickly. Hugh pulled a handgun from his waistband and pointed it at the occupants, the chief explained. After shots were fired, Moore, though mortally wounded, focused on saving his passenger. 'Even after being shot, he acted selflessly and courageously, driving his passenger to safety at a nearby fire station,' Araujo said. Moore later died from his injuries at a local hospital. Technology's Role in a Swift Arrest Araujo also revealed how technology was critical in tracking down the suspect. He said Milner, who is homeless, fled the scene in a vehicle. Flock license plate readers helped investigators track the car as it traveled south into Broward County. This real-time intelligence allowed the Broward Sheriffs Office to quickly locate and stop the car, Araujo said. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

Prosecutors told jurors they would present emails, witness testimony, and city documents to support their case. They alleged Mimms used his position to influence the bidding process for the development of city-owned properties. Mimms carefully, skillfully steered the bid for the development of this property so that it would end up in the hands of two city employees. And one of those employees was Mr. Mimms' niece," Bridges said. "The state puts a lot of emphasis on the fact that she is my client's niece, and she is, but she can fairly be called a distant niece if that's at all possible," Murrell said. The defense argued that Mimms did not conspire to commit the crime. "If you follow the law, you follow the facts, and we're comfortable at the end of this case you will find that Mr. Mimms is not guilty," Murrell said. entry.article_text: The Martin County Medical examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy an accidental drowning. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County Sheriff John Budenseik said the child's parents called 911. "We received one of the most heart wrenching 911 calls you can get," Budenseik said. According to investigators, Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in the area of Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive in Port Salerno and was found unresponsive in a pond on his family’s property in Port Salerno. The toddler was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he went missing for a short time. According to investigators, the child slipped out of sight for a short time. When Pablo’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and ultimately found him in the pond. "At some point there had been a fence around the pond, but it had been trampled down or broke down over time, so it wasn't really a functional fence,' Budensiek said. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, but despite lifesaving efforts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said. Charlene Lyons is the President and CEO for the YMCA Treasure Coast. She said she was devastated when she heard the news, "I started at the 'Y' as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me,' Lyons said She wants the public to know they can contact the YMCA for information about swim lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time. For more information about swim lessons, log on to the YMCA Treasure Coast website posted here. entry.title: As Buc-ee's nears construction, development interest builds in northern St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: As Buc-ee's nears construction, development interest builds in northern St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

entry.article_text: A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    WPEC
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

entry.article_text: Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

entry.article_text: Lucie City Council unanimously approved a reduction in the city's property tax rate for the 11th consecutive year, lowering the millage rate from 4.9750 to 4.8750 for the fiscal year beginning Oct. 1.The decision, made during the formal adoption of the city's $971.6 million budget on Monday, continues a trend of tax relief that officials said has saved the average homeowner nearly $2,000 over the past decade.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie property tax rate going downSince 2016, Port St. Lucie has reduced its millage rate by 25%, giving the city the third-lowest municipal tax rate among Florida's 20 largest cities. The millage rate represents the amount of tax charged per $1,000 of taxable property value.Officials said the tax cuts come despite the city's rapid population growth. More than 60,000 new residents have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, requiring substantial investments in infrastructure including roads, drainage systems, utilities and public safety services."Our goal is to provide the services our residents value most while being good stewards of taxpayer dollars," said Mayor Shannon M. "By taking a measured approach to lowering property tax rates, we have been able to continue meeting the needs of our growing community while remaining fiscally responsible."The city's ability to maintain services while reducing taxes reflects what officials describe as smart financial planning designed to support the rapidly expanding community without burdening existing property owners.The fiscal year 2026-27 budget totals $971.6 million across the city's operating and capital funds, supporting services for a population that has grown substantially in recent years while maintaining the city's commitment to keeping property tax rates low.The new millage rate takes effect Thursday.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

entry.title: Jupiter Fire Rescue Department now in service
entry.summary: The Town of Jupiter officially launched its own fire rescue department at 12:01 a.m. Thursday, marking a historic milestone for the community's emergency services. JFRD Day 1 The Jupiter Fire Rescue Department (JFRD) has assumed full responsibility for fire suppression and emergency medical services throughout the town, operating from three strategically located stations. The new department represents the culmination of more than three years of intensive planning and preparation to build a municipal fire rescue operation from scratch. WATCH: WPTV speaks to Jupiter Fire Rescue Department minutes after official launch Jupiter Fire Rescue Department now in service JFRD operates from Station 10 at 500 N. U.S. Highway 1 near Burt Reynolds Park, Temporary Station 11 at Abacoa Community Park, and Station 12 at 2197 W. Indiantown Road adjacent to Cinquez Park. The department employs 94 operational personnel, maintaining a minimum of 23 firefighters on duty during each shift to ensure round-the-clock coverage. Beyond emergency response, the town has also taken over fire prevention and inspection services through JFRD's Fire Prevention Division. This includes conducting fire inspections, reviewing building plans, and implementing other fire safety measures throughout Jupiter. Just before midnight, JFRD personnel gathered simultaneously at all three stations for ceremonial flag raisings and bell ceremonies. The traditional bell ceremony honored previous emergency responders while symbolically marking the beginning of JFRD's service to the community. Fire Chief Darrel Donatto officially placed the department in service after reading the department's mission statement and core values. We are tightly aligned with Palm Beach Gardens Fire Rescue,' Donatto said. 'Our two cities operate as one fire department with nine stations. Thats a big department and were ready. JFRD operates under the mission statement 'Your Life, Our Mission.' Jupiter residents calling 911 for fire or medical emergencies will now be served exclusively by Jupiter Fire Rescue Department personnel.

entry.article_text: A 23-month-old boy died Tuesday evening after he was found in a pond on his family's property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office . Deputies identified the child as Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo, who is remembered by loved ones for his bright smile and joyful spirit. Investigators say Pablo was outside with family members in the yard of a home along Darling Street in Port Salerno shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday when he went out of sight. His mother and aunt realized he was missing and began searching. They later found him in a pond on the property Sheriff John Budensiek said the father was mowing the yard while the mother and her sister played with other children. Budensiek said there had been a fence around the pond at one point, but it had broken down over time and was no longer working. "It's a pond where if you walk in two feet, it drops off. And if you don't know how to swim, you're going to be in trouble," Budensiek said. "And in this case, sadly, our two-year-old did not know how to swim." Family members took the child to Cleveland Clinic South Hospital. The sheriff's office said he was pronounced dead in the emergency room despite lifesaving efforts. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Family members told investigators the boy was out of sight for no more than 10 minutes, according to the sheriff's office. MCSO criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene and are reviewing the circumstances of the child's death. Budensiek said Wednesday that the medical examiner ruled the death an accidental drowning after an autopsy. "From all indications, everything that we've got through our investigation, this is a tragic accident," Budensiek said. One relative, Virginia Maldonado, said she hopes people remember Pablo by his smile and keep the family in their prayers. Others told CBS12 News Pablo was deeply loved by a large extended family spanning beyond Florida. According to the sheriff, investigators found no signs that the parents were reckless or inattentive. "Parents get distracted, I know that. So no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning," Budensiek said. Budensiek encouraged parents to get young children into swim lessons and said the YMCA offers free classes for children as young as 2. Mindy York, president and co-founder of Baby Otter Swim School, said supervision is the most important way to prevent drownings. She also recommended door alarms, locked pool gates, and CPR training for parents. She said teaching children to swim is just as important. "We want to make sure that a child knows what to do if they fall into a body of water. Teach your children how to swim. It's like here in Florida, right? It's the leading cause of death in children under the age of five. With this death, now we're at 99," York said. She said children are never too young to start swim lessons. "I'm telling you, they absorb everything. So, we start at nine months, and we. We go all the way up to adults. So they're not too young to learn anything. They understand everything you say. And with a proper technique and speaking to them, they get it," York said. A GoFundMe has been established to help Pablo Mendoza-Arroyo's family with expenses following his tragic death. entry.title: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie man arrested after police say cocaine, meth and gun found in home with baby    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man was charged after police said a search of his home found suspected cocaine , methamphetamine, marijuana, stolen identification documents, cash, a revolver and ammunition. Lucie police SWAT officers served a search warrant about 5:30 a.m. 22 at 406 SW Fields Ave., where Bruce Alexander Francis, 30, and five other people exited the home, according to arrest reports. Francis told detectives that any drugs in the home belonged to him, but declined to provide further information, police said. He also denied having a phone, though investigators said they found the cellphone allegedly used in a prior cocaine transaction. A separate arrest affidavit said police used a confidential informant earlier in September to buy about 3.5 grams of cocaine from Francis at the home. The substance later tested presumptively positive for cocaine and weighed about 4 grams, the report said. Francis was also charged with selling cocaine and using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony in that case. A woman told police she shared the home’s master bedroom with Francis and a baby. She said Francis stayed home with the children during the day and that she did not know what he did for work, according to the report. "To me, that is absolutely ludicrous. There's no way that that should happen in this community. So I'm very upset that that is in our neighborhood," said Gail Lucas, a neighbor. Lucas said she has seen three children at the house. She said she was saddened that police found drugs in the home where there were kids. It's just, oh, it gives me the creeps," Lucas said. Detectives said they found suspected cocaine in the master bedroom and bathroom, including bags in and around a toilet. SWAT officers reported seeing Francis run from the bedroom to the bathroom and throw something before closing the door, the affidavit said. Police also reported finding a Fanta bottle containing a green liquid in the refrigerator that tested presumptively positive for methamphetamine. The liquid weighed about 180.5 grams, according to the report. The search also turned up $2,560 in cash, a .22-caliber revolver, .22-caliber and 9mm ammunition, scales, plastic baggies, suspected marijuana and THC products, police said. See also: Florida counties declare local emergencies as dengue cases rise In the master bedroom closet and elsewhere in the home, police said they found driver’s licenses, Social Security cards, debit cards and credit cards belonging to several other people. The report identifies documents belonging to people in Texas and Florida. Francis was charged with trafficking in methamphetamine, possession of cocaine with intent to sell, marijuana possession, possession of drug equipment, three counts of possessing another person’s identification without consent, evidence tampering and two counts of possession of a weapon or ammunition by a convicted felon. He was also charged in the earlier alleged cocaine sale investigation. "I'm glad that they did, you know, take care of that," Lucas said after she learned Francis has been arrested. Police said Francis had a 2014 felony conviction. His bond was set at $530,000 on Tuesday.

entry.title: Port St. Lucie pauses Flock program; 18 cameras set for removal Sept. 30 - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Port St. Lucie pauses Flock program; 18 cameras set for removal Sept. 30    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Lucie officials said 18 Flock cameras installed in county and state rights-of-way are scheduled to be removed by the vendor by Sept. 30, as the city pauses its automated license plate reader program amid continued privacy concerns. The update came during public comment at a City Council meeting on Monday, where several residents urged council members to permanently remove the cameras from city streets and prohibit future permits for Flock and other automated vehicle-tracking systems. Casey Huneycutt called for a citywide ban on Flock cameras and similar systems, arguing they pose privacy and surveillance concerns. "We've grown up in this country understanding that mass surveillance is wrong," Huneycutt said during an interview with CBS12 a day after the council meeting. "Authoritarian governments use it against their citizens and we don't want that." Huneycutt lives just around the corner from a license plate reader in his neighborhood. "It makes me very nervous," Huneycutt said. "These license plate readers have wrong readings, so I'm subject to being mistaken for a criminal." Port St. Lucie resident Jorge Borges directly asked council members to remove the cameras and take further action. He asked the city to stop issuing permits for automated license plate readers and other vehicle-tracking systems in city-owned or city-controlled rights-of-way, and to pursue removal of existing cameras. "It's just dangerous," Borges told CBS12 News. "I just believe that the benefits don't outweigh the risks." Borges said Port St. Lucie police announced Sept. 1 that the department would pause the program and remove seven cameras. He told council he counted eight of 22 cameras still standing at locations he believed required state right-of-way review. Steven Greer also addressed the council, saying he has sued the city, Mayor Shannon Martin and Flock in federal court. His lawsuit allegations were not discussed by the council during the meeting. Lucie resident James Reynolds joined the criticism, telling council members the city had previously achieved its public safety goals without Flock cameras. See also: Sheriff’s office warns of renewed inappropriate activity at DJ Wilcox Preserve During Monday night's city council meeting, city leaders said they'd weigh their options. We need to make sure there’s punishments for misuse; we need to make sure that retention periods are addressed; our audit is complete, Councilman Anthony Bonna said. I know there have been local incidents of misuse, and so this isn’t something abstract. Councilman Bonna said he was not calling for all cameras to be taken down immediately. What I’m calling for is to pause the program, and when I say pause, I mean pause, and let’s get this policy right, so it protects both our liberties and safety, Bonna said. During the discussion, city officials said the police chief’s white paper calls for nine cameras in county rights-of-way and nine in state rights-of-way to be removed by the vendor. The city can’t take them down; the vendor needs to take them down, an unidentified city official said. Those 18 cameras will be taken down. An unidentified city staff member later confirmed the scheduled removal date. 30 that the cameras will be taken down, the staff member said. Lucie police had previously announced an operational pause on its Flock and Axon license plate reader systems after the Florida Department of Transportation revoked approvals for the technology in state highway rights of way. At that time, police said seven city cameras located in FDOT rights-of-way would be removed. The city’s pause limits use of the remaining systems to cases involving an immediate threat to life, including missing or endangered people, with authorization from Police Chief Leo Niemczyk . The discussion follows a broader debate in St. Earlier this month, county commissioners voted 3-2 to stop new permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers in county-controlled rights of way, review existing permits and issue removal notices where appropriate. The county action went beyond FDOT’s order, which applied only to state highway rights-of-way. The county vote did not apply to cameras on private property or devices mounted in law enforcement vehicles. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said his office would comply with the state directive while tightening internal rules for deputies’ use of the technology. "The issue is not that they have the cameras," said Jorge Borges of Port St. "The issue is the mistakes that can happen with the cameras and the consequences of those mistakes."

entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District's attorney resigned minutes after a heated special fire board meeting Wednesday, as fallout from an alleged hazing investigation continues to threaten district leadership.Attorney Kim Sabol submitted her resignation letter effective in 90 days. She is the subject of several complaints tied to the hazing investigation.WATCH BELOW: St. Lucie County fire district attorney resigns amid hazing falloutNearly a dozen people spoke at the special meeting, which was called to address what board members described as a major gap in district policy: who investigates complaints against the district's own leaders."Since this district's inception, we have not had a policy on how they handle complaints against themselves," St. Lucie County Commissioner and Fire District Board Member Jamie Fowler said. "They — being those positions— have essentially been able to investigate themselves." Those positions include the fire chief, assistant fire chief and district attorney. The issue stems from an alleged hazing incident we reported on earlier this year. A third-party investigator concluded that videos showing firefighters using a modified bug zapper to shock probationary firefighters depicted hazing. Three veteran firefighters — Doug Boudrias, Jordan Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin — were fired as a result."It was just us in our downtime, joking around, having fun," Hutchinson said."We're all still friends," Boudrias said. "Us and the victims, there was no ill intent." Months before the incident came to light, in September 2025, Boudrias and Hutchinson filed a complaint against Fire Chief Jeff Lee and Sabol. That complaint was denied by the district officials who were themselves named in it."That's not a good process," Fowler said. The board is now asking two outside law firms to help draft a new complaint policy. Meanwhile, firefighters are casting ballots in a no-confidence vote regarding Lee."It basically says whether or not they trust and believe in him to lead this district," Fowler said. "So that is a huge thing if you have the majority of the men and women underneath you saying they can no longer serve under you, that's a pretty impactful message." Lee acknowledged the district lacks a clear complaint process. He told Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey: "I'm glad this board is finally taking this as a serious issue," adding he "welcomes any investigation from any agency."Per Sabol's resignation, Lee said it's a "sad day." "She's been a tremendous attorney for the district," Lee said of Sabol. As for the vote of no confidence, Lee said he didn't have much to say until it's over with "We'll see what the men and women decide," Lee told Hussey. "I came up on the labor side; I've always fought for our men and women on the line." Tension inside district headquarters was evident throughout Wednesday's meeting."This system is so broken," one attendee said."Everybody is fed up. They want action," said retired fire captain Mike Jenkins.As the union's legal fight to reinstate the three firefighters continues, calls are growing for the fire board to bypass arbitration and bring them back to work. When asked whether the board has that authority, Fowler said, "I think we might actually," adding, "The chief wants them back. The union is saying they want to come back. I'm going to ask the board in a week from now — what do we want to do? What's the process?" Firefighters are still casting ballots in the no-confidence vote. There is no word yet on when results will be released.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. entry.title: As Buc-ee's nears construction, development interest builds in northern St. Lucie County - cbs12.com
entry.summary: As Buc-ee's nears construction, development interest builds in northern St. Lucie County    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

entry.title: Race, then head home: Inside St. Lucie County’s P1 Motor Club - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Race, then head home: Inside St. Lucie County’s P1 Motor Club    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: The 650-acre development plans nearly 10 miles of driving surfaces, trackside homes and country club amenities. Membership currently starts at $192,000. P1 Motor Club expects to welcome members onto its first racetrack within a month, offering an early taste of a community where owners will eventually be able to drive on a circuit and head home overlooking it. The 650-acre development on Okeechobee Road is taking shape on a former orange grove. Plans include multiple driving circuits, trackside homes, a motorsports business park and amenities ranging from a pool to walking trails. The easiest way to describe it that most people understand is think of a high-end golf club, but a racetrack, said Chris Duplessis, P1’s director of fun. So no golf balls, we’ve got fancy race cars instead. CBS12 News took a ride with Duplessis for a firsthand look at the three-mile track, which he said is about 85% complete. Remaining work includes finishing sections of guardrail while the newly laid asphalt cures. Construction on what visitors see today started about a year ago, following several years of planning and approvals, he said. See also: Citadel CEO's historic $3 billion gift is bringing Carnegie Mellon to Miami Eventually, the property will have just under 10 miles of driving surfaces. A planned 4.5-mile circuit will include elevation changes and a crossover bridge where the track passes over itself. Other plans include karting, rally and drifting areas. Duplessis said construction on the larger circuit and real estate portion is expected to begin around the start of 2027. P1 plans to pay for a water line connecting the development to county water service. Homes with a view of the action For some members, P1 will be a place to spend the day. For others, it will become a home or weekend getaway. Duplessis said the club already has 280 members and has sold 68 real estate units. The planned garage townhomes will combine ground-floor vehicle space with living areas upstairs. Each unit will overlook a track, he said. These are fully livable, garage on the ground level, beautiful living space upstairs, Duplessis said. Every unit is overlooking the track, so they all have track view as well as community view. P1 also plans trackside residences. Duplessis estimated the development will eventually include roughly 200 residential units, with many buyers expected to use them as second or third homes. Only members can purchase real estate. Membership currently starts at $192,000, with yearly dues in addition. Duplessis quoted real estate at $1.4 million, purchased separately. Residents could begin moving in in about two years, he said. The full development is expected to take approximately five years to complete. A fleet of cars and coaching for beginners Members will not necessarily need to bring their own car to get behind the wheel. Duplessis said P1’s partnership with Mercedes will provide a fleet of vehicles for members to drive. He also described plans for Mercedes-hosted driving experiences that would give nonmembers opportunities to use the track. While luxury cars are part of the appeal, Duplessis said the vehicles on the circuit could range from Mazda Miatas to Porsches, Ferraris and Mercedes models. Some members have racing experience. Others have never driven on a track. For beginners, P1 plans to provide instructors who teach driving fundamentals and track rules before building toward more advanced skills. We get them an instructor, an expert, teach them all the basics, all the rules of the road, let’s say, and then they start driving, Duplessis said. The circuit has no posted speed limit, but drivers will be expected to stay within their abilities. New drivers will work with coaches who control the pace as they learn. Members whose skills qualify them will also have opportunities to participate in club races. Beyond the racetrack The development’s plans include a clubhouse, pool, pickleball and other sport courts, lakes and walking trails. Duplessis said a rooftop bar at the clubhouse will offer views of the activity below. He said the team is also considering nature as it lays out the property, including pond locations intended to support bird life. An area with mature trees is planned for slower, technical off-road driving. The team is exploring water sports on the property’s lakes, though those activities are still being considered. P1 also plans space for motorsports-related businesses. Duplessis said the club intends to host community events where nonmembers can visit and watch, along with driving training for law enforcement. He said local workers and contractors are already involved in the project. For Duplessis, a four-time national rally champion, the development is personal. He plans to make it his home. I will live right here, he said. It’ll be a big sense of community for all our members. Duplessis said P1 will bring jobs and use local contractors and businesses, noting a track he previously ran employed about 150 people; he did not provide a hiring estimate for P1. He expects little traffic impact, saying many homes will be used only occasionally and a busy day would draw about 100 members.

entry.title: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route - cbs12.com
entry.summary: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route    cbs12.com
entry.article_text: A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

entry.title: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart - cw34.com
entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

entry.title: Only 17% approve of Trump’s handling of cost of living weeks before midterms
entry.summary: Americans are deeply frustrated with President Donald Trump's handling of the economy and rising prices, with most panning his performance and blaming his policies as higher costs threaten his party's chances in November. A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of the Republican president's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low. A majority, 65%, of U.S. adults now blame Trumps policies for persistently high costs more than factors outside of his control, signaling growing weariness over his aggressive use of tariffs and continued unhappiness with the war with Iran. The dismal numbers come just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress and while Trump is hitting the campaign trail with an aggressive schedule of rallies. But Trump who has asked voters to pretend that he is on the ballot as he tries to bolster turnout remains deeply unpopular, with even many Republicans faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief. RELATED STORY | Fed raises rates despite pressure from Trump to cut borrowing costs I was hoping it would be better or different, but its not really good,' said Robert Gault, 66, a retired factory worker from Bradford, Pennsylvania, who describes himself as a Republican. Our president, I thought, was going to help the country, and so far he has not really seemed to have done that with the economy or in general. Hes not really done what I was hoping he would,' said Gault. 'He said, 'Make America Great Again.' And I have not seen him do that. Costs drag on Trump as the economic pain keeps coming Over the last few months, Americans have grown more worried about being able to afford basics like groceries and gas. About half of U.S. adults now say they are extremely or very concerned about being able to fill their tanks, up from 39% in July. About half are also highly concerned about being able to afford food. Prices are 'extremely exorbitant. Just the cost of everything is going up as a result of fuel, said Pedro Sanchez, 52, of Perris, California, who voted for Trump and works in law enforcement. I used to have a lot more disposable income. I dont have that any more. Its gotten eaten up because of all these increases in the cost of everything.
