entry.title: Jupiter Fire Rescue firefighter honored for lifesaving actions on hockey rink
entry.summary: As Jupiter Fire Rescue officially began its first day on Thursday, one of the departments new firefighters is already being recognized for the life-saving work she does. At a recent Jupiter Town Council meeting, Jessica Herman was honored for her heroic actions that helped save a retired NYPD officer who went into cardiac arrest. WATCH: Jupiter Firefighter Honored for Lifesaving Rescue Jupiter Firefighter Honored After Helping Save Retired NYPD Officer During Hockey Game Jupiter Fire Rescue Deputy Chief Jason Sekula read a letter to Herman before she was given the Phoenix Life Saving Award. 'Although you recently joined JFRD, you demonstrated the character, leadership, and heart of a veteran firefighter,' Sekula said. Herman was at a first responders tournament in Coral Springs on 9/11 when Joe Gomes felt something was off. 'I just got this odd feeling over my entire body, and to myself, I said, 'that feels weird,'' Gomes said. He lay down and was able to walk off the ice on his own, but within seconds, his teammates realized this was an emergency. Herman ran toward Gomes, whom she'd known since he used to referee her junior hockey games. 'I checked your pulse,' Herman recalled. 'I said, 'I don't have a pulse.' She coordinated a team of six firefighters from different South Florida fire rescue departments to save Gomes. 'Roll call. I'm doing this. You're doing that. He's doing this. They're doing that, and we just got to work,' Herman said. She began CPR compressions, and an AED defibrillator was brought out. 'At one point, the bright white light came out,' Gomes told WPTV. Herman said this was a true team effort. 'I'm very humbled, and I'm extremely grateful for all the attention it's bringing. I keep reminding people I wasn't the only one,' Herman said. Gomes says the experience left him with a new mission making sure others are as lucky as he was that day. 'There should be someone at all times working at the rink that knows CPR,' he said. Now, Herman is bringing that same readiness to Jupiter as the town's new fire department starts its first day.

entry.title: Mosquito-borne illness advisory issued for Martin County
entry.summary: The Florida Department of Health in Martin County is informing residents that several sentinel chickens have tested positive for West Nile virus. The department and Martin County Mosquito Control said they are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts by enhanced monitoring for mosquitoes and diseases, as well as targeted mosquito treatment to reduce the risk of disease transmission. Individuals with symptoms of fever, chills, sweats, nausea/vomiting, and headache should seek immediate medical attention, the department said. The health department is reminding the community to avoid being bitten by mosquitoes by taking these basic precautions: Spray yourself with mosquito repellent Cover your arms and legs with clothing Drain standing water Mosquitoes breed by laying eggs in and near standing water and as little as one bottle cap of water standing for more than one week is enough for mosquitoes to multiply, the health department said. entry.summary: CROS Ministries seeks volunteers as demand for senior meal deliveries grows. CROS Ministries says its Caring Kitchen program has reached capacity serving seniors and homebound residents in the Delray Beach area, and now the nonprofit is looking for more volunteers as it works to expand. The free meal delivery program serves seniors and homebound residents in Delray Beach and parts of Boca Raton. entry.title: Fort Pierce city clerk testifies about meetings in former city manager Nick Mimms corruption trial - wflx.com
entry.summary: Fort Pierce city clerk testifies about meetings in former city manager Nick Mimms corruption trial    wflx.com
entry.article_text: Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day. Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. The jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D. The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization’s board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee. According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater. Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information. “Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. “Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?” Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said. Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid. WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city manager Under cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms’ niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time. “You knew they were city employees,” Murrell said. “And it bothered you that they were doing this?” Murrell said. “I thought it was a little odd,” Cox said. “You didn’t raise any objections,” Murrell said. Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney’s presence at the meetings. “He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?” Murrell said. “He didn’t raise any objections or concerns, did he?” Murrell said. “Not at the meeting,” Cox said. Not that I know of,” Cox said. The trial is expected to last at least a week.

entry.title: Two men arrested in separate Port St. Lucie hit-and-run cases - WPEC
entry.summary: Two men arrested in separate Port St. Lucie hit-and-run cases    WPEC
entry.article_text: Two men are out of jail on bond after being arrested in two separate hit-and-run cases in Port St. Lucie this week, according to the Port St. According to an arrest affidavit, 23-year-old Giovanny Barthelemy was driving a silver Toyota Highlander around 8:40 p.m. Tuesday when it collided with a 16-year-old riding an electric motorcycle on Southwest Roma Way near Southwest Lorenzo Way. A security camera at the community clubhouse recorded the crash. The officer wrote that the video shows the SUV turning into the community entrance as the teen crossed in front of it. The teen was thrown from the motorcycle. The affidavit says the SUV then backed up and drove away while the injured teen lay on the ground waving his arms. The teen was taken to Tradition Medical Center and then flown to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. Police said he broke his left femur and hurt his left ankle, and he was listed in serious but stable condition. See also: Rapper Rick Ross arrested in Florida on domestic violence charges, enters not guilty plea One witness told police the electric motorcycle had no headlights. Two witnesses said both vehicles were going fast. The SUV's owner, the father of Barthelemy's girlfriend, called 911. He told police Barthelemy said he had hit someone on a bike and then driven home. Officers found Barthelemy at his home on Southwest Ridgecrest Drive. According to the affidavit, after being read his rights, Barthelemy told police he felt and heard the crash and knew right away he had hit a person. He told police he should have stopped but didn't, and said his phone was dead, according to the affidavit. Barthelemy is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving injuries, which is a felony. He was also given a traffic citation. He was released on a $7,500 bond. The second case happened earlier that afternoon. Lucie officer clocked a silver Toyota going 85 mph in a 40-mph zone, according to an arrest affidavit. The officer turned around and tried to stop the car. The affidavit says the driver went over a concrete median into the opposite lanes, ran a red light, and hit a traffic sign at Southwest Becker Road and Southwest Hallmark Street before getting on northbound Interstate 95. The officer turned off his lights and siren but kept the car in sight. Police said the car later broke down on the side of I-95. Officers said the driver, 19-year-old Christian Johnson, got out and ran toward the back of the car. Lucie detective, a Florida Highway Patrol trooper, and the officer surrounded the car, and Johnson was taken into custody. According to the affidavit, Johnson's license had been suspended three times in St. Johnson is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving property damage, reckless driving and driving with a suspended or revoked license. All three charges are misdemeanors. He was released on a $12,500 bond. In a statement about both arrests, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said drivers are legally required to stop, whether it's for a traffic stop or after a crash. "Fleeing from law enforcement or leaving the scene of a crash can have serious consequences," the department said.

entry.title: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge - WPEC
entry.summary: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie man whose TikTok and Twich bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sept. on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records. His bond was set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped. The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women’s electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile’s bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman’s password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking. The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts. See also: Florida Education Department eyes dress code to ban head coverings, Crocs, short skirts The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea’s booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

entry.title: 'Ready to answer the call': Jupiter Fire Rescue officially in service, marking historic transition
entry.summary: The new Jupiter Fire Rescue department is officially in service, taking over all fire and emergency response duties for the town as of 12 a.m., Oct. 1. The historic transition from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue was marked by a ceremony where Fire Chief Darrel Donatto made the first official radio call, declaring the new agency 'in service and ready to answer the call.' The launch is the culmination of a months-long journey, closely followed by WPTV, from the initial swearing-in of firefighters to the traditional 'push-in' ceremony for the new fire engines. WATCH: Jupiter's new fire department officially launches Jupiter Fire Rescue Department now in service A New Era of Service At a ceremony held at the Jupiter fire station to commemorate the official start of operations, Chief Donatto addressed the firefighters and the community, acknowledging the significance of the moment. 'Jupiter Fire Rescue will assume official responsibility for providing fire and emergency services to this community,' Donatto said. 'We gather here to recognize those who came before us and to reflect on the responsibility that we now inherit and to reaffirm the mission and principles that will guide this department from its very first call.' 'Ready to Answer the Call' Just before midnight, the chief's voice came over the radio, making the transition official and signaling to dispatchers and surrounding agencies that the new department was operational. 'Jupiter Chief, thank you to everyone. We look forward to serving together. Jupiter Fire Rescue is in service and ready to answer the call,' Donatto announced. For residents, dialing 911 for an emergency will not change. However, calls will now be dispatched to the new municipal department, and a Jupiter Fire Rescue engine and crew will respond. The move gives the Town of Jupiter direct control over its emergency services, staffing, and equipment for the first time in decades. entry.title: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart - cw34.com
entry.summary: Rabies alert issued in Martin County after raccoon tests positive in Stuart    cw34.com
entry.article_text: A rabid raccoon found in Stuart prompted the Florida Department of Health in Martin County to issue a 60-day alert Wednesday. The raccoon was captured Sunday off South Kanner Highway and later tested positive for rabies , according to the department. The alert covered an area bounded by Southeast Tressler Drive to the south, Southeast Federal Highway to the east and South Kanner Highway to the west. Health officials said rabies was present among wild animals in the area and urged residents and visitors to avoid contact with raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats, coyotes and other wildlife. Rabies is a deadly viral disease most commonly transmitted through the bite or scratch of an infected animal. An animal with rabies may appear healthy and can behave unusually friendly or aggressively. People who are bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal should wash the wound with soap and water, seek medical attention and report the incident to the Department of Health in Martin County at 772-221-4030 . Treatment administered after an exposure can prevent the disease. Officials recommended that residents take several precautions: Keep pets and livestock current on rabies vaccinations. Keep pets leashed and under direct supervision. Avoid handling or feeding wild and stray animals. Do not leave pet food or unsecured garbage outdoors. Prevent bats and other wildlife from entering homes, schools and other occupied buildings. Contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator rather than bringing a wild animal into a home. See also: Florida mother leaves 4 children home alone while on Carnival cruise to Bahamas: Police Anyone whose pet or livestock is bitten should immediately contact a veterinarian and Martin County Animal Control at 772-463-3211 . Residents can also call animal control to report stray animals in their neighborhoods. More information is available at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies .

entry.title: Martin County sheriff investigates toddler death in pond - WPBF
entry.summary: Martin County sheriff investigates toddler death in pond    WPBF
entry.article_text: The Martin County Medical examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy an accidental drowning. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County Sheriff John Budenseik said the child's parents called 911. "We received one of the most heart wrenching 911 calls you can get," Budenseik said. According to investigators, Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in the area of Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive in Port Salerno and was found unresponsive in a pond on his family’s property in Port Salerno. The toddler was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he went missing for a short time. According to investigators, the child slipped out of sight for a short time. When Pablo’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and ultimately found him in the pond. "At some point there had been a fence around the pond, but it had been trampled down or broke down over time, so it wasn't really a functional fence,' Budensiek said. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, but despite lifesaving efforts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said. Charlene Lyons is the President and CEO for the YMCA Treasure Coast. She said she was devastated when she heard the news, "I started at the 'Y' as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me,' Lyons said She wants the public to know they can contact the YMCA for information about swim lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time. For more information about swim lessons, log on to the YMCA Treasure Coast website posted here. entry.title: King tides, full moon erode Fort Pierce road for second time in a week - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides, full moon erode Fort Pierce road for second time in a week    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to repair a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and recent rain continue to affect parts of South Florida. Skid loaders were working along the narrow roadway beside the Indian River Lagoon, adding dirt and sand to reinforce an area where erosion has left the road’s edge vulnerable. Crews brought 32 loads of dirt to the site Sept. But only days later, the embankment again needed repairs. Resident Gene Barnes said the recurring work is not a long-term solution. We’re losing ground year by year, Barnes said. Until the Corps of Engineers or something like that comes and puts a headwall in to stabilize it, it’s not going to be an easy fix. The road has faced erosion problems before. Heavy rain damaged sections in 2014, and Hurricane Nicole caused additional washouts in 2022. Barnes said continued rain and tidal action could undermine the roadway itself. See also: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge If we keep getting rains like this, it’s going to undermine the road, and then the road is going to collapse and the school bus is going to fall in the hole, he said. The latest repairs follow an emergency sand operation at nearby Jetty Park that cost taxpayers nearly $500,000. While repairs on South Indian River Drive may be less costly, residents said the erosion is likely to remain a concern as more rain and tidal action are forecast.

entry.article_text: Fort Pierce City Clerk Linda Cox took the stand Wednesday as the trial of former city manager Nick Mimms entered its third day.Mimms was arrested in 2024 on charges of bid tampering and official misconduct.WATCH BELOW: Fort Pierce city clerk takes the stand in Nick Mimms trialThe jury heard first from Cox, who testified about a series of city meetings shown in video evidence by the state. One meeting, held in October 2019, showed a representative with Allegany Franciscan Ministries presenting a community center concept on behalf of the Lincoln Park Young Professionals for two vacant lots along Avenue D.The Lincoln Park Young Professionals had been awarded a $500,000 grant from Allegany Franciscan Ministries for the project. Among the organization's board members was Caleta Scott, the niece of Mimms, as well as a city employee.According to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Mimms had begun the process of having the Avenue D land declared as surplus, even though it had been designated for use as parking for the nearby Lincoln Theater.Prosecutors questioned Cox about whether the city board relied on Mimms for accurate information."Does the board also expect the defendant to give them correct information?" Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said."Yes," Cox said."Do they rely on the defendant to give correct information?" Assistant State Attorney Brandon White said."Yes," Cox said.Attorneys also showed footage from future meetings of the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency, where the board voted to declare the lots surplus and later announced that the Lincoln Park Young Professionals had won the bid.WATCH BELOW: Opening statements begin in trial of former city managerUnder cross-examination, the defense argued it was no secret that Mimms' niece was among those seeking to obtain the property. Defense attorney Donald Murrell questioned Cox about whether she had raised any concerns at the time."You knew they were city employees," Murrell said."I did," Cox said."And it bothered you that they were doing this?" Murrell said."I thought it was a little odd," Cox said."You didn't raise any objections," Murrell said."I did not," Cox said.Murrell also questioned Cox about the city attorney's presence at the meetings."He saw the same slideshow you saw, the same PowerPoint?" Murrell said."Yes," Cox said."He didn't raise any objections or concerns, did he?" Murrell said."Not at the meeting," Cox said."Ever?" Murrell said."I wouldn't know. Not that I know of," Cox said.The trial is expected to last at least a week.

entry.title: New Northstar Day school opens in Palm Beach Gardens for neurodivergent children
entry.summary: A new school designed specifically for neurodivergent children has opened in Palm Beach Gardens, bringing education and therapy services together under one roof. Leaders at Northstar Day say the facility is designed to support children with conditions such as ADHD, dyslexia, autism and other learning differences while making life easier for families seeking specialized care. The school officially celebrated its grand opening with a ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by local leaders, educators and community members. New Northstar Day school opens in Palm Beach Gardens for neurodivergent children For many families, finding support for neurodivergent children often means traveling between schools, therapists and specialists in different locations. Northstar Day's founders say their model aims to streamline that process by providing multiple services in a single setting. Education and therapy in one place School leaders say Northstar Day is built around a comprehensive approach that combines academics and therapeutic services for students with diverse learning needs. 'This is a shift in the way we think of mental health for young people,' said Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg during the grand opening. Founder and CEO James McManus said the goal is to create a different approach to care and education for neurodivergent children. 'We're trailblazers, and what we want to do is show the community and show the world that there's something different than the neurodivergent treatment that's being used currently,' McManus said. He added that reducing challenges for parents can also improve outcomes for children. 'The easier we can make the parents' life, the easier we're going to make the child's life, and that's our goal,' McManus said. entry.title: Downtown Boca Raton wellness club project along Sanborn Square moves forward, sparking mixed reactions
entry.summary: A proposed private social and wellness club in downtown Boca Raton is moving forward after receiving unanimous approval from the city's planning and zoning board. The eight-story project, planned near Sanborn Square, would add restaurants, fitness and wellness facilities, and rooftop amenities to an area already experiencing significant redevelopment. The proposal comes as multiple major projects are reshaping the downtown corridor, including the Aletto mixed-use development and the previously approved Mizner Plaza hotel project. Supporters say the club could bring new customers and tax revenue to the area, while some residents worry about increased traffic, parking demand and what they consider overdevelopment. For people who live, work and spend time downtown, the decision could affect everything from traffic patterns to the future look and feel of one of Boca Raton's most recognizable public gathering spaces. Project planned between major downtown developments The proposed club would replace an existing building along Northeast First Avenue near Sanborn Square. According to plans presented to city officials, the development would total 54,681 square feet and include private social spaces, dining options, fitness facilities and wellness-focused amenities. A rooftop component is also planned as part of the project. The proposal would sit near two high-profile developments already underway or approved in the area. Nearby, construction continues on the Aletto, a mixed-use office and retail project. Just down the block, a 12-story Mizner Plaza hotel has also received approval. Planning documents presented to the city indicate the project could require as many as 183 parking spaces. Every place I’ve gone, we win,” Trump said during a speech at a truck facility in Denton, northwest of Dallas. He said some have suggested his “heart isn't in it. My heart is in it,” and if not, he'd promised he'd be “home right now.”“My heart is in it like never before,” Trump said of the run-up to the midterms.Vance, meanwhile, stumped in Florida, putting the Republican Party’s highest-ranking officials in areas where GOP candidates once expected to have glide paths to victory but are now facing tougher races.The vice president tried to cast the GOP as representing common sense in the face of a Democratic push to the left.“I have the easiest job in the world,” the vice president said in Lakeland, Florida. “I get to talk about how crazy the Democrats are.”RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground statesTrump and Vance could have their work cut out for them, though.A new poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds that only 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Just 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.Republicans have expressed growing pessimism about their chances in the election, which will determine control of Congress, as the president has repeatedly dismissed concerns about high costs and gas prices as his unpopular war in Iran drags on.According to Trump, his party has merely done a poor job of public relations in promoting his administration's accomplishments.“Maybe we’re doing a bad job selling it,” Trump said in Texas.Still, the president spent far more time scoffing at his predecessor, President Joe Biden, reliving his 2024 presidential campaign and defending the war in Iran than he did talking about how he'll help lower the cost of living.Trump scoffed at questions about affordability, insisting that they'd been caused by Biden, who left office more than two years ago. He also insisted that prices were actually on the decline.“I think inflation is very real, but they’re the ones that caused the inflation,” he said. “I’m the one that’s bringing it down, and we have to be able to get that word out somehow because they’re using the word affordability.”Democrats say Trump is desperateThe Democratic National Committee said Trump and Vance are “desperately trying to rally their base as the midterm elections approach and Republicans face defeat.”“Donald Trump and JD Vance started a deadly and costly war with Iran that sent the economy spiraling and pushed prices even higher, and now — in the final stretch to the midterms — they’re desperately pleading with voters to 'give (them) another chance,'” said DNC deputy communications director Kendall Witmer.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | 'Pretend that I'm on the ballot': Trump courts Republicans at unusual GOP midterm conventionIn Oklahoma, Trump campaigned with Republican Mike Mazzei, who is running against Democratic state House Minority Leader Cyndi Munson for governor. That event was held on the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, putting Trump in the company of just a handful of U.S. presidents who have visited tribal nations while in office.Before his evening Oklahoma stop, Trump toured the truck facility and chatted with workers in Texas, where Republicans are spending heavily to try to bolster state Attorney General Ken Paxton in a Senate race that could be closer than long expected. Paxton is facing Democratic state Rep. James Talarico,Paxton attended the event and Trump joked that he “could be a pain in the ass sometimes” but also noted, “We need Ken so badly, and that’s why I’m here.”Trump didn't summon Paxton to the stage. He also shouted out, but didn't invite to speak, an unlikely traveler accompanying him, former NBA star Dennis Rodman. Trump praised Rodman as his longtime friend and said Rodman had become close with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.Trump promises a travel blitz coming upThe president will be campaigning in more politically competitive areas in the weeks ahead as he embarks on his travel sprint. But Republican officials will not send him to places where they think his presence could drag down their candidates, according to a person familiar with the party’s strategy who was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.Trump’s Oklahoma visit, and likewise one on Friday to Alabama, aimed at hitting two targets with one stop, the person said.Republican officials have noted that even his Oklahoma stop brought Trump close to the Dallas-Fort Worth media market, meaning the president's message reached Texas voters who could back Paxton.His Friday stop in Mobile, Alabama, is aimed not only at boosting Sen. Tommy Tuberville as he runs for Alabama governor but also at shoring up support in Florida’s adjacent panhandle for Republican Rep. Byron Donalds.Donalds is running for Florida governor against David Jolly, the Republican-turned-independent who is now running as a Democrat. Donalds' campaign in heavily GOP Florida comes as Republicans there have faced some turbulence and voter concerns about affordability and artificial intelligence data centers have become central issues.With Trump in Oklahoma and Texas, Vance's central Florida stop on Thursday was for Donalds. That came a day after the vice president campaigned in Texas, rallying with Republican candidate Eric Flores, who is in a tight U.S. House race in south Texas.Trump will also campaign on Saturday in Vandalia, Ohio, and on Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska.Trump is expected to campaign for the GOP almost dailyIn a meeting on Capitol Hill this week, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles described privately to GOP senators that Trump will have a near-daily sprint of campaigning ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.West Virginia Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito said that White House officials are “acknowledging the headwinds” but that “they have a strategy, and we have a strategy,” including money that the president’s operation will continue to deploy.Capito also defended the White House’s plan to send Trump to traditionally conservative territory, arguing that he can motivate the Republican base not just where he travels but elsewhere in the country because he has such a broad reach.“He can get more of his voters out — that are going to be our voters — than anybody else,” Capito said.

entry.title: Returning Stuart city manager Michael Mortell vows to improve city structure, restore public trust
entry.summary: Stuart's returning city manager says he has unfinished business and a plan to bring more structure to City Hall. Michael Mortell is back in his role as Stuart city manager. In his first interview since officially returning to the role Friday, Mortell told me he still has more to give the city. WATCH BELOW: Returning Stuart city manager vows to restore public trust Returning Stuart city manager Michael Mortell vows to improve city structure 'There's something drawing me. I feel the need to go back and finish the unwritten book or the unwritten chapter,' Mortell said. 'I felt like there was things that were left that needed to be corrected and needed to be finished.' After his dismissal last October, Mortell worked for the 19th Judicial Circuit, where he says he learned practices that could help the city run more efficiently. 'We need to really focus on defining administration defining whatwho are the policymakers, who the administrators, who is the chain of command, and how we need to disseminate information,' Mortell said. 'Implementing more structure and defining it will help all of us make the city a better place and I think residents will know exactly what to expect.' Over the past year, a divided Stuart Commission and leadership turnover have left some residents questioning their confidence in city government. Resident David Kelman voiced those concerns at a previous city commission meeting. 'You all represent this city. You need to step back and unite because what you're doing ain't going to work. It's three versus two here,' Kelman said. I asked Mortell how he plans to restore the community's faith in the city. He says it starts with teamwork. 'We really identify everybody's strengths ... and find ways to work more as a team so that everybody feels like they're contributing to the outcome and that everybody has the common goal of what's best for Stuart in mind and rather than being divisive at all to try to find ways to work together,' Mortell said. A city manager with a long history working for the city, Mortell is returning to the job with a fresh approach. entry.title: Jupiter launches its own fire department, aims to improve service and save taxpayers millions
entry.summary: Jupiter on Thursday started its first day of having its own fire department. It comes with the promise of protection and a hope to save taxpayers' money. Town leaders started the process three years ago to have their own fire rescue department. The decision came after frustration with the rising cost of paying for services from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. WATCH BELOW: Jupiter aims to improve fire rescue service, save taxpayers millions Jupiter Fire Rescue launches with hope of saving money 'I think its a great thing,' said David, who was out along Indiantown Road with his family. 'I don't think it matters, to be honest with you. I think a lot of people, whether it's Palm Beach County or Jupiter they just want to feel safe.' In 2023, town leaders had pointed to a study that estimated a budget savings of $68 million over 10 years if they started their own fire department. Residents saw the old county assessment fee replaced by a new one for Jupiter. The new fire department has 94 firefighters in three stations. The new fire department also comes along just one month before Florida voters will decide on the Amendment 3 referendum that aims to raise the Homestead Exemption and lower revenues for municipalities and counties.

entry.summary: FDLE testimony focuses on RFP process in ex-Fort Pierce manager Nick Mimms' trial    WPEC
entry.article_text: Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms is on trial over allegations that he improperly influenced a city bidding process involving two vacant lots in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park area. Mimms faces charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors allege he steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included Mimms' niece and another city employee. On Thursday, much of the testimony focused on who controlled the RFP process and how closely Mimms remained involved after it was turned over to the city's purchasing department. FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails and other records collected during the investigation. One focus was the nearby Lincoln Theater and its need for parking. Brisky testified Mimms had told the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency that the RFP would include language addressing the theater's parking needs. But that language was not included in the request Mimms sent to the purchasing department. Brisky also testified investigators found no evidence Mimms filed a 2019 memorandum concerning the parking plans in the relevant city records. The defense questioned the significance of that omission and emphasized that the purchasing department was responsible for putting together and publishing the RFP after receiving the project's specifications. See also: NTSB report clarifies Amazon plane crash timeline that killed 5 on Sept. 6 Defense attorneys also challenged the state's characterization of the process as a sole-source arrangement. Brisky acknowledged the RFP was not technically a sole-source contract. The state, meanwhile, pointed to emails showing Mimms continued to communicate with city employees about the RFP, including its evaluation criteria and the evaluation committee. Other emails showed city employees knew there had been one submission after the RFP was posted. An LPYP email address was copied on one of those communications. The defense also questioned the investigation's treatment of other city employees involved in the process, including a purchasing official who was not charged. Later, former Fort Pierce employee Kalita Scott testified about LPYP and its efforts to develop the Lincoln Park properties. She described the organization as a group of young professionals focused on community development and said the need for parking near the Lincoln Theater was known in the community. Prosecutors allege Mimms manipulated the city's process to ensure LPYP received the lease. The defense has argued Mimms did not improperly favor the organization and that the evidence does not establish a criminal conspiracy. The trial is continuing in St.

entry.article_text: Lucie man whose TikTok and Twich bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sept. on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records. His bond was set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped. The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women’s electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile’s bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman’s password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking. The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts. See also: Florida Education Department eyes dress code to ban head coverings, Crocs, short skirts The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea’s booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

entry.title: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route - WPEC
entry.summary: Martin County rejected a plan for homes, a new state law offers another route    WPEC
entry.article_text: A new Florida law could offer another path toward housing on 396 acres near Kanner Highway, after Martin County commissioners voted against advancing a residential proposal for the land last year. The property, known as Waterside, lies south of SW 96th Street, between Kanner Highway and the St. The applicant previously sought to change its designation from agricultural to low-density residential. Commissioners voted 5 0 in November 2025 not to advance that request. Now, Kanner/96th Street Investments LLC has asked commissioners to certify the property as an agricultural enclave under a state law that took effect July 1. Florida business records list The Kolter Group as the LLC’s manager. A hearing on the certification request is scheduled for October 13. Senior Planner Jenna Knobbe said the application requests a density of about 3.1 homes per acre, or roughly 1,200 single-family homes. That is a proposed figure, not an approved home count. Jim Harvey, president of Brookfield Kolter Land Partners, declined to comment on the request. We have no comment at this time, Harvey said in an email to CBS12 News. The law is meant for certain agricultural properties that are already surrounded by development or land planned for it. To qualify, an applicant must meet specific requirements involving the property’s agricultural history, surrounding land, size and access to services such as roads, water and sewer. Whether Waterside meets those requirements is what commissioners must decide. Commissioners can deny certification if the land does not qualify. But they must base their decision on the law’s criteria not simply whether they want homes built there. A denial requires written findings, which the applicant can challenge in court. If the county takes no action within 90 days of receiving an application, state law says the land must be certified. See also: Woman accused of driving wrong way with 0.20 BAC in deadly crash gets house arrest Certification would not approve a subdivision. It would let the applicant later submit qualifying housing plans based on what is allowed on neighboring land. The law says those plans must be treated as an allowed use even if the county’s existing growth plan or zoning would otherwise prohibit it. County staff would still review the plans, but the law does not require another commission hearing on them. It does take away some of the local control for local governments for deciding where development may or may not take place, Knobbe said in an interview. She said certification is the only part of this process that would go before commissioners. If certified, the property owner could submit development plans for administrative review without another commission hearing or vote on those plans. Martin County has long tried to keep new neighborhoods from spreading into rural areas. The new law raises a question: If this land qualifies, can commissioners still stop homes from being built outside the county’s planned growth area? Greg Braun, executive director of The Guardians of Martin County, said his organization wants development to follow the county’s existing growth plan. Tallahassee legislators seem to think that they know better about what’s going on locally than our local elected officials, and we think that that’s wrong, Braun said. Gil Smart, advocacy director for Friends of the Everglades, said his organization opposed the law because of concerns about development and public involvement. People value the open space, the green space, as they see them being taken away and bulldozed flat so we can build more housing, Smart said. People are going to have something to say about that, and they need to have a say in that. Commissioners did not decide the Waterside request Tuesday. They unanimously approved fees for reviewing applications under the new law: $8,150 to review whether property qualifies and $16,600 to review development plans submitted later. Knobbe said the law puts staff on a tight schedule. The county has 30 days to review a certification application and issue a report. A public hearing must follow within another 30 days. We've kind of had to drop everything that we're working on and prioritize that application, Knobbe told commissioners Tuesday. A separate deadline would apply if the land is certified and the applicant submits development plans: County staff would have no more than 180 days to review them. These are very expedited timeframes for what we typically will do for a major development plan type of review, because there’s a lot of moving parts, Knobbe said. The property is outside the county’s urban service district, where the county generally directs more intensive development and plans for supporting services. Knobbe said the county had not necessarily planned for that level of development on these properties. Roads, drainage, water and sewer would still need review. Knobbe said the county would need to negotiate with the developer over who pays for any needed infrastructure improvements. I think the effect is going to be more traffic. I think the effect is going to be more sprawl. I think the effect is going to be municipal services overextended, Smart said. No homes were approved Tuesday. The October 13 hearing is about whether Waterside qualifies for the new process, not approval of a housing site plan.

entry.title: 'Most heart-wrenching': Toddler drowns in Martin County Pond, sheriff calls it a tragic accident - wpbf.com
entry.summary: 'Most heart-wrenching': Toddler drowns in Martin County Pond, sheriff calls it a tragic accident    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: The Martin County Medical examiner has ruled the drowning death of a 23-month-old boy an accidental drowning. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Martin County Sheriff John Budenseik said the child's parents called 911. "We received one of the most heart wrenching 911 calls you can get," Budenseik said. According to investigators, Pablo Mendoza-Arrojo drowned in the area of Southeast Darling Street and Southeast Taylor Drive in Port Salerno and was found unresponsive in a pond on his family’s property in Port Salerno. The toddler was outside in the yard with family members shortly after 5 p.m. when he went missing for a short time. According to investigators, the child slipped out of sight for a short time. When Pablo’s mother and aunt realized he was missing, they began a frantic search and ultimately found him in the pond. "At some point there had been a fence around the pond, but it had been trampled down or broke down over time, so it wasn't really a functional fence,' Budensiek said. The family rushed him to Cleveland Clinic South, but despite lifesaving efforts, he was pronounced dead in the emergency room. Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said. Charlene Lyons is the President and CEO for the YMCA Treasure Coast. She said she was devastated when she heard the news, "I started at the 'Y' as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me,' Lyons said She wants the public to know they can contact the YMCA for information about swim lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time. For more information about swim lessons, log on to the YMCA Treasure Coast website posted here. entry.title: 'Not knowing where he is': Family searches for missing Port St. Lucie father - WPEC
entry.summary: 'Not knowing where he is': Family searches for missing Port St. Lucie father    WPEC
entry.article_text: Eight months after a Port St. Lucie father vanished, his family says they are still searching for answers and living with the painful uncertainty of not knowing where he is. "I'm stuck in this cycle of not knowing where he is," said Aubrey Finley, whose brother, Robert La Polla , disappeared Jan. 8 after being released from a hospital in Fort Pierce. The 47-year-old father has not been seen or heard from since, according to his family. Detectives have no confirmed sightings, and the case remains unsolved. Finley said La Polla struggled with depression following the deaths of their parents, but the siblings remained close and talked often. "Everything kind of fell apart," she said. "But we still managed to communicate a lot. We were still there for each other all the time." Also read: Search underway for missing autistic man last seen at Jensen Beach home Thursday morning Because of that bond, Finley said her brother's disappearance is completely out of character. In the months since he vanished, family members and friends have organized search efforts across Fort Pierce, checking wooded areas and busy corridors near HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. "We've gone through woods, under bridges, talking to people everywhere in Fort Pierce, trying to find anything that brings us to him," Finley said. The search has also taken an emotional toll on La Polla's young daughter, who continues to wait for her father to come home. She misses him," Finley said. "He's got a family that love him." The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office (SLCSO) said La Polla has been entered into a national missing persons database. Investigators have also collected DNA from family members in case it is needed for identification and continue to follow up on leads. Anyone with information about La Polla's whereabouts is asked to contact Detective Cpl. Drawdy at 772-462-3230 or call 911.

entry.summary: Niece testifies in trial involving former Fort Pierce city manager    wpbf.com
entry.article_text: The trial of former Fort Pierce City Manager Nicholas Mimms, who faces accusations of bid tampering and official misconduct, continued with testimony from his niece and a lead investigator. The first witness called to the stand was one of the lead investigators in the case, and cross-examination became tense at times. The prosecution’s key witness was Mimms’ niece, Caleta Scott, who is one of the founders of the nonprofit Lincoln Park Young Professionals. Mimms was my uncle when I applied," Scott said during her testimony. When asked about her relationship with Mimms, Scott said, "I respected him in the role of city manager and called him Mr. Mimms." Mimms is accused of using his position to help Lincoln Park Young Professionals secure a lease to develop two city-owned properties. The prosecution argues that Scott received special treatment because of her relationship with Mimms, presenting it as a conflict of interest. The defense has previously argued that Mimms and Scott have a distant relationship and that Mimms did not conspire to commit the alleged crimes. Testimony also included statements from the lead investigator in the case for the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, with cross-examination becoming tense at times. entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight - cw34.com
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.

entry.title: As Buc-ee's nears construction, development interest builds in northern St. Lucie County - WPEC
entry.summary: As Buc-ee's nears construction, development interest builds in northern St. Lucie County    WPEC
entry.article_text: Buc-ee’s may be best known for its massive travel centers, barbecue sandwiches and loyal fan base, but on the Treasure Coast, county leaders say the proposed development could signal something even bigger: a wave of growth along the Indrio Road corridor in northern St. After years of planning and review, the proposed Buc-ee’s at Interstate 95 and Indrio Road has completed the county’s planning process, bringing the long-discussed project one step closer to reality. The proposed 76,000-square-foot travel center would feature approximately 120 fuel pumps and could become the largest Buc-ee’s location in Florida. Buc-ee’s Nearing Construction Phase According to St. Lucie County Planning and Development Services Director Benjamin Balcer, the project has cleared its local planning hurdles. "They are completely 100% finished with the planning process," Balcer said. "Our board will not see this again." Balcer said the company is now awaiting final approvals from the Florida Department of Transportation and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection before construction can begin. "As far as the county is concerned, their building permit and their site development permit is pretty much at the tail end and ready to go," Balcer said. "It's really just pulling the trigger on Buc-ee's end to start the process." Buc-ee's has previously targeted a 2028 opening date. Development Interest Growing Along Indrio Road While the travel center itself would bring jobs and tax revenue, county officials say its presence also shines a spotlight on a corridor already attracting significant development interest. For now, much of the area remains undeveloped, with cattle grazing across wide stretches of rural land. But Balcer said developers are increasingly looking at opportunities along Indrio Road. "It's kind of an untapped resource," he said. "At the moment, we're seeing a lot of development interest, whether that's pre-application meetings, developers coming in and talking about concept plans, or actual formal applications." Balcer stopped short of calling Buc-ee's the direct catalyst for that interest, but acknowledged that a major national company can influence future investment decisions. "I don't know if Buc-ee's is a catalyst that actually drives development," he said. "But whenever you have a large national commercial entity like Buc-ee's, it does move the needle whenever people see that type of investment." Why the Corridor Is Attracting Attention The area has benefited from recent road and utility improvements, making it increasingly attractive for future residential and commercial projects. County officials say they are already seeing proposals emerge throughout the area. "But all through that Indrio Road corridor, we do see more retail, mixed-use residential projects that are starting to come in and gain traction," Balcer said. Several large developments are either proposed or moving through the review process near the future Buc-ee's site. The proposed Club at Indrio Creek , located south of Indrio Road, could bring hundreds of new homes to the area. Another proposal, Indrio Town Center , would transform approximately 85 acres near Indrio Road and Emerson Avenue into a mixed-use development featuring retail, office space and residential uses. Perhaps the most controversial proposal was Indrio Groves , a development planned near Spanish Lakes Fairways that could add more than 3,000 homes to the area. The size of that proposal has raised concerns among nearby residents who worry about traffic and infrastructure demands. The discussion was tabled over the summer. Residents Voice Infrastructure Concerns But as development proposals continue to stack up, some residents worry infrastructure isn't keeping pace. "That's what people are concerned about," said Jeff Bourassa, president of the Spanish Lakes Fairways Homeowners Association. If they put another 3,000 homes, we're in trouble." Bourassa said residents are worried local roads are not equipped to handle the level of growth being proposed. They're cowpaths," Bourassa said. "There's nothing that was put in for infrastructure." County officials say they understand those concerns. "People are concerned," Balcer said. "Traffic impacts, changing their lifestyle. This is a historical agricultural kind of community." Looking Ahead Whether Buc-ee's ultimately becomes a transformational project remains to be seen. County leaders say the larger story is what comes next for the surrounding area. If Buc-ee's opens and several proposed developments move forward, the character of the Indrio Road corridor could change dramatically over the next decade. "If Buc-ee's does come online, and the projects that are in the pipeline do develop," Balcer said, "you'll see a big difference in the Indrio Road corridor."

entry.title: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge - cw34.com
entry.summary: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man whose TikTok and Twich bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sept. on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records. His bond was set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped. The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women’s electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile’s bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman’s password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking. The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts. See also: Florida Education Department eyes dress code to ban head coverings, Crocs, short skirts The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea’s booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

entry.title: King tides, full moon erode Fort Pierce road for second time in a week - WPEC
entry.summary: King tides, full moon erode Fort Pierce road for second time in a week    WPEC
entry.article_text: Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to repair a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and recent rain continue to affect parts of South Florida. Skid loaders were working along the narrow roadway beside the Indian River Lagoon, adding dirt and sand to reinforce an area where erosion has left the road’s edge vulnerable. Crews brought 32 loads of dirt to the site Sept. But only days later, the embankment again needed repairs. Resident Gene Barnes said the recurring work is not a long-term solution. We’re losing ground year by year, Barnes said. Until the Corps of Engineers or something like that comes and puts a headwall in to stabilize it, it’s not going to be an easy fix. The road has faced erosion problems before. Heavy rain damaged sections in 2014, and Hurricane Nicole caused additional washouts in 2022. Barnes said continued rain and tidal action could undermine the roadway itself. See also: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge If we keep getting rains like this, it’s going to undermine the road, and then the road is going to collapse and the school bus is going to fall in the hole, he said. The latest repairs follow an emergency sand operation at nearby Jetty Park that cost taxpayers nearly $500,000. While repairs on South Indian River Drive may be less costly, residents said the erosion is likely to remain a concern as more rain and tidal action are forecast.

Family members told investigators that Pablo had been out of sight for no more than 10 minutes. Martin County Sheriff’s Office criminal investigators interviewed everyone at the scene. The sheriff said it does not appear that anyone was being reckless. "Parents get distracted, I know that," Budensiek said. "So, no one is disparaging the parents. In this case, this was an accidental drowning. But we have to remember where we live and take the time and the effort or spend the money. Whatever you have to do to try to drown proof your child," Budensiek said. Charlene Lyons is the President and CEO for the YMCA Treasure Coast. She said she was devastated when she heard the news, "I started at the 'Y' as a lifeguard, so aquatic safety is paramount to me,' Lyons said She wants the public to know they can contact the YMCA for information about swim lessons. "Drowning is the great equalizer — it goes across every demographic, socioeconomic status — it doesn't matter, so it's important for everyone to learn to swim," Lyons. The family has set up a GoFundMe account to assist during this difficult time. For more information about swim lessons, log on to the YMCA Treasure Coast website posted here. It has been just under two months since Martin County deputies took 36 dogs out of O'Donnell's feces-filled home on Aug. The county condemned it days after the Border Collies were rescued. Ferraro said O'Donnell is staying elsewhere while the house is under repair. O'Donnell faces an animal cruelty and improper confinement charge for each dog and has pleaded not guilty. "Everybody's got a right to a fair trial and to due process," Ferraro said. The next hearing in O'Donnell's case is scheduled for Dec. While the outcome of the case remains uncertain, most of O'Donnell's former dogs have found loving homes. According to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, 30 of the dogs have been adopted, five have gone or are about to go to animal rescues, and one remains up for adoption. Lucie and Colleen Tilley near Deltona each adopted one of the rescued border collies. "She's just has an endless amount of energy and just wants to expend it at all times," Cale said. entry.summary: King tides, full moon erode Fort Pierce road for second time in a week    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Crews returned to South Indian River Drive in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to repair a washed-out embankment for the second time in a week, as king tides and recent rain continue to affect parts of South Florida. Skid loaders were working along the narrow roadway beside the Indian River Lagoon, adding dirt and sand to reinforce an area where erosion has left the road’s edge vulnerable. Crews brought 32 loads of dirt to the site Sept. But only days later, the embankment again needed repairs. Resident Gene Barnes said the recurring work is not a long-term solution. We’re losing ground year by year, Barnes said. Until the Corps of Engineers or something like that comes and puts a headwall in to stabilize it, it’s not going to be an easy fix. The road has faced erosion problems before. Heavy rain damaged sections in 2014, and Hurricane Nicole caused additional washouts in 2022. Barnes said continued rain and tidal action could undermine the roadway itself. See also: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge If we keep getting rains like this, it’s going to undermine the road, and then the road is going to collapse and the school bus is going to fall in the hole, he said. The latest repairs follow an emergency sand operation at nearby Jetty Park that cost taxpayers nearly $500,000. While repairs on South Indian River Drive may be less costly, residents said the erosion is likely to remain a concern as more rain and tidal action are forecast.

entry.title: FDLE testimony focuses on RFP process in ex-Fort Pierce manager Nick Mimms' trial - WPEC
entry.summary: FDLE testimony focuses on RFP process in ex-Fort Pierce manager Nick Mimms' trial    WPEC
entry.article_text: Former Fort Pierce City Manager Nick Mimms is on trial over allegations that he improperly influenced a city bidding process involving two vacant lots in Fort Pierce's Lincoln Park area. Mimms faces charges of bid tampering and official misconduct. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors allege he steered the process toward Lincoln Park Young Professionals, a nonprofit whose board included Mimms' niece and another city employee. On Thursday, much of the testimony focused on who controlled the RFP process and how closely Mimms remained involved after it was turned over to the city's purchasing department. FDLE Agent Derek Brisky testified about emails and other records collected during the investigation. One focus was the nearby Lincoln Theater and its need for parking. Brisky testified Mimms had told the Fort Pierce Redevelopment Agency that the RFP would include language addressing the theater's parking needs. But that language was not included in the request Mimms sent to the purchasing department. Brisky also testified investigators found no evidence Mimms filed a 2019 memorandum concerning the parking plans in the relevant city records. The defense questioned the significance of that omission and emphasized that the purchasing department was responsible for putting together and publishing the RFP after receiving the project's specifications. See also: NTSB report clarifies Amazon plane crash timeline that killed 5 on Sept. 6 Defense attorneys also challenged the state's characterization of the process as a sole-source arrangement. Brisky acknowledged the RFP was not technically a sole-source contract. The state, meanwhile, pointed to emails showing Mimms continued to communicate with city employees about the RFP, including its evaluation criteria and the evaluation committee. Other emails showed city employees knew there had been one submission after the RFP was posted. An LPYP email address was copied on one of those communications. The defense also questioned the investigation's treatment of other city employees involved in the process, including a purchasing official who was not charged. Later, former Fort Pierce employee Kalita Scott testified about LPYP and its efforts to develop the Lincoln Park properties. She described the organization as a group of young professionals focused on community development and said the need for parking near the Lincoln Theater was known in the community. Prosecutors allege Mimms manipulated the city's process to ensure LPYP received the lease. The defense has argued Mimms did not improperly favor the organization and that the evidence does not establish a criminal conspiracy. The trial is continuing in St.

entry.title: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge - cw34.com
entry.summary: Case reopened: Port St. Lucie TikTok creator jailed on computer-access charge    cw34.com
entry.article_text: Lucie man whose TikTok and Twich bios identify him as a cybersecurity engineer was jailed Wednesday after police reopened an investigation that had been closed in May. Mark Stephen Asea, 36, was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail on Sept. on one pending count of offense against computer users, according to jail records. His bond was set at $35,000. An earlier stalking charge appears to have been dropped. The charge stems from an earlier investigation in which detectives accused Asea of gaining access to women’s electronic devices and using TikTok posts to discuss information they said was private. In a warrant affidavit, a detective described reviewing videos from an account linked to Asea. The profile’s bio identifies its user as a narcissistic abuse survivor, former satanist, empath, cybersecurity engineer and woodsman. Police said one video included references to a woman’s password, device information, banking activity, license plate number and possible location tracking. The woman told investigators the password had been shared only in a closed TikTok group chat and that she had not given Asea permission to share it. Another woman told police Asea previously had remote access to her computer to help with an application. She became concerned, investigators said, after an image from a private Telegram message appeared in one of his TikTok posts. See also: Florida Education Department eyes dress code to ban head coverings, Crocs, short skirts The earlier affidavit alleged Asea posted more than 100 TikTok videos mentioning one of the women, including as many as six in a day. Detectives also cited videos that appeared to show computer equipment and coding as they investigated whether he had accessed devices without authorization. Asea’s booking photo shows him with long dark hair and prominent geometric tattoos across his face.

entry.summary: Floridians who want to cast a ballot in the 2026 General Election have until Monday, Oct. 5, to register to vote or update their voter registration information. Voters are encouraged to verify that their registration details, including their name, address and party affiliation, are accurate before the deadline. Voters are also urged to confirm their Election Day polling location. Election Day is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Residents can register to vote or update their registration online through Florida's voter registration website , by mail or in person using a Florida Voter Registration Application. Applications are also available at Supervisor of Elections Offices and other designated voter registration agencies. St. Lucie County: Oct. 1931 from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily, including Sunday, Oct. 25. The county will have eight early-voting locations across the county. Indian River County: Oct. 19-31 from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. with extended hours on Thursdays from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. Four early-voting locations will be available throughout the county. Vote-by-mail ballots must be received by the Supervisor of Elections office by 7 p.m. Election Day to be counted and may be returned to a secure ballot intake station located at each early voting location during early voting hours, or in person to the Supervisor of Elections office. Okeechobee County: Oct. 24-31 from 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. at one location: 307 NW 5th Avenue in Okeechobee Election Day: Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Voters must cast their ballot at their assigned precinct.

entry.title: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight - WPEC
entry.summary: St. Lucie County Fire District attorney gives 90-day notice amid firefighter hazing fight    WPEC
entry.article_text: Lucie County Fire District Attorney Kim Sabol is leaving the department, submitting her 90-day notice Wednesday as the agency faces an ongoing fight with its firefighters' union over the termination of three employees accused of hazing rookies. Sabol confirmed she submitted her notice Wednesday. It was not immediately clear whether her departure is connected to the ongoing dispute. My employment agreement requires 90 days' notice because it's a 3-year contract," Sabol told CBS12. "My last work day will be 12/31/2026." Sabol has served as the district's attorney since 2017, advising the Fire Board, fire chief and administration on legal matters including labor and employment issues and collective bargaining. Her departure comes as Professional Firefighters and Paramedics of St. Lucie County Local 1377 fights the discipline of five firefighters. The union has formally demanded arbitration for three terminated firefighters and two suspended personnel, arguing there was no just cause for the discipline. See also: Beyond the dashcam: FHP begins equipping troopers with body cameras The firefighters were disciplined after an outside investigation into videos showing senior personnel using a modified bug zapper to administer electric shocks to newer firefighters in incidents in March and September 2024. Fire District officials called the conduct hazing and said it violated department policies and created a culture of intimidation between senior and junior employees. According to previous reports , Local 1377 President Ryan Sapp said the incidents amounted to consensual station horseplay, pointing to an earlier Fort Pierce Police Department investigation that found no criminal wrongdoing. There was no kind of hazing whatsoever, and I could not believe that that's what was found," Sapp told CBS12. The union has also challenged the fairness of the Fire District's investigation, which was conducted by outside attorney John "J.K." Keller IV. Sapp said union attorneys believe the investigation was not impartial and that some questions appeared to be designed to reach a predetermined conclusion. The union also raised concerns that the law firm involved in the investigation has since been retained by the district for the upcoming arbitration. Two terminated firefighters, Jordon Hutchinson and Christopher Baldwin, have separately alleged whistleblower retaliation. Lucie County Fire District received a 90-day notice of a resignation from its legal counsel today. The District Attorney is eligible for retirement, and the notice provides for continued service during the 90-day period," St. Lucie County Fire Rescue said in a statement. "The District will not speculate regarding the circumstances surrounding the resignation or any connection to other matters. Sapp said the union remains willing to negotiate a resolution that could avoid arbitration, but any compromise would need to include reinstatement of the terminated firefighters. Sabol's 90-day notice means she is expected to remain with the district during that period unless the terms of her departure change.
